Short Answer (i) Define class limits

The minimum and maximum values defined for a class or group are called its class limits; the minimum value is the lower class limit and the maximum value is the upper class limit.

Short Answer (ii) Define class mark

The class mark (midpoint) of a class is the average of its class limits: class mark = (lower limit + upper limit)/2. It represents the whole class in computations.

Short Answer (iii) What is cumulative frequency?

The cumulative frequency of a class is the total of the frequencies of that class and all the classes before it, i.e. the total frequency up to the upper class limit or boundary.

Short Answer (iv) Define a frequency distribution

A frequency distribution is a tabular arrangement that classifies data into different groups (classes) and shows the number of observations (frequency) falling in each group.

Short Answer (v) What is a Histogram?

A histogram is a graph of adjacent rectangles constructed on the XY-plane: rectangles are erected on the class intervals (boundaries) with heights proportional to the class frequencies. It is a graph of a frequency distribution.

Short Answer (vi) Name two measures of central tendency

Any two of: Arithmetic mean, Median (also: Mode, Geometric mean, Harmonic mean, Quartiles).

Short Answer (vii) Define Arithmetic mean

Arithmetic mean is a measure that determines a value of the variable under study by dividing the sum of all values (observations) of the variable by their number: X-bar = (sum of X)/n.

Short Answer (viii) Write three properties of Arithmetic mean

(1) The mean of a variable whose observations are all the same constant k is k itself. (2) The mean is affected by change in origin (adding a constant to every observation adds it to the mean). (3) The mean is affected by change in scale (multiplying every observation by a constant multiplies the mean by it). (Also: the sum of the deviations of X from its mean is always zero.)

Short Answer (ix) Define Median

Median is the middlemost observation in an arranged data set; it divides the data set into two equal parts.

Short Answer (x) Define Mode

Mode is defined as the most frequent occurring observation of the variable or data.

Short Answer (xi) What do you mean by Harmonic mean?

Harmonic mean refers to the value obtained by reciprocating the mean of the reciprocals of the observations: H.M. = n/(sum of 1/X).

Short Answer (xii) Define Geometric mean

Geometric mean of a variable X is the n-th positive root of the product of the n observations: G.M. = (x1.x2...xn)^(1/n).

Short Answer (xiii) What is Range?

Range is the difference between the maximum and minimum observations of a data set; it measures the extent of variation between the two extreme observations.

Short Answer (xiv) Define Standard deviation

Standard deviation is defined as the positive square root of the mean of the squared deviations of the observations from their arithmetic mean: S = sqrt{[sum of (X - X-bar)^2]/n}.

mcqs.q: A grouped frequency table is also called a:
mcqs.why: A tabular arrangement that classifies data into groups (classes) and shows the number of observations in each group is called a frequency distribution. A grouped frequency table is exactly such an arrangement.

mcqs.q: A histogram is a set of adjacent:
mcqs.why: A histogram is a graph of a frequency distribution made of adjacent rectangles erected on the class intervals (boundaries), with heights proportional to the class frequencies.

mcqs.q: A frequency polygon is a many-sided:
mcqs.why: A frequency polygon is drawn by plotting points at the class midpoints with the class frequencies and joining them by straight line segments, then closing it to the x-axis — so it is a many-sided closed figure.

mcqs.q: In a cumulative frequency polygon (ogive), frequencies are plotted against:
mcqs.why: In a 'less than' cumulative frequency polygon, the cumulative frequencies are plotted against the upper class boundaries, starting from the lower boundary of the first class with cumulative frequency 0.

mcqs.q: Data in the form of a frequency distribution is called:
mcqs.why: When data is presented in the form of a frequency distribution (classes with their frequencies), it is called grouped data. Data in its original, unarranged form is ungrouped or raw data.

mcqs.q: The mean of a variable whose observations are all the same constant k is:
mcqs.why: If every observation equals k, then sum of X = nk and X-bar = nk / n = k. So the mean of constant observations is the constant k itself — one of the basic properties of the arithmetic mean.

mcqs.q: The sum of the deviations of the variable X from its arithmetic mean is always:
mcqs.why: Sum of (X − X-bar) = sum of X − n·X-bar = sum of X − sum of X = 0. So the sum of the deviations of the observations from their mean is always zero — a standard property of the arithmetic mean.

mcqs.q: The n-th positive root of the product of the observations x1, x2, ..., xn is called the:
mcqs.why: By definition, the geometric mean is G.M. = (x1 · x2 · ... · xn)^(1/n), the n-th positive root of the product of the n observations.

mcqs.q: The value obtained by reciprocating the mean of the reciprocals of the observations is called the:
mcqs.why: By definition, the harmonic mean is H.M. = n / (sum of 1/X): first take the reciprocals of the observations, find their mean, and then reciprocate that mean.

mcqs.q: The most frequently occurring observation in a data set is called the:
mcqs.why: The mode is defined as the most frequent occurring observation of the variable or data set — the value that appears the maximum number of times.

mcqs.q: The measure which determines the middlemost observation in a data set is called the:
mcqs.why: The median is the middlemost observation in an arranged (ordered) data set; it divides the data into two equal parts, with half the observations below it and half above it.

mcqs.q: The observations that divide a data set into four equal parts are called:
mcqs.why: Quartiles are the three values Q1, Q2 and Q3 that divide an arranged data set into four equal parts. (Deciles divide it into ten equal parts and percentiles into a hundred.)

mcqs.q: The spread or scatter of observations in a data set is called:
mcqs.why: The spread or scatter of observations in a data set is called dispersion. Measures of dispersion (range, variance, standard deviation) tell us the degree or extent of this variation.

mcqs.q: The extent of variation between the two extreme observations of a data set is measured by the:
mcqs.why: The range is the difference between the maximum and minimum observations of a data set, so it measures the extent of variation between the two extreme observations.

mcqs.q: The positive square root of the mean of the squared deviations of the observations from their arithmetic mean is called:
mcqs.why: By definition, the standard deviation is S = sqrt{ [sum of (X − X-bar)^2] / n } — the positive square root of the variance, which is itself the mean of the squared deviations from the arithmetic mean.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Locate the following angles (state the quadrant and direction of rotation): (i) 30 deg (ii) 22.5 deg (iii) 135 deg (iv) 225 deg (v) -60 deg (vi) -120 deg (vii) -150 deg (viii) -225 deg

In standard position the initial side is the positive x-axis; positive angles rotate anticlockwise, negative angles clockwise.

(i) 30 deg: first quadrant, 30 deg anticlockwise from the x-axis.

(ii) 22.5 deg: first quadrant, 22.5 deg anticlockwise.

(iii) 135 deg: second quadrant (between 90 and 180 deg).

(iv) 225 deg: third quadrant (between 180 and 270 deg).

(v) -60 deg: fourth quadrant, 60 deg clockwise.

(vi) -120 deg: third quadrant, 120 deg clockwise (terminal side at 240 deg position).

(vii) -150 deg: third quadrant, 150 deg clockwise (terminal side at 210 deg position).

(viii) -225 deg: second quadrant, 225 deg clockwise (terminal side at 135 deg position).

Q2 Express the following sexagesimal measures of angles in decimal form: (i) 45 deg 30 min (ii) 60 deg 30 min 30 sec (iii) 125 deg 22 min 50 sec

Rules: 1 deg = 60 min, 1 min = 60 sec, so decimal degrees = deg + min/60 + sec/3600.

(i) 45 + 30/60 = 45.5 deg.

(ii) 60 + 30/60 + 30/3600 = 60 + 0.5 + 0.0083 = 60.5083 deg.

(iii) 125 + 22/60 + 50/3600 = 125 + 0.3667 + 0.0139 = 125.3806 deg.

Q3 Express the following into D M S (degrees-minutes-seconds) form: (i) 47.36 deg (ii) 125.45 deg (iii) 225.75 deg (iv) -22.5 deg (v) -67.58 deg (vi) 315.18 deg

Method: multiply the decimal part by 60 to get minutes; multiply the remaining decimal by 60 to get seconds.

(i) 0.36 x 60 = 21.6 min; 0.6 x 60 = 36 sec: 47 deg 21 min 36 sec.

(ii) 0.45 x 60 = 27 min exactly: 125 deg 27 min 0 sec.

(iii) 0.75 x 60 = 45 min: 225 deg 45 min 0 sec.

(iv) -22 deg 30 min 0 sec.

(v) 0.58 x 60 = 34.8 min; 0.8 x 60 = 48 sec: -67 deg 34 min 48 sec.

(vi) 0.18 x 60 = 10.8 min; 0.8 x 60 = 48 sec: 315 deg 10 min 48 sec.

Q4 Express the following angles into radians: (i) 30 deg (ii) 60 deg (iii) 135 deg (iv) 225 deg (v) -150 deg (vi) -225 deg (vii) 300 deg (viii) 315 deg

Formula: radians = degrees x (pi/180).

(i) 30 x pi/180 = pi/6.

(ii) 60 x pi/180 = pi/3.

(iii) 135 x pi/180 = 3pi/4.

(iv) 225 x pi/180 = 5pi/4.

(v) -150 x pi/180 = -5pi/6.

(vi) -225 x pi/180 = -5pi/4.

(vii) 300 x pi/180 = 5pi/3.

(viii) 315 x pi/180 = 7pi/4.

Q5 Convert each of the following to degrees: (i) 3pi/4 (ii) 5pi/6 (iii) 7pi/8 (iv) 13pi/16 (v) 3 (vi) 4.5 (vii) -7pi/8 (viii) -13pi/16

Formula: degrees = radians x (180/pi).

(i) (3pi/4)(180/pi) = 135 deg.

(ii) (5pi/6)(180/pi) = 150 deg.

(iii) (7pi/8)(180/pi) = 157.5 deg.

(iv) (13pi/16)(180/pi) = 146.25 deg.

(v) 3 x (180/pi) = 540/pi = 171.89 deg (approx).

(vi) 4.5 x (180/pi) = 810/pi = 257.83 deg (approx).

(vii) -157.5 deg.

(viii) -146.25 deg.

mcqs.q: In standard position, in which quadrant does an angle of 135 degrees lie?
mcqs.why: Quadrants are counted from the positive x-axis anticlockwise. Formula for range: Quadrant II is 90 degrees < angle < 180 degrees. Since 90 < 135 < 180, the terminal side of 135 degrees lies in the second quadrant.

mcqs.q: In standard position, an angle of -60 degrees lies in which quadrant and is measured in which direction?
mcqs.why: Positive angles rotate anticlockwise and negative angles rotate clockwise from the positive x-axis. Step 1: -60 degrees means 60 degrees clockwise. Step 2: A clockwise rotation of 60 degrees puts the terminal side between 270 degrees and 360 degrees in position, which is the fourth quadrant.

mcqs.q: Express 45 degrees 30 minutes in decimal form.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: decimal degrees = degrees + minutes/60 + seconds/3600, with 1 degree = 60 minutes. Step 1: 30 minutes = 30/60 = 0.5 degree. Step 2: 45 + 0.5 = 45.5 degrees.

mcqs.q: Express 60 degrees 30 minutes 30 seconds in decimal form (approx.).
mcqs.why: Use the formula: decimal degrees = degrees + minutes/60 + seconds/3600. Step 1: 30/60 = 0.5. Step 2: 30/3600 = 0.0083 approx. Step 3: 60 + 0.5 + 0.0083 = 60.5083 degrees.

mcqs.q: Express 47.36 degrees in degrees-minutes-seconds (DMS) form.
mcqs.why: Method: multiply the decimal part by 60 to get minutes, then multiply the remaining decimal by 60 to get seconds. Step 1: 0.36 x 60 = 21.6 minutes. Step 2: 0.6 x 60 = 36 seconds. So 47.36 degrees = 47 degrees 21 minutes 36 seconds.

mcqs.q: Express -67.58 degrees in degrees-minutes-seconds form.
mcqs.why: Method: multiply the decimal part by 60 for minutes and the remaining decimal by 60 for seconds, keeping the negative sign. Step 1: 0.58 x 60 = 34.8 minutes. Step 2: 0.8 x 60 = 48 seconds. So -67.58 degrees = -67 degrees 34 minutes 48 seconds.

mcqs.q: Express 30 degrees in radians.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: radians = degrees x (pi/180). Step 1: 30 x pi/180. Step 2: Simplify 30/180 = 1/6. So the result is pi/6 radians.

mcqs.q: Express 225 degrees in radians.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: radians = degrees x (pi/180). Step 1: 225 x pi/180. Step 2: Simplify 225/180 = 5/4. So the result is 5pi/4 radians, which lies in the third quadrant.

mcqs.q: Convert 3pi/4 radians to degrees.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: degrees = radians x (180/pi). Step 1: (3pi/4) x (180/pi). Step 2: pi cancels, 3 x 180 / 4 = 540/4 = 135 degrees.

mcqs.q: Convert 3 radians to degrees (approx.).
mcqs.why: Use the formula: degrees = radians x (180/pi). Step 1: 3 x 180/pi = 540/pi. Step 2: 540 / 3.1416 = 171.89 degrees approx. Note 3 is in radians here, not 3 degrees.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Find theta when: (i) l = 2 cm, r = 3.5 cm (ii) l = 4.5 m, r = 2.5 m

Formula: l = r x theta, where theta is in radians; also 1 deg = pi/180 radian.

(i) theta = l/r = 2/3.5 = 4/7 = 0.571 radian (approx).

(ii) theta = l/r = 4.5/2.5 = 1.8 radians.

Q2 Find l when: (i) theta = 180 deg, r = 4.9 cm (ii) theta = 60 deg 30 min, r = 15 mm

Formula: l = r x theta, where theta is in radians; also 1 deg = pi/180 radian.

(i) theta = 180 deg = pi radian. l = r.theta = 4.9 x pi = 15.4 cm (approx).

(ii) theta = 60.5 deg = 60.5 x pi/180 = 1.056 radian. l = 15 x 1.056 = 15.83 mm (approx).

Q3 Find r when: (i) l = 4 cm, theta = 1/4 radian (ii) l = 52 cm, theta = 45 deg

Formula: l = r x theta, where theta is in radians; also 1 deg = pi/180 radian.

(i) r = l/theta = 4/(1/4) = 16 cm.

(ii) theta = 45 deg = pi/4 radian. r = 52/(pi/4) = 208/pi = 66.2 cm (approx).

Q4 In a circle of radius 12 m, find the length of an arc which subtends a central angle theta = 1.5 radian

Formula: l = r x theta, where theta is in radians; also 1 deg = pi/180 radian.

l = r.theta = 12 x 1.5 = 18 m.

Q5 In a circle of radius 10 m, find the distance travelled by a point moving on this circle if the point makes 3.5 revolutions (3.5 revolutions = 7pi)

Step 1: One revolution = 2pi radians, so 3.5 revolutions = 7pi radians.

Step 2: Distance = l = r.theta = 10 x 7pi = 70pi = 219.9 m (approx).

Q6 What is the circular measure of the angle between the hands of a watch at 3 o'clock?

Step 1: At 3 o'clock the minute hand points at 12 and the hour hand at 3, a quarter of the full circle apart.

Step 2: Angle = (1/4) x 360 deg = 90 deg = 90 x pi/180 = pi/2 radian.

Answer: pi/2 radian.

Q7 What is the length of the arc APB? (From the figure: circle of radius 8 cm, centre angle AOB = 90 deg, P on the minor arc AB)

Formula: l = r x theta, where theta is in radians; also 1 deg = pi/180 radian.

Step 1: theta = 90 deg = pi/2 radian, r = 8 cm.

Step 2: Arc APB is the minor arc AB, so l = r.theta = 8 x pi/2 = 4pi = 12.57 cm (approx).

Q8 In a circle of radius 12 cm, how long an arc subtends a central angle of 84 deg?

Formula: l = r x theta, where theta is in radians; also 1 deg = pi/180 radian.

Step 1: theta = 84 deg = 84pi/180 = 1.466 radian.

Step 2: l = r.theta = 12 x 1.466 = 17.59 cm (exactly 5.6pi cm).

Q9 Find the area of the sectors OPR: (a) radius 6 cm, angle at O = 60 deg (b) radius OP = 20 cm, angle at O = 45 deg

Formula: Area of a sector = (1/2) r^2 theta, theta in radians.

(a) theta = 60 deg = pi/3. Area = (1/2)(6^2)(pi/3) = 6pi = 18.85 cm^2 (approx).

(b) theta = 45 deg = pi/4. Area = (1/2)(20^2)(pi/4) = 50pi = 157.08 cm^2 (approx).

mcqs.q: Find theta (in radians) when arc length l = 2 cm and radius r = 3.5 cm.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: l = r x theta, so theta = l/r, where theta is in radians. Step 1: theta = 2 / 3.5. Step 2: 2/3.5 = 4/7 = 0.571 radian approx.

mcqs.q: Find theta (in radians) when l = 4.5 m and r = 2.5 m.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: l = r x theta, so theta = l/r. Step 1: theta = 4.5 / 2.5. Step 2: 4.5/2.5 = 1.8. So theta = 1.8 radians.

mcqs.q: Find arc length l when theta = 180 degrees and r = 4.9 cm.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: l = r x theta, theta in radians. Step 1: Convert 180 degrees = 180 x pi/180 = pi radian. Step 2: l = 4.9 x pi = 15.4 cm approx.

mcqs.q: Find radius r when l = 4 cm and theta = 1/4 radian.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: l = r x theta, so r = l/theta. Step 1: r = 4 / (1/4). Step 2: Dividing by 1/4 means multiplying by 4, so r = 16 cm.

mcqs.q: Find radius r when l = 52 cm and theta = 45 degrees.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: l = r x theta, so r = l/theta, theta in radians. Step 1: 45 degrees = pi/4 radian. Step 2: r = 52 / (pi/4) = 208/pi. Step 3: 208/3.1416 = 66.2 cm approx.

mcqs.q: In a circle of radius 12 m, find the length of an arc which subtends a central angle theta = 1.5 radian.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: l = r x theta, theta in radians. Step 1: l = 12 x 1.5. Step 2: 12 x 1.5 = 18. So the arc length is 18 m.

mcqs.q: A point moves on a circle of radius 10 m and makes 3.5 revolutions. Find the distance travelled.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: l = r x theta. Step 1: One revolution = 2pi radians, so 3.5 revolutions = 3.5 x 2pi = 7pi radians. Step 2: Distance = 10 x 7pi = 70pi. Step 3: 70 x 3.1416 = 219.9 m approx.

mcqs.q: What is the circular measure of the angle between the hands of a watch at 3 o'clock?
mcqs.why: Step 1: At 3 o'clock the hands are a quarter of the full circle apart. Step 2: Angle = (1/4) x 360 degrees = 90 degrees. Step 3: Use radians = degrees x pi/180, so 90 x pi/180 = pi/2 radian.

mcqs.q: In a circle of radius 8 cm with centre angle AOB = 90 degrees, find the length of the minor arc APB.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: l = r x theta, theta in radians. Step 1: 90 degrees = pi/2 radian, r = 8 cm. Step 2: l = 8 x pi/2 = 4pi. Step 3: 4 x 3.1416 = 12.57 cm approx. This is the minor arc AB.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a sector with radius 6 cm and angle at the centre = 60 degrees.
mcqs.why: Use the formula: Area of a sector = (1/2) r^2 theta, theta in radians. Step 1: 60 degrees = pi/3 radian. Step 2: Area = (1/2)(6^2)(pi/3) = (1/2)(36)(pi/3) = 6pi. Step 3: 6 x 3.1416 = 18.85 cm^2 approx.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.3
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Locate each angle in standard position and find a positive and a negative angle coterminal with it: (i) 170 deg (ii) 780 deg (iii) -100 deg (iv) -500 deg

Coterminal angles differ by whole multiples of 360 deg: theta + 360k.

(i) 170 deg lies in quadrant II. Positive coterminal: 170 + 360 = 530 deg. Negative coterminal: 170 - 360 = -190 deg.

(ii) 780 deg = 720 + 60, so its terminal side is that of 60 deg (quadrant I). Positive coterminal: 780 - 360 = 420 deg. Negative coterminal: 60 - 360 = -300 deg.

(iii) -100 deg: terminal side at 260 deg position (quadrant III). Positive coterminal: -100 + 360 = 260 deg. Negative coterminal: -100 - 360 = -460 deg.

(iv) -500 deg = -720 + 220, terminal side that of 220 deg (quadrant III). Positive coterminal: -500 + 720 = 220 deg. Negative coterminal: -500 - 360 = -860 deg.

Q2 Identify the closest quadrantal angles between which the following angles lie: (i) 156 deg (ii) 318 deg (iii) 572 deg (iv) -330 deg

(i) 156 deg lies between 90 deg and 180 deg.

(ii) 318 deg lies between 270 deg and 360 deg.

(iii) 572 deg = 360 + 212, so it lies between 180 deg and 270 deg.

(iv) -330 deg has the terminal side of 30 deg, so it lies between 0 deg and 90 deg.

Q3 Write the closest quadrantal angles between which the angle lies (answer in radian measure): (i) pi/3 (ii) 3pi/4 (iii) -pi/4 (iv) -3pi/4

(i) pi/3 lies between 0 and pi/2.

(ii) 3pi/4 lies between pi/2 and pi.

(iii) -pi/4 lies between -pi/2 and 0 (quadrant IV).

(iv) -3pi/4 lies between -pi and -pi/2 (quadrant III).

Q4 In which quadrant does theta lie when: (i) sin theta > 0, tan theta < 0 (ii) cos theta < 0, sin theta < 0 (iii) sec theta > 0, sin theta < 0 (iv) cos theta < 0, tan theta < 0 (v) cosec theta > 0, cos theta > 0 (vi) sin theta < 0, sec theta < 0

Sign chart: QI all positive; QII sin, cosec positive; QIII tan, cot positive; QIV cos, sec positive.

(i) sin positive and tan negative: Quadrant II.

(ii) Both sin and cos negative: Quadrant III.

(iii) cos positive (sec > 0) and sin negative: Quadrant IV.

(iv) cos negative and tan negative: Quadrant II.

(v) sin positive and cos positive: Quadrant I.

(vi) sin negative and cos negative (sec < 0): Quadrant III.

Q5 Fill in the blank: cos(-150 deg) = _______ cos 150 deg

Answer: +

Q5 Fill in the blank: sin(-310 deg) = _______ sin 310 deg

Answer: -

Q5 Fill in the blank: tan(-210 deg) = _______ tan 210 deg

Answer: -

Q5 Fill in the blank: cot(-45 deg) = _______ cot 45 deg

Answer: -

Q5 Fill in the blank: sec(-60 deg) = _______ sec 60 deg

Answer: +

Q5 Fill in the blank: cosec(-137 deg) = _______ cosec 137 deg

Answer: -

Q6 The given point P lies on the terminal side of theta. Find the quadrant of theta and all six trigonometric ratios: (i) P(-2, 3) (ii) P(-3, -4) (iii) P(sqrt(2), 1)

Method: r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2); sin theta = y/r, cos theta = x/r, tan theta = y/x, cot theta = x/y, sec theta = r/x, cosec theta = r/y.

(i) P(-2, 3): quadrant II. r = sqrt(4 + 9) = sqrt(13). sin theta = 3/sqrt(13); cos theta = -2/sqrt(13); tan theta = -3/2; cot theta = -2/3; sec theta = -sqrt(13)/2; cosec theta = sqrt(13)/3.

(ii) P(-3, -4): quadrant III. r = 5. sin theta = -4/5; cos theta = -3/5; tan theta = 4/3; cot theta = 3/4; sec theta = -5/3; cosec theta = -5/4.

(iii) P(sqrt(2), 1): quadrant I. r = sqrt(2 + 1) = sqrt(3). sin theta = 1/sqrt(3); cos theta = sqrt(2)/sqrt(3); tan theta = 1/sqrt(2); cot theta = sqrt(2); sec theta = sqrt(3)/sqrt(2); cosec theta = sqrt(3).

Q7 If cos theta = -2/3 and the terminal arm of theta is in quadrant II, find the values of the remaining trigonometric functions

Step 1: Use sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1: sin^2 theta = 1 - 4/9 = 5/9. In quadrant II sin theta is positive: sin theta = sqrt(5)/3.

Step 2: tan theta = sin/cos = (sqrt(5)/3)/(-2/3) = -sqrt(5)/2.

Step 3: cot theta = -2/sqrt(5); sec theta = -3/2; cosec theta = 3/sqrt(5).

Q8 If tan theta = 4/3 and sin theta < 0, find the values of the other trigonometric functions at theta

Step 1: tan theta positive with sin theta negative places theta in quadrant III (sin and cos both negative).

Step 2: sec^2 theta = 1 + tan^2 theta = 1 + 16/9 = 25/9, so cos theta = -3/5 (negative in QIII) and sec theta = -5/3.

Step 3: sin theta = tan theta x cos theta = (4/3)(-3/5) = -4/5. cot theta = 3/4; cosec theta = -5/4.

Q9 If sin theta = -1/sqrt(2) and the terminal side of the angle is not in quadrant III, find the values of tan theta, sec theta and cosec theta

Step 1: sin theta negative and not in QIII means theta is in quadrant IV, where cos theta is positive.

Step 2: cos^2 theta = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2, so cos theta = 1/sqrt(2).

Step 3: tan theta = sin/cos = -1. sec theta = sqrt(2). cosec theta = -sqrt(2).

Q10 If cosec theta = 13/12 and sec theta > 0, find the remaining trigonometric functions

Step 1: sin theta = 12/13 (positive). sec theta > 0 means cos theta > 0, so theta is in quadrant I.

Step 2: cos^2 theta = 1 - 144/169 = 25/169, so cos theta = 5/13 and sec theta = 13/5.

Step 3: tan theta = sin/cos = 12/5; cot theta = 5/12.

Q11 Find the values of the trigonometric functions at the indicated angle theta in the right triangle: (i) hypotenuse 4, side adjacent to theta = 3 (ii) hypotenuse 17, side opposite theta = 8, side adjacent = 15 (iii) hypotenuse 7, side adjacent to theta = 3

Definitions: sin theta = opposite/hypotenuse, cos theta = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan theta = opposite/adjacent; the third side comes from Pythagoras.

(i) Opposite side = sqrt(16 - 9) = sqrt(7). sin theta = sqrt(7)/4; cos theta = 3/4; tan theta = sqrt(7)/3; cot theta = 3/sqrt(7); sec theta = 4/3; cosec theta = 4/sqrt(7).

(ii) sin theta = 8/17; cos theta = 15/17; tan theta = 8/15; cot theta = 15/8; sec theta = 17/15; cosec theta = 17/8. (Check: 8^2 + 15^2 = 289 = 17^2.)

(iii) Opposite side = sqrt(49 - 9) = sqrt(40) = 2sqrt(10). sin theta = 2sqrt(10)/7; cos theta = 3/7; tan theta = 2sqrt(10)/3; cot theta = 3/(2sqrt(10)); sec theta = 7/3; cosec theta = 7/(2sqrt(10)).

Q12 Find the values of the trigonometric functions (do not use tables or calculator): (i) tan 30 deg (ii) tan 330 deg (iii) sec 330 deg (iv) cot(pi/4) (v) cos(2pi/3) (vi) cosec(2pi/3) (vii) cos(-450 deg) (viii) tan(-9pi) (ix) cos(-5pi/6) (x) sin(7pi/6) (xi) cot(7pi/6) (xii) cos 225 deg

Use the standard values at 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 deg with quadrant signs.

(i) tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3).

(ii) 330 deg is in QIV: tan 330 = -tan 30 = -1/sqrt(3).

(iii) sec 330 = sec 30 = 2/sqrt(3) (cos positive in QIV).

(iv) cot(pi/4) = cot 45 = 1.

(v) 2pi/3 = 120 deg, QII: cos = -cos 60 = -1/2.

(vi) cosec(2pi/3) = cosec 60 = 2/sqrt(3) (sin positive in QII).

(vii) cos(-450) = cos 450 = cos(360 + 90) = cos 90 = 0.

(viii) tan(-9pi) = -tan(9pi) = 0 (tan(n.pi) = 0).

(ix) cos(-5pi/6) = cos(5pi/6) = -cos(pi/6) = -sqrt(3)/2.

(x) 7pi/6 = 210 deg, QIII: sin = -sin 30 = -1/2.

(xi) cot(7pi/6) = cot 30 = sqrt(3) (tan, cot positive in QIII).

(xii) 225 deg, QIII: cos 225 = -cos 45 = -1/sqrt(2).

mcqs.q: Which angle is a positive coterminal angle with 170 degrees?
mcqs.why: Coterminal angles differ by whole multiples of 360 degrees: formula theta + 360k. Step 1: For a positive coterminal angle take k = 1. Step 2: 170 + 360 = 530 degrees. The angle -190 degrees is the negative coterminal angle.

mcqs.q: If sin theta > 0 and tan theta < 0, in which quadrant does theta lie?
mcqs.why: Sign chart: Quadrant I all positive; Quadrant II sin and cosec positive only; Quadrant III tan and cot positive only; Quadrant IV cos and sec positive only. Sin positive restricts theta to I or II, and tan negative excludes I, so theta is in Quadrant II.

mcqs.q: cos(-150 degrees) is equal to which expression?
mcqs.why: Cosine is an even function, so the formula is cos(-theta) = +cos theta for every theta. Therefore cos(-150 degrees) = +cos 150 degrees, with no change of sign.

mcqs.q: sin(-310 degrees) is equal to which expression?
mcqs.why: Sine is an odd function, so the formula is sin(-theta) = -sin theta. Therefore sin(-310 degrees) = -sin 310 degrees. The same odd rule applies to tan, cot and cosec, while cos and sec are even.

mcqs.q: Point P(-3, -4) lies on the terminal side of theta. What is sin theta?
mcqs.why: Use the formulas: r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) and sin theta = y/r. Step 1: r = sqrt((-3)^2 + (-4)^2) = sqrt(9+16) = 5. Step 2: P is in Quadrant III, x = -3, y = -4. Step 3: sin theta = -4/5.

mcqs.q: If cos theta = -2/3 and theta is in Quadrant II, what is sin theta?
mcqs.why: Use the identity sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1. Step 1: sin^2 theta = 1 - (-2/3)^2 = 1 - 4/9 = 5/9. Step 2: In Quadrant II sin theta is positive, so take the positive root. Step 3: sin theta = sqrt(5)/3.

mcqs.q: If tan theta = 4/3 and sin theta < 0, what is cos theta?
mcqs.why: Step 1: Tan positive with sin negative places theta in Quadrant III, where cos is also negative. Step 2: Use sec^2 theta = 1 + tan^2 theta = 1 + 16/9 = 25/9, so |cos theta| = 3/5. Step 3: With the Quadrant III sign, cos theta = -3/5.

mcqs.q: If sin theta = -1/sqrt(2) and the terminal side is NOT in Quadrant III, what is tan theta?
mcqs.why: Step 1: Sin negative and not in Quadrant III means theta is in Quadrant IV, where cos is positive. Step 2: Use cos^2 theta = 1 - sin^2 theta = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2, so cos theta = 1/sqrt(2). Step 3: Formula tan theta = sin theta / cos theta = (-1/sqrt(2))/(1/sqrt(2)) = -1.

mcqs.q: What is the value of tan 330 degrees?
mcqs.why: Step 1: 330 degrees lies in Quadrant IV, where tan is negative. Step 2: Its reference angle is 360 - 330 = 30 degrees. Step 3: tan 330 degrees = -tan 30 degrees = -1/sqrt(3).

mcqs.q: If cosec theta = 13/12 and sec theta > 0, what is tan theta?
mcqs.why: Step 1: Formula sin theta = 1/cosec theta = 12/13, positive. Sec > 0 means cos > 0, so theta is in Quadrant I. Step 2: Use cos^2 theta = 1 - 144/169 = 25/169, so cos theta = 5/13. Step 3: Formula tan theta = sin theta / cos theta = (12/13)/(5/13) = 12/5.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.4
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Simplify to a single trigonometric function: sin^2 x / cos^2 x

sin^2 x / cos^2 x = (sin x/cos x)^2 = tan^2 x.

Answer: tan^2 x.

Q2 Simplify to a single trigonometric function: tan x . sin x . sec x

Step 1: Write in sine and cosine: tan x = sin x/cos x and sec x = 1/cos x.

Step 2: tan x . sin x . sec x = (sin x/cos x)(sin x)(1/cos x) = sin^2 x/cos^2 x = tan^2 x.

Answer: tan^2 x.

Q3 Simplify to a single trigonometric function: tan x / sec x

tan x/sec x = (sin x/cos x)/(1/cos x) = sin x.

Answer: sin x.

Q4 Simplify to a single trigonometric function: 1 - cos^2 x

By the identity sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1: 1 - cos^2 x = sin^2 x.

Answer: sin^2 x.

Q5 Simplify to a single trigonometric function: sec^2 x - 1

By the identity 1 + tan^2 x = sec^2 x: sec^2 x - 1 = tan^2 x.

Answer: tan^2 x.

Q6 Simplify to a single trigonometric function: sin^2 x . cot^2 x

Step 1: cot^2 x = cos^2 x/sin^2 x.

Step 2: sin^2 x . (cos^2 x/sin^2 x) = cos^2 x.

Answer: cos^2 x.

Q7 Verify the identity: (1 - sin theta)(1 + sin theta) = cos^2 theta

L.H.S = 1 - sin^2 theta (difference of squares).

By sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1, 1 - sin^2 theta = cos^2 theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q8 Verify the identity: (sin theta + cos theta)/cos theta = 1 + tan theta

L.H.S = sin theta/cos theta + cos theta/cos theta = tan theta + 1 = R.H.S. Verified.

Q9 Verify the identity: (tan theta + cot theta) tan theta = sec^2 theta

Step 1: tan theta + cot theta = sin theta/cos theta + cos theta/sin theta = (sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta)/(sin theta cos theta) = 1/(sin theta cos theta).

Step 2: Multiply by tan theta = sin theta/cos theta: [1/(sin theta cos theta)] x (sin theta/cos theta) = 1/cos^2 theta = sec^2 theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q10 Verify the identity: (cot theta + cosec theta)(tan theta - sin theta) = sec theta - cos theta

Step 1: cot theta + cosec theta = cos theta/sin theta + 1/sin theta = (1 + cos theta)/sin theta.

Step 2: tan theta - sin theta = sin theta/cos theta - sin theta = sin theta(1 - cos theta)/cos theta.

Step 3: Product = [(1 + cos theta)/sin theta] x [sin theta(1 - cos theta)/cos theta] = (1 - cos^2 theta)/cos theta = 1/cos theta - cos theta = sec theta - cos theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q11 Verify the identity: (sin theta + cos theta)/(tan^2 theta - 1) = cos^2 theta/(sin theta - cos theta)

Step 1: tan^2 theta - 1 = sin^2 theta/cos^2 theta - 1 = (sin^2 theta - cos^2 theta)/cos^2 theta = (sin theta - cos theta)(sin theta + cos theta)/cos^2 theta.

Step 2: L.H.S = (sin theta + cos theta) x cos^2 theta/[(sin theta - cos theta)(sin theta + cos theta)] = cos^2 theta/(sin theta - cos theta) = R.H.S. Verified.

Q12 Verify the identity: cos^2 theta/sin theta + sin theta = cosec theta

L.H.S = (cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta)/sin theta = 1/sin theta = cosec theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q13 Verify the identity: sec theta - cos theta = tan theta sin theta

L.H.S = 1/cos theta - cos theta = (1 - cos^2 theta)/cos theta = sin^2 theta/cos theta = (sin theta/cos theta) sin theta = tan theta sin theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q14 Verify the identity: sin^2 theta/cos theta + cos theta = sec theta

L.H.S = (sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta)/cos theta = 1/cos theta = sec theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q15 Verify the identity: tan theta + cot theta = sec theta cosec theta

L.H.S = sin theta/cos theta + cos theta/sin theta = (sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta)/(sin theta cos theta) = 1/(sin theta cos theta) = (1/cos theta)(1/sin theta) = sec theta cosec theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q16 Verify the identity: (tan theta + cot theta)(cos theta + sin theta) = sec theta + cosec theta

Step 1: From Q15, tan theta + cot theta = 1/(sin theta cos theta).

Step 2: L.H.S = (sin theta + cos theta)/(sin theta cos theta) = 1/cos theta + 1/sin theta = sec theta + cosec theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q17 Verify the identity: sin theta (tan theta + cot theta) = sec theta

L.H.S = sin theta x [1/(sin theta cos theta)] (using tan + cot = 1/(sin theta cos theta)) = 1/cos theta = sec theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q18 Verify the identity: (1 + cos theta)/sin theta + sin theta/(1 + cos theta) = 2 cosec theta

Step 1: Common denominator sin theta(1 + cos theta): numerator = (1 + cos theta)^2 + sin^2 theta = 1 + 2cos theta + cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta = 2 + 2cos theta = 2(1 + cos theta).

Step 2: L.H.S = 2(1 + cos theta)/[sin theta(1 + cos theta)] = 2/sin theta = 2 cosec theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q19 Verify the identity: 1/(1 - cos theta) + 1/(1 + cos theta) = 2 cosec^2 theta

Step 1: Common denominator (1 - cos theta)(1 + cos theta) = 1 - cos^2 theta = sin^2 theta.

Step 2: Numerator = (1 + cos theta) + (1 - cos theta) = 2.

Step 3: L.H.S = 2/sin^2 theta = 2 cosec^2 theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q20 Verify the identity: (1 + sin theta)/(1 - sin theta) - (1 - sin theta)/(1 + sin theta) = 4 tan theta sec theta

Step 1: Common denominator (1 - sin theta)(1 + sin theta) = cos^2 theta.

Step 2: Numerator = (1 + sin theta)^2 - (1 - sin theta)^2 = (1 + 2sin theta + sin^2 theta) - (1 - 2sin theta + sin^2 theta) = 4 sin theta.

Step 3: L.H.S = 4 sin theta/cos^2 theta = 4 (sin theta/cos theta)(1/cos theta) = 4 tan theta sec theta = R.H.S. Verified.

Q21 Verify the identity: sin^3 theta = sin theta - sin theta cos^2 theta

R.H.S = sin theta(1 - cos^2 theta) = sin theta x sin^2 theta = sin^3 theta = L.H.S. Verified.

Q22 Verify the identity: cos^4 theta - sin^4 theta = (cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta)

L.H.S = (cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta)(cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta) (difference of squares).

Since cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta = 1, L.H.S = (cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta)(1) = R.H.S. Verified.

Q23 Verify the identity: sqrt[(1 + cos theta)/(1 - cos theta)] = sin theta/(1 - cos theta)

Step 1: Multiply numerator and denominator inside the root by (1 - cos theta): (1 + cos theta)(1 - cos theta)/(1 - cos theta)^2 = (1 - cos^2 theta)/(1 - cos theta)^2 = sin^2 theta/(1 - cos theta)^2.

Step 2: Taking the square root (for sin theta > 0): sin theta/(1 - cos theta) = R.H.S. Verified.

Q24 Verify the identity: sqrt[(sec theta + 1)/(sec theta - 1)] = (sec theta + 1)/tan theta

Step 1: Multiply numerator and denominator inside the root by (sec theta + 1): (sec theta + 1)^2/(sec^2 theta - 1).

Step 2: By 1 + tan^2 theta = sec^2 theta, sec^2 theta - 1 = tan^2 theta, so the fraction = (sec theta + 1)^2/tan^2 theta.

Step 3: Taking the square root: (sec theta + 1)/tan theta = R.H.S. Verified.

mcqs.q: Simplify sin^2 x / cos^2 x to a single trigonometric function.
mcqs.why: Use the formula tan x = sin x / cos x. Step 1: sin^2 x / cos^2 x = (sin x / cos x)^2. Step 2: (sin x / cos x)^2 = tan^2 x. So the simplified form is tan^2 x.

mcqs.q: Simplify tan x / sec x to a single trigonometric function.
mcqs.why: Write everything in sine and cosine using tan x = sin x / cos x and sec x = 1 / cos x. Step 1: tan x / sec x = (sin x / cos x) / (1 / cos x). Step 2: The cos x terms cancel, leaving sin x.

mcqs.q: Simplify 1 - cos^2 x.
mcqs.why: Use the Pythagorean identity sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1. Step 1: Rearranging gives 1 - cos^2 x = sin^2 x directly. So the simplified form is sin^2 x.

mcqs.q: Simplify sec^2 x - 1.
mcqs.why: Use the identity 1 + tan^2 x = sec^2 x. Step 1: Subtract 1 from both sides. Step 2: sec^2 x - 1 = tan^2 x. So the simplified form is tan^2 x.

mcqs.q: Simplify sin^2 x . cot^2 x.
mcqs.why: Use the formula cot^2 x = cos^2 x / sin^2 x. Step 1: sin^2 x . cot^2 x = sin^2 x . (cos^2 x / sin^2 x). Step 2: The sin^2 x terms cancel, leaving cos^2 x.

mcqs.q: (1 - sin theta)(1 + sin theta) simplifies to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: By difference of squares, (1 - sin theta)(1 + sin theta) = 1 - sin^2 theta. Step 2: Use the identity sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1, so 1 - sin^2 theta = cos^2 theta.

mcqs.q: (sin theta + cos theta) / cos theta simplifies to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Split the fraction: (sin theta + cos theta)/cos theta = sin theta/cos theta + cos theta/cos theta. Step 2: sin theta/cos theta = tan theta and cos theta/cos theta = 1. So the result is 1 + tan theta.

mcqs.q: cos^2 theta / sin theta + sin theta simplifies to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Take a common denominator sin theta: (cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta)/sin theta. Step 2: Use cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta = 1, giving 1/sin theta. Step 3: By definition 1/sin theta = cosec theta.

mcqs.q: sec theta - cos theta is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Write sec theta = 1/cos theta, so L.H.S. = 1/cos theta - cos theta = (1 - cos^2 theta)/cos theta. Step 2: Use 1 - cos^2 theta = sin^2 theta, giving sin^2 theta / cos theta. Step 3: sin^2 theta / cos theta = (sin theta/cos theta) x sin theta = tan theta sin theta.

mcqs.q: tan theta + cot theta is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: tan theta + cot theta = sin theta/cos theta + cos theta/sin theta = (sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta)/(sin theta cos theta). Step 2: Numerator = 1, so this is 1/(sin theta cos theta). Step 3: 1/(sin theta cos theta) = (1/cos theta)(1/sin theta) = sec theta cosec theta.

mcqs.q: 1/(1 - cos theta) + 1/(1 + cos theta) is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Common denominator (1 - cos theta)(1 + cos theta) = 1 - cos^2 theta = sin^2 theta. Step 2: Numerator = (1 + cos theta) + (1 - cos theta) = 2. Step 3: Result = 2 / sin^2 theta = 2 cosec^2 theta.

mcqs.q: (1 + sin theta)/(1 - sin theta) - (1 - sin theta)/(1 + sin theta) is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Common denominator (1 - sin theta)(1 + sin theta) = 1 - sin^2 theta = cos^2 theta. Step 2: Numerator = (1 + sin theta)^2 - (1 - sin theta)^2 = 4 sin theta. Step 3: Result = 4 sin theta / cos^2 theta = 4 (sin theta/cos theta)(1/cos theta) = 4 tan theta sec theta.

mcqs.q: cos^4 theta - sin^4 theta is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Factorise by difference of squares: cos^4 theta - sin^4 theta = (cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta)(cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta). Step 2: Use cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta = 1. Step 3: The product becomes (cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta)(1) = cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta.

mcqs.q: sqrt[(1 + cos theta)/(1 - cos theta)] is equal to (for sin theta > 0):
mcqs.why: Step 1: Multiply numerator and denominator inside the root by (1 - cos theta): the fraction becomes (1 - cos^2 theta)/(1 - cos theta)^2. Step 2: Use 1 - cos^2 theta = sin^2 theta, giving sin^2 theta/(1 - cos theta)^2. Step 3: Taking the square root (sin theta > 0) gives sin theta/(1 - cos theta).

mcqs.q: sin theta (tan theta + cot theta) simplifies to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: From tan theta + cot theta = 1/(sin theta cos theta). Step 2: Multiply by sin theta: sin theta x 1/(sin theta cos theta) = 1/cos theta. Step 3: By definition 1/cos theta = sec theta.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.5
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Find the angle of elevation of the sun if a 6 feet man casts a 3.5 feet shadow

Step 1: The man is the perpendicular (6 ft) and his shadow the base (3.5 ft); the sun's elevation theta satisfies tan theta = opposite/adjacent = 6/3.5 = 1.7143.

Step 2: theta = tan^-1(1.7143) = 59.7 deg (approx).

Answer: about 59.7 degrees.

Q2 A tree casts a 40 meter shadow when the angle of elevation of the sun is 25 deg. Find the height of the tree

Step 1: tan 25 = height/shadow = h/40.

Step 2: h = 40 x tan 25 = 40 x 0.4663 = 18.65 m.

Answer: about 18.65 meters.

Q3 A 20 feet long ladder is leaning against a wall. The bottom of the ladder is 5 feet from the base of the wall. Find the acute angle (angle of elevation) the ladder makes with the ground

Step 1: The ladder is the hypotenuse (20 ft); the distance from the wall is the side adjacent to the ground angle: cos theta = 5/20 = 0.25.

Step 2: theta = cos^-1(0.25) = 75.5 deg (approx).

Answer: about 75.5 degrees.

Q4 The base of a rectangle is 25 feet and the height of the rectangle is 13 feet. Find the angle that the diagonal of the rectangle makes with the base

Step 1: The diagonal, base and height form a right triangle with tan theta = height/base = 13/25 = 0.52.

Step 2: theta = tan^-1(0.52) = 27.5 deg (approx).

Answer: about 27.5 degrees.

Q5 A rocket is launched and climbs at a constant angle of 80 deg. Find the altitude of the rocket after it travels 5000 meter

Step 1: The path of the rocket is the hypotenuse (5000 m); altitude is the side opposite the 80 deg angle: sin 80 = altitude/5000.

Step 2: Altitude = 5000 x sin 80 = 5000 x 0.9848 = 4924 m.

Answer: about 4924 meters.

Q6 An aeroplane pilot flying at an altitude of 4000 m wishes to make an approach to an airport at an angle of 50 deg with the horizontal. How far from the airport will the plane be when the pilot begins to descend?

Step 1: The descent angle (angle of depression) is 50 deg; altitude 4000 m is opposite this angle and the ground distance d is adjacent: tan 50 = 4000/d.

Step 2: d = 4000/tan 50 = 4000/1.1918 = 3356 m.

Answer: about 3356 meters (3.36 km) from the airport.

Q7 A guy wire (supporting wire) runs from the middle of a utility pole to the ground. The wire makes an angle of 78.2 deg with the ground and touches the ground 3 meters from the base of the pole. Find the height of the pole

Step 1: The wire meets the pole at its middle, say at height h/2, and the ground distance is 3 m: tan 78.2 = (h/2)/3.

Step 2: h/2 = 3 x tan 78.2 = 3 x 4.777 = 14.33 m.

Step 3: Full height h = 2 x 14.33 = 28.66 m.

Answer: about 28.66 meters.

Q8 A road is inclined at an angle 5.7 deg. Suppose that we drive 2 miles up this road starting from sea level. How high above sea level are we?

Step 1: The 2 miles driven is the hypotenuse; the height is opposite the 5.7 deg angle: sin 5.7 = height/2.

Step 2: Height = 2 x sin 5.7 = 2 x 0.0993 = 0.199 mile (approx), about 1050 feet.

Answer: about 0.2 mile above sea level.

Q9 A television antenna of 8 feet height is located on the top of a house. From a point on the ground the angle of elevation to the top of the house is 17 deg and the angle of elevation to the top of the antenna is 21.8 deg. Find the height of the house

Step 1: Let the house height be h and the distance of the point from the house be d. Then tan 17 = h/d and tan 21.8 = (h + 8)/d.

Step 2: From the first, d = h/tan 17. Substitute in the second: h + 8 = h x (tan 21.8/tan 17) = h x (0.4001/0.3057) = 1.3088h.

Step 3: 8 = 0.3088h, so h = 8/0.3088 = 25.9 feet.

Answer: about 25.9 feet.

Q10 From an observation point, the angles of depression of two boats in line with this point are found to be 30 deg and 45 deg. Find the distance between the two boats if the point of observation is 4000 feet high

Step 1: Distance of the nearer boat (depression 45 deg) from the foot of the observation point: d1 = 4000/tan 45 = 4000/1 = 4000 ft.

Step 2: Distance of the farther boat (depression 30 deg): d2 = 4000/tan 30 = 4000 x sqrt(3) = 6928 ft.

Step 3: Distance between the boats = d2 - d1 = 6928 - 4000 = 2928 ft.

Answer: about 2928 feet.

Q11 Two ships, which are in line with the base of a vertical cliff, are 120 meters apart. The angles of depression from the top of the cliff to the ships are 30 deg and 45 deg (see the book diagram: A = far ship, B = near ship, C = base of cliff, D = top of cliff). (a) Calculate the distance BC. (b) Calculate the height CD of the cliff

Step 1: Let the cliff height CD = h. For the near ship B (depression 45 deg): tan 45 = h/BC, so BC = h.

Step 2: For the far ship A (depression 30 deg): tan 30 = h/AC, so AC = h/tan 30 = h x sqrt(3) = 1.732h.

Step 3: AB = AC - BC = 1.732h - h = 0.732h = 120, so h = 120/0.732 = 163.9 m.

(a) BC = h = 163.9 m (approx).

(b) CD = h = 163.9 m (approx).

Q12 Suppose that we are standing on a bridge 30 feet above a river watching a log (piece of wood) floating towards us. If the angle with the horizontal to the front of the log is 16.7 deg and the angle with the horizontal to the back of the log is 14 deg, how long is the log?

Step 1: The front (nearer end) has the larger angle of depression, 16.7 deg. Its distance from the foot of the bridge: d1 = 30/tan 16.7 = 30/0.3000 = 100 ft.

Step 2: The back (farther end), depression 14 deg: d2 = 30/tan 14 = 30/0.2493 = 120.3 ft.

Step 3: Length of the log = d2 - d1 = 120.3 - 100 = 20.3 ft.

Answer: about 20.3 feet. (Note: the book's diagram labels the height 30 m while the text says 30 feet; the solution follows the text, 30 feet.)

mcqs.q: A 6 feet man casts a 3.5 feet shadow. Find the angle of elevation of the sun.
mcqs.why: The man is the perpendicular (6 ft) and the shadow is the base (3.5 ft). Use the formula tan theta = opposite/adjacent. Step 1: tan theta = 6/3.5 = 1.7143. Step 2: theta = tan^-1(1.7143) = 59.7 degrees approx.

mcqs.q: A tree casts a 40 m shadow when the angle of elevation of the sun is 25 degrees. Find the height of the tree.
mcqs.why: Use the formula tan theta = height/shadow, so height = shadow x tan theta. Step 1: h = 40 x tan 25 degrees. Step 2: tan 25 = 0.4663. Step 3: h = 40 x 0.4663 = 18.65 m approx.

mcqs.q: A 20 feet ladder leans against a wall with its bottom 5 feet from the wall. Find the angle the ladder makes with the ground.
mcqs.why: The ladder is the hypotenuse (20 ft) and the 5 ft distance is adjacent to the ground angle. Use the formula cos theta = adjacent/hypotenuse. Step 1: cos theta = 5/20 = 0.25. Step 2: theta = cos^-1(0.25) = 75.5 degrees approx.

mcqs.q: A rectangle has base 25 feet and height 13 feet. Find the angle its diagonal makes with the base.
mcqs.why: The diagonal, base and height form a right triangle. Use the formula tan theta = height/base. Step 1: tan theta = 13/25 = 0.52. Step 2: theta = tan^-1(0.52) = 27.5 degrees approx.

mcqs.q: A rocket climbs at a constant angle of 80 degrees and travels 5000 m. Find its altitude.
mcqs.why: The path is the hypotenuse (5000 m) and altitude is opposite the 80 degree angle. Use the formula sin theta = altitude/hypotenuse. Step 1: Altitude = 5000 x sin 80 degrees. Step 2: sin 80 = 0.9848. Step 3: Altitude = 5000 x 0.9848 = 4924 m approx.

mcqs.q: A pilot at altitude 4000 m approaches an airport at 50 degrees to the horizontal. How far from the airport does descent begin?
mcqs.why: Altitude 4000 m is opposite the 50 degree descent angle and ground distance d is adjacent. Use the formula tan 50 = 4000/d, so d = 4000/tan 50. Step 1: tan 50 = 1.1918. Step 2: d = 4000/1.1918 = 3356 m approx, about 3.36 km.

mcqs.q: A guy wire from the middle of a pole makes 78.2 degrees with the ground and touches the ground 3 m from the pole. Find the height of the pole.
mcqs.why: Let the pole height be h; the wire meets it at h/2, with ground distance 3 m. Use the formula tan theta = opposite/adjacent. Step 1: tan 78.2 = (h/2)/3. Step 2: h/2 = 3 x tan 78.2 = 3 x 4.777 = 14.33 m. Step 3: h = 2 x 14.33 = 28.66 m approx.

mcqs.q: A road is inclined at 5.7 degrees. Driving 2 miles up it from sea level, how high above sea level are you?
mcqs.why: The 2 miles driven is the hypotenuse and the height is opposite the 5.7 degree angle. Use the formula sin theta = height/hypotenuse. Step 1: Height = 2 x sin 5.7 degrees. Step 2: sin 5.7 = 0.0993. Step 3: Height = 2 x 0.0993 = 0.199 mile approx, about 1050 feet.

mcqs.q: An 8 feet antenna is on a house. From a ground point, elevation to top of house is 17 degrees and to top of antenna is 21.8 degrees. Find the height of the house.
mcqs.why: Let house height be h and distance be d. Use tan theta = height/distance. Step 1: tan 17 = h/d and tan 21.8 = (h+8)/d, so d = h/tan 17. Step 2: h + 8 = h x (tan 21.8 / tan 17) = h x (0.4001/0.3057) = 1.3088h. Step 3: 8 = 0.3088h, so h = 8/0.3088 = 25.9 feet approx.

mcqs.q: From a point 4000 feet high, angles of depression of two boats in line are 30 degrees and 45 degrees. Find the distance between the boats.
mcqs.why: Use the formula distance = height / tan(depression angle). Step 1: Nearer boat (45 degrees): d1 = 4000/tan 45 = 4000/1 = 4000 ft. Step 2: Farther boat (30 degrees): d2 = 4000/tan 30 = 4000 x sqrt(3) = 6928 ft. Step 3: Distance between boats = d2 - d1 = 6928 - 4000 = 2928 ft approx.

lessons.title: Miscellaneous Exercise 7
lessons.notes_html:
MCQ (i) The union of two non-collinear rays, which have a common end point, is called

(a) an angle
(b) a degree
(c) a minute
(d) a radian
Correct answer: an angle

MCQ (ii) The system of measurement in which the angle is measured in radians is called

(a) CGS system
(b) sexagesimal system
(c) MKS system
(d) circular system
Correct answer: circular system

MCQ (iii) 20 degrees =

(a) 360 min
(b) 630 min
(c) 1200 min
(d) 3600 min
Correct answer: 1200 min

MCQ (iv) 3pi/4 radians =

(a) 115 deg
(b) 135 deg
(c) 150 deg
(d) 30 deg
Correct answer: 135 deg

MCQ (v) If tan theta = sqrt(3), then theta is equal to

(a) 90 deg
(b) 45 deg
(c) 60 deg
(d) 30 deg
Correct answer: 60 deg

MCQ (vi) sec^2 theta =

(a) 1 - sin^2 theta
(b) 1 + tan^2 theta
(c) 1 + cos^2 theta
(d) 1 - tan^2 theta
Correct answer: 1 + tan^2 theta

MCQ (vii) 1/(1 + sin theta) + 1/(1 - sin theta) =

(a) 2 sec^2 theta
(b) 2cos^2 theta
(c) sec^2 theta
(d) cos theta
Correct answer: 2 sec^2 theta

MCQ (viii) (1/2) cosec 45 deg =

(a) 1/(2sqrt(2))
(b) 1/sqrt(2)
(c) sqrt(2)
(d) sqrt(3)/2
Correct answer: 1/sqrt(2)

MCQ (ix) sec theta . cot theta =

(a) sin theta
(b) 1/cos theta
(c) 1/sin theta
(d) sin theta/cos theta
Correct answer: 1/sin theta

MCQ (x) cosec^2 theta - cot^2 theta =

(a) -1
(b) 1
(c) 0
(d) tan theta
Correct answer: 1

Short Answer (i) Define an angle

An angle is the union of two non-collinear rays which have a common end point (the vertex); one ray is the initial side and the other the terminal side.

Short Answer (ii) What is the sexagesimal system of measurement of angles?

The sexagesimal system is the system in which an angle is measured in degrees, minutes and seconds: a right angle is divided into 90 equal parts called degrees, each degree into 60 minutes and each minute into 60 seconds (1 deg = 60 min, 1 min = 60 sec).

Short Answer (iii) How many minutes are there in two right angles?

Two right angles = 180 deg. Each degree has 60 minutes, so 180 x 60 = 10,800 minutes.

Short Answer (iv) Define radian measure of an angle

One radian is the measure of the central angle of a circle whose intercepted arc has length equal to the radius of the circle. In general, theta (radians) = arc length/radius = l/r.

Short Answer (v) Convert pi/4 radians to degree measure

pi/4 x (180/pi) = 45 degrees.

Short Answer (vi) Convert 15 degrees to radians

15 x (pi/180) = pi/12 radian = 0.2618 radian (approx).

Short Answer (vii) What is the radian measure of the central angle of an arc 50 m long on the circle of radius 25 m?

Formula: theta = l/r = 50/25 = 2 radians.

Short Answer (viii) Find r when l = 56 cm and theta = 45 deg

Step 1: theta = 45 deg = pi/4 radian.

Step 2: Formula l = r.theta gives r = l/theta = 56/(pi/4) = 224/pi = 71.3 cm (approx).

Short Answer (ix) Find tan theta when cos theta = 9/41 and the terminal side of theta is in the fourth quadrant

Step 1: sin^2 theta = 1 - 81/1681 = 1600/1681, so sin theta = -40/41 (negative in quadrant IV).

Step 2: tan theta = sin theta/cos theta = (-40/41)/(9/41) = -40/9.

Short Answer (x) Prove that (1 - sin^2 theta)(1 + tan^2 theta) = 1

Step 1: 1 - sin^2 theta = cos^2 theta (Pythagorean identity).

Step 2: 1 + tan^2 theta = sec^2 theta.

Step 3: Product = cos^2 theta x sec^2 theta = cos^2 theta x (1/cos^2 theta) = 1. Proved.

Fill in the blank (i) pi radians = _______ degree.

Answer: 180

Fill in the blank (ii) The terminal side of angle 235 deg lies in _______ quadrant.

Answer: third (III)

Fill in the blank (iii) Terminal side of the angle -30 deg lies in _______ quadrant.

Answer: fourth (IV)

Fill in the blank (iv) Area of a circular sector is _______.

Answer: (1/2) r^2 theta (theta in radians)

Fill in the blank (v) If r = 2 cm and theta = 3 radian, then area of the circular sector is _______.

Answer: 6 cm^2

Fill in the blank (vi) The general form of the angle 480 deg is _______.

Answer: 360 deg x n + 120 deg (n an integer)

Fill in the blank (vii) If sin theta = 1/2, then theta = _______.

Answer: 30 deg

Fill in the blank (viii) If theta = 300 deg, then sec(-300 deg) = _______.

Answer: 2

Fill in the blank (ix) 1 + cot^2 theta = _______.

Answer: cosec^2 theta

Fill in the blank (x) sec theta - tan theta = _______.

Answer: 1/(sec theta + tan theta)

mcqs.q: The union of two non-collinear rays, which have a common end point, is called
mcqs.why: By definition in the book, an angle is the union of two non-collinear rays which have a common end point. The common end point is the vertex, one ray is the initial side and the other is the terminal side.

mcqs.q: The system of measurement in which the angle is measured in radians is called
mcqs.why: Angles measured in degrees, minutes and seconds belong to the sexagesimal system. Angles measured in radians belong to the circular system, where one radian is the central angle whose arc length equals the radius.

mcqs.q: 20 degrees =
mcqs.why: Use the conversion 1 degree = 60 minutes. Step 1: 20 degrees = 20 x 60 minutes. Step 2: 20 x 60 = 1200 minutes.

mcqs.q: 3pi/4 radians =
mcqs.why: Use the formula degrees = radians x (180/pi). Step 1: (3pi/4) x (180/pi). Step 2: pi cancels and 3 x 180/4 = 135 degrees.

mcqs.q: If tan theta = sqrt(3), then theta is equal to
mcqs.why: Use the standard values table: tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3), tan 45 = 1, tan 60 = sqrt(3). Since tan theta = sqrt(3), theta = 60 degrees for the acute value given in the book.

mcqs.q: sec^2 theta =
mcqs.why: Use the Pythagorean identity 1 + tan^2 theta = sec^2 theta. This follows by dividing sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1 throughout by cos^2 theta, giving tan^2 theta + 1 = sec^2 theta.

mcqs.q: 1/(1 + sin theta) + 1/(1 - sin theta) =
mcqs.why: Step 1: Common denominator (1 + sin theta)(1 - sin theta) = 1 - sin^2 theta = cos^2 theta. Step 2: Numerator = (1 - sin theta) + (1 + sin theta) = 2. Step 3: Result = 2/cos^2 theta = 2 sec^2 theta.

mcqs.q: (1/2) cosec 45 deg =
mcqs.why: Step 1: Standard value cosec 45 degrees = 1/sin 45 = sqrt(2). Step 2: (1/2) x sqrt(2) = sqrt(2)/2. Step 3: Rationalising, sqrt(2)/2 = 1/sqrt(2).

mcqs.q: sec theta . cot theta =
mcqs.why: Write in sine and cosine: sec theta = 1/cos theta and cot theta = cos theta/sin theta. Step 1: Product = (1/cos theta) x (cos theta/sin theta). Step 2: cos theta cancels, leaving 1/sin theta, which is cosec theta.

mcqs.q: cosec^2 theta - cot^2 theta =
mcqs.why: Use the identity 1 + cot^2 theta = cosec^2 theta. Step 1: Rearranging gives cosec^2 theta - cot^2 theta = 1 for all theta where the functions are defined.

mcqs.q: pi radians = _______ degree.
mcqs.why: Use the formula degrees = radians x (180/pi). Step 1: pi x (180/pi). Step 2: pi cancels, giving 180 degrees. This is the key conversion used throughout the unit.

mcqs.q: The terminal side of angle 235 degrees lies in _______ quadrant.
mcqs.why: Quadrant ranges: III is 180 degrees < angle < 270 degrees. Since 180 < 235 < 270, the terminal side of 235 degrees lies in the third quadrant.

mcqs.q: If r = 2 cm and theta = 3 radian, the area of the circular sector is:
mcqs.why: Use the formula Area of a sector = (1/2) r^2 theta, theta in radians. Step 1: Area = (1/2) x (2)^2 x 3. Step 2: (1/2) x 4 x 3 = 6. So the area is 6 cm^2.

mcqs.q: 1 + cot^2 theta =
mcqs.why: Use the Pythagorean identity 1 + cot^2 theta = cosec^2 theta. It follows by dividing sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1 throughout by sin^2 theta, giving 1 + cot^2 theta = cosec^2 theta.

mcqs.q: How many minutes are there in two right angles?
mcqs.why: Step 1: Two right angles = 2 x 90 degrees = 180 degrees. Step 2: Use 1 degree = 60 minutes. Step 3: 180 x 60 = 10800 minutes.

chapters.title: Unit 8 - Projection of a Side of a Triangle

lessons.title: Theorems of Unit 8
lessons.notes_html:
Theorem 1 (8.1(i)) In an obtuse-angled triangle, the square on the side opposite to the obtuse angle is equal to the sum of the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle together with twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides, and the projection on it of the other

Given: ABC is a triangle having an obtuse angle BAC at A. Draw CD perpendicular to BA produced, so that AD is the projection of AC on BA produced. Take BC = a, CA = b, AB = c, AD = x and CD = h.

To prove: (BC)^2 = (AC)^2 + (AB)^2 + 2(AB)(AD), i.e. a^2 = b^2 + c^2 + 2cx.

Proof:

Step 1: In right triangle CDA, angle CDA = 90 deg, so by Pythagoras: (AC)^2 = (AD)^2 + (CD)^2, i.e. b^2 = x^2 + h^2 ... (i)

Step 2: In right triangle CDB, angle CDB = 90 deg, so (BC)^2 = (BD)^2 + (CD)^2. Since BD = BA + AD = c + x: a^2 = (c + x)^2 + h^2 = c^2 + 2cx + x^2 + h^2 ... (ii)

Step 3: Using (i) in (ii): a^2 = c^2 + 2cx + b^2.

Hence (BC)^2 = (AC)^2 + (AB)^2 + 2(AB)(AD). Proved.

Theorem 2 (8.1(ii)) In any triangle, the square on the side opposite to an acute angle is equal to the sum of the squares on the sides containing that acute angle diminished by twice the rectangle contained by one of those sides and the projection on it of the other

Given: Triangle ABC with an acute angle CAB at A. Take BC = a, CA = b, AB = c. Draw CD perpendicular to AB so that AD is the projection of AC on AB. Also AD = x and CD = h.

To prove: (BC)^2 = (AC)^2 + (AB)^2 - 2(AB)(AD), i.e. a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2cx.

Proof:

Step 1: In right triangle CDA, angle CDA = 90 deg, so (AC)^2 = (AD)^2 + (CD)^2, i.e. b^2 = x^2 + h^2 ... (i)

Step 2: In right triangle CDB, (BC)^2 = (BD)^2 + (CD)^2. Since BD = AB - AD = c - x: a^2 = (c - x)^2 + h^2 = c^2 - 2cx + x^2 + h^2 ... (ii)

Step 3: Using (i) in (ii): a^2 = c^2 - 2cx + b^2.

Hence (BC)^2 = (AC)^2 + (AB)^2 - 2(AB)(AD). Proved.

Theorem 3 (8.1(iii)) - Apollonius' Theorem: In any triangle, the sum of the squares on any two sides is equal to twice the square on half the third side together with twice the square on the median which bisects the third side

Given: In triangle ABC, the median AD bisects BC, i.e. BD = CD.

To prove: (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 = 2(BD)^2 + 2(AD)^2.

Construction: Draw AF perpendicular to BC.

Proof:

Step 1: In triangle ADB, angle ADB is acute at D, so by Theorem 2: (AB)^2 = (BD)^2 + (AD)^2 - 2(BD)(FD) ... (i)

Step 2: In triangle ADC, angle ADC is obtuse at D (supplement of angle ADB), so by Theorem 1: (AC)^2 = (CD)^2 + (AD)^2 + 2(CD)(FD) = (BD)^2 + (AD)^2 + 2(BD)(FD), using CD = BD ... (ii)

Step 3: Add (i) and (ii): the terms -2(BD)(FD) and +2(BD)(FD) cancel, giving (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 = 2(BD)^2 + 2(AD)^2. Proved.

mcqs.q: Theorem 1 (obtuse-angled triangle): If angle A of triangle ABC is obtuse, with AD the projection of AC on BA produced, then (BC)^2 equals:
mcqs.why: Theorem 1 states: in an obtuse-angled triangle, the square on the side opposite the obtuse angle equals the sum of the squares on the sides containing it together with twice the rectangle by one side and the projection of the other. With a=BC, b=CA, c=AB, x=AD: a^2 = b^2 + c^2 + 2cx. The sign is PLUS because the angle is obtuse.

mcqs.q: Theorem 2 (acute angle): If angle A of triangle ABC is acute, with AD the projection of AC on AB, then (BC)^2 equals:
mcqs.why: Theorem 2 states: the square on the side opposite an acute angle equals the sum of the squares on the sides containing it diminished by twice the rectangle by one side and the projection of the other. With a=BC, b=CA, c=AB, x=AD: a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2cx. The sign is MINUS because the angle is acute.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 1, CD is drawn perpendicular to:
mcqs.why: Given triangle ABC with obtuse angle BAC at A, the construction draws CD perpendicular to BA produced, because the foot D must fall outside segment AB on its extension. Then AD is the projection of AC on BA produced.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 1, with BD = BA + AD = c + x and CD = h, the step for (BC)^2 in triangle CDB gives:
mcqs.why: In right triangle CDB, angle CDB = 90 degrees, so by Pythagoras (BC)^2 = (BD)^2 + (CD)^2. Step 1: BD = BA + AD = c + x because D is on BA produced. Step 2: a^2 = (c + x)^2 + h^2 = c^2 + 2cx + x^2 + h^2. Step 3: Using b^2 = x^2 + h^2 from triangle CDA gives a^2 = b^2 + c^2 + 2cx.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 2, BD is equal to:
mcqs.why: In Theorem 2 the angle at A is acute, so the foot D of the perpendicular from C falls on AB itself. Therefore BD = AB - AD = c - x. This is why (c - x)^2 produces the minus term -2cx in a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2cx.

mcqs.q: Apollonius' Theorem states that in any triangle, (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 equals (D is the midpoint of BC):
mcqs.why: Apollonius' Theorem: the sum of the squares on any two sides equals twice the square on half the third side together with twice the square on the median which bisects the third side. Since D bisects BC, half the third side is BD, and the median is AD, giving (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 = 2(BD)^2 + 2(AD)^2.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Apollonius' Theorem, adding the results from triangles ADB and ADC causes which terms to cancel?
mcqs.why: Step 1: In triangle ADB, angle ADB is acute, so by Theorem 2: (AB)^2 = (BD)^2 + (AD)^2 - 2(BD)(FD). Step 2: In triangle ADC, angle ADC is obtuse, so by Theorem 1: (AC)^2 = (BD)^2 + (AD)^2 + 2(BD)(FD), using CD = BD. Step 3: Adding, -2(BD)(FD) and +2(BD)(FD) cancel, leaving 2(BD)^2 + 2(AD)^2.

mcqs.q: In Apollonius' Theorem, AD is:
mcqs.why: By the statement of Apollonius' Theorem, AD is the median which bisects the third side BC, so BD = CD. The altitude in the proof is the separate construction AF perpendicular to BC, not AD itself unless the triangle is isosceles.

mcqs.q: In both Theorems 1 and 2, the relation obtained from right triangle CDA (with AD = x, CD = h, AC = b) is:
mcqs.why: In right triangle CDA, angle CDA = 90 degrees, so by Pythagoras the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: (AC)^2 = (AD)^2 + (CD)^2, i.e. b^2 = x^2 + h^2. This relation (i) is then substituted into the expression for a^2 in both proofs.

mcqs.q: The essential difference between Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 in the final formula a^2 = b^2 + c^2 +/- 2cx is:
mcqs.why: For the obtuse angle (Theorem 1) the projection falls on the side produced and BD = c + x, giving a^2 = b^2 + c^2 + 2cx with a PLUS sign. For the acute angle (Theorem 2) the projection falls on the side itself and BD = c - x, giving a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2cx with a MINUS sign.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Given AC = 1 cm, BC = 2 cm, angle C = 120 deg. Compute the length AB and the area of triangle ABC. (Hint: (AB)^2 = (AC)^2 + (BC)^2 + 2(AC).(CD) where CD = (BC) cos(180 deg - angle C); use Theorem 1)

Step 1: Angle C = 120 deg is obtuse, so use Theorem 1 with the projection CD of BC on CA produced: CD = BC x cos(180 - 120) = 2 x cos 60 = 2 x (1/2) = 1 cm.

Step 2: (AB)^2 = (AC)^2 + (BC)^2 + 2(AC)(CD) = 1 + 4 + 2(1)(1) = 7.

Step 3: AB = sqrt(7) = 2.65 cm (approx).

Step 4 (Area): Area = (1/2)(AC)(BC) sin C = (1/2)(1)(2) sin 120 = sin 120 = sqrt(3)/2 = 0.87 cm^2 (approx).

Answer: AB = sqrt(7) cm (2.65 cm); Area = 0.87 cm^2.

Q2 Find AC if in triangle ABC, BC = 6 cm, AB = 4sqrt(2) cm and angle ABC = 135 deg

Step 1: Angle B = 135 deg is obtuse, so use Theorem 1: (AC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (BC)^2 + 2(AB)(projection of BC on BA produced).

Step 2: Projection of BC on BA produced = BC x cos(180 - 135) = 6 x cos 45 = 6/sqrt(2) = 3sqrt(2) cm.

Step 3: (AC)^2 = (4sqrt(2))^2 + 6^2 + 2(4sqrt(2))(3sqrt(2)) = 32 + 36 + 48 = 116.

Step 4: AC = sqrt(116) = 2sqrt(29) = 10.77 cm (approx).

Answer: AC = 2sqrt(29) cm (10.77 cm).

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, AC = 1 cm, BC = 2 cm and angle C = 120 degrees. The projection CD of BC on CA produced is:
mcqs.why: Angle C = 120 degrees is obtuse, so use Theorem 1. Formula for projection: CD = (BC) cos(180 degrees - angle C). Step 1: CD = 2 x cos(180 - 120) = 2 x cos 60. Step 2: cos 60 = 1/2, so CD = 2 x 1/2 = 1 cm.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, AC = 1 cm, BC = 2 cm and angle C = 120 degrees. (AB)^2 equals:
mcqs.why: Use Theorem 1 (obtuse angle): formula (AB)^2 = (AC)^2 + (BC)^2 + 2(AC)(CD), with CD = 1 cm from the projection step. Step 1: (AB)^2 = 1^2 + 2^2 + 2(1)(1). Step 2: = 1 + 4 + 2 = 7.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, AC = 1 cm, BC = 2 cm and angle C = 120 degrees. The length AB is:
mcqs.why: Use Theorem 1: (AB)^2 = (AC)^2 + (BC)^2 + 2(AC)(CD) = 1 + 4 + 2(1)(1) = 7. Step 1: Take the square root of both sides. Step 2: AB = sqrt(7) = 2.65 cm approx.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, AC = 1 cm, BC = 2 cm and angle C = 120 degrees. The area of triangle ABC is:
mcqs.why: Use the formula Area = (1/2)(AC)(BC) sin C. Step 1: Area = (1/2)(1)(2) sin 120 degrees = sin 120 degrees. Step 2: sin 120 = sqrt(3)/2 = 0.87. So the area is 0.87 cm^2 approx.

mcqs.q: For angle C = 120 degrees in Exercise 8.1 Q1, which theorem is applied and why?
options: Theorem 2, because angle C is acute
Theorem 1, because angle C is obtuse
Apollonius' Theorem, because C is a midpoint
Pythagoras only, because angle C is 90 degrees
mcqs.why: Theorem 1 applies to the side opposite an obtuse angle, with a PLUS 2(side)(projection) term. Angle C = 120 degrees is greater than 90 degrees, so it is obtuse, the projection is taken on CA produced, and Theorem 1 must be used.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, BC = 6 cm, AB = 4sqrt(2) cm and angle ABC = 135 degrees. The projection of BC on BA produced is:
mcqs.why: Angle B = 135 degrees is obtuse. Formula for projection: projection = (BC) cos(180 degrees - angle B). Step 1: = 6 x cos(180 - 135) = 6 x cos 45. Step 2: cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2), so projection = 6/sqrt(2) = 3sqrt(2) cm.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, BC = 6 cm, AB = 4sqrt(2) cm and angle B = 135 degrees. (AC)^2 equals:
mcqs.why: Use Theorem 1: formula (AC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (BC)^2 + 2(AB)(projection), projection = 3sqrt(2) cm. Step 1: (4sqrt(2))^2 = 32 and 6^2 = 36. Step 2: 2(4sqrt(2))(3sqrt(2)) = 48. Step 3: (AC)^2 = 32 + 36 + 48 = 116.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, BC = 6 cm, AB = 4sqrt(2) cm and angle B = 135 degrees. The length AC is:
mcqs.why: From Theorem 1, (AC)^2 = 32 + 36 + 48 = 116. Step 1: AC = sqrt(116). Step 2: Simplify sqrt(116) = sqrt(4 x 29) = 2sqrt(29). Step 3: 2sqrt(29) = 10.77 cm approx.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 8.1 Q2, the value cos(180 degrees - 135 degrees) used for the projection is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 180 degrees - 135 degrees = 45 degrees, the supplementary acute angle outside the obtuse angle at B. Step 2: The standard value cos 45 degrees = 1/sqrt(2). This is multiplied by BC = 6 cm to get the projection 3sqrt(2) cm.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 8.1 Q1, the value sin 120 degrees used in the area formula equals:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 120 degrees is in Quadrant II, where sin is positive. Step 2: Its reference angle is 180 - 120 = 60 degrees. Step 3: sin 120 = sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2, so Area = (1/2)(1)(2)(sqrt(3)/2) = sqrt(3)/2 = 0.87 cm^2 approx.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 In a triangle ABC calculate BC when AB = 6 cm, AC = 4 cm and angle A = 60 deg

Step 1: Angle A = 60 deg is acute, so use Theorem 2: (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - 2(AB)(projection of AC on AB).

Step 2: Projection of AC on AB = AC x cos 60 = 4 x (1/2) = 2 cm.

Step 3: (BC)^2 = 36 + 16 - 2(6)(2) = 52 - 24 = 28.

Step 4: BC = sqrt(28) = 2sqrt(7) = 5.29 cm (approx).

Answer: BC = 2sqrt(7) cm (5.29 cm).

Q2 In a triangle ABC, AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm, AC = 9 cm and D is the mid-point of side AC. Find the length of the median BD

Step 1: By Apollonius' Theorem (Theorem 3) applied to the median BD: (AB)^2 + (BC)^2 = 2(AD)^2 + 2(BD)^2, where AD = AC/2 = 9/2 = 4.5 cm.

Step 2: Substitute: 6^2 + 8^2 = 2(4.5)^2 + 2(BD)^2, i.e. 36 + 64 = 40.5 + 2(BD)^2.

Step 3: 2(BD)^2 = 100 - 40.5 = 59.5, so (BD)^2 = 29.75.

Step 4: BD = sqrt(29.75) = 5.45 cm (approx).

Answer: BD = 5.45 cm.

Q3 In a parallelogram ABCD prove that (AC)^2 + (BD)^2 = 2[(AB)^2 + (BC)^2]

Step 1: In a parallelogram the diagonals AC and BD bisect each other; let them meet at O, so O is the midpoint of AC and AO = AC/2, BO = BD/2.

Step 2: In triangle ABC, BO is a median to side AC. By Apollonius' Theorem: (AB)^2 + (BC)^2 = 2(AO)^2 + 2(BO)^2.

Step 3: Substitute AO = AC/2 and BO = BD/2: (AB)^2 + (BC)^2 = 2(AC/2)^2 + 2(BD/2)^2 = (AC)^2/2 + (BD)^2/2.

Step 4: Multiply by 2: 2[(AB)^2 + (BC)^2] = (AC)^2 + (BD)^2. Proved.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, AB = 6 cm, AC = 4 cm and angle A = 60 degrees. The projection of AC on AB is:
mcqs.why: Angle A = 60 degrees is acute. Formula for projection: projection = (AC) cos A. Step 1: = 4 x cos 60. Step 2: cos 60 = 1/2, so projection = 4 x 1/2 = 2 cm.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, AB = 6 cm, AC = 4 cm and angle A = 60 degrees. BC equals:
options: sqrt(28) cm is wrong, BC = 28 cm
mcqs.why: Use Theorem 2 (acute angle): formula (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - 2(AB)(projection), projection = 2 cm. Step 1: (BC)^2 = 36 + 16 - 2(6)(2) = 52 - 24 = 28. Step 2: BC = sqrt(28) = 2sqrt(7) = 5.29 cm approx.

mcqs.q: For angle A = 60 degrees in Exercise 8.2 Q1, which theorem is applied?
mcqs.why: Angle A = 60 degrees is less than 90 degrees, so it is acute. Theorem 2 therefore applies: the square on the opposite side is diminished by twice the rectangle, i.e. the formula carries a MINUS 2(AB)(projection) term.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm, AC = 9 cm and D is the midpoint of AC. AD equals:
mcqs.why: D is the midpoint of AC, so formula AD = AC/2. Step 1: AC = 9 cm. Step 2: AD = 9/2 = 4.5 cm. This AD is the half-side used in Apollonius' Theorem for median BD.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm, AC = 9 cm, D midpoint of AC. (BD)^2 equals:
In triangle ABC, AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm, AC = 9 cm, D midpoint of AC. The median BD equals:
mcqs.why: By Apollonius' Theorem, (BD)^2 = 29.75 (from 100 = 40.5 + 2(BD)^2). Step 1: Take the square root: BD = sqrt(29.75). Step 2: sqrt(29.75) = 5.45 cm approx.

mcqs.q: Which theorem is used to find median BD in Exercise 8.2 Q2?
mcqs.why: BD is a median because D is the midpoint of AC. Apollonius' Theorem relates the squares on the two sides AB and BC to twice the square on half of AC and twice the square on the median BD, which is exactly the relation needed to solve for BD.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram ABCD, (AC)^2 + (BD)^2 equals:
mcqs.why: In a parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other, so in triangle ABC, BO is a median to AC. By Apollonius: (AB)^2 + (BC)^2 = 2(AO)^2 + 2(BO)^2 = (AC)^2/2 + (BD)^2/2. Multiplying by 2 gives (AC)^2 + (BD)^2 = 2[(AB)^2 + (BC)^2].

mcqs.q: In the proof for parallelogram ABCD, the diagonals AC and BD meet at O. O is:
mcqs.why: A property used in the proof is that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. Therefore their intersection O is the midpoint of AC and also the midpoint of BD, so AO = AC/2 and BO = BD/2, which allows Apollonius' Theorem to be applied in triangle ABC.

mcqs.q: In the parallelogram proof, BO in triangle ABC is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: O is the midpoint of AC because the diagonals bisect each other. Step 2: A line from vertex B to the midpoint of the opposite side AC is by definition a median. So BO is a median to side AC in triangle ABC, and Apollonius' Theorem applies to it.

lessons.title: Miscellaneous Exercise 8
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 In triangle ABC, angle A = 60 deg. Prove that (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - (AB).(AC)

Step 1: Angle A is acute, so by Theorem 2: (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - 2(AB)(projection of AC on AB).

Step 2: Projection of AC on AB = AC x cos 60 = AC x (1/2) = AC/2.

Step 3: (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - 2(AB)(AC/2) = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - (AB)(AC). Proved.

Q2 In triangle ABC, angle A = 45 deg. Prove that (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - sqrt(2)(AB).(AC)

Step 1: By Theorem 2: (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - 2(AB)(projection of AC on AB).

Step 2: Projection of AC on AB = AC x cos 45 = AC/sqrt(2).

Step 3: (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - 2(AB)(AC/sqrt(2)) = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - sqrt(2)(AB)(AC). Proved.

Q3 In triangle ABC, calculate BC when AB = 5 cm, AC = 4 cm, angle A = 60 deg

Step 1: By Theorem 2 (angle A acute): (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - 2(AB)(projection of AC on AB).

Step 2: Projection of AC on AB = AC x cos 60 = 4 x (1/2) = 2 cm.

Step 3: (BC)^2 = 25 + 16 - 2(5)(2) = 41 - 20 = 21.

Step 4: BC = sqrt(21) = 4.58 cm (approx).

Answer: BC = sqrt(21) cm (4.58 cm).

Q4 In triangle ABC, calculate AC when AB = 5 cm, BC = 4sqrt(2) cm, angle B = 45 deg

Step 1: Angle B is acute, so by Theorem 2: (AC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (BC)^2 - 2(BC)(projection of AB on BC).

Step 2: Projection of AB on BC = AB x cos 45 = 5/sqrt(2) cm.

Step 3: (AC)^2 = 25 + (4sqrt(2))^2 - 2(4sqrt(2))(5/sqrt(2)) = 25 + 32 - 40 = 17.

Step 4: AC = sqrt(17) = 4.12 cm (approx).

Answer: AC = sqrt(17) cm (4.12 cm).

Q5 In a triangle ABC, BC = 21 cm, AC = 17 cm, AB = 10 cm. Measure the length of projection of AC upon BC

Step 1: Let p be the projection of AC on BC (the foot of the perpendicular from A divides BC). By Theorem 2 applied at angle C: (AB)^2 = (AC)^2 + (BC)^2 - 2(BC)(p).

Step 2: Substitute: 10^2 = 17^2 + 21^2 - 2(21)p, i.e. 100 = 289 + 441 - 42p.

Step 3: 42p = 730 - 100 = 630, so p = 15 cm.

Answer: The projection of AC upon BC is 15 cm.

Q6 In a triangle ABC, BC = 21 cm, AC = 17 cm, AB = 10 cm. Calculate the projection of AB upon BC

Step 1: Let p be the projection of AB on BC. By Theorem 2 applied at angle B: (AC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (BC)^2 - 2(BC)(p).

Step 2: Substitute: 17^2 = 10^2 + 21^2 - 2(21)p, i.e. 289 = 100 + 441 - 42p.

Step 3: 42p = 541 - 289 = 252, so p = 6 cm.

Answer: The projection of AB upon BC is 6 cm. (Check with Q5: 15 + 6 = 21 = BC, as the foot of the altitude lies between B and C.)

Q7 In triangle ABC, a = 17, b = 15 and c = 8 cm. Find angle A (a, b, c are the sides opposite to A, B, C respectively)

Step 1: By Theorem 2 (cosine form): (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - 2(AB)(AC) cos A, i.e. a^2 = c^2 + b^2 - 2bc cos A.

Step 2: Substitute: 17^2 = 8^2 + 15^2 - 2(8)(15) cos A, i.e. 289 = 64 + 225 - 240 cos A = 289 - 240 cos A.

Step 3: 240 cos A = 0, so cos A = 0.

Answer: Angle A = 90 deg (the triangle is right-angled at A).

Q8 In triangle ABC, a = 17, b = 15 and c = 8 cm. Find angle B

Step 1: By the cosine form of Theorem 2 at angle B: b^2 = a^2 + c^2 - 2ac cos B.

Step 2: Substitute: 15^2 = 17^2 + 8^2 - 2(17)(8) cos B, i.e. 225 = 289 + 64 - 272 cos B = 353 - 272 cos B.

Step 3: 272 cos B = 353 - 225 = 128, so cos B = 128/272 = 8/17 = 0.4706.

Step 4: Angle B = cos^-1(0.4706) = 61.9 deg (approx).

Answer: Angle B = 61.9 degrees.

Q9 Whether the triangle with sides 5 cm, 7 cm, 8 cm is acute, obtuse or right angled

Step 1: Test the largest side (8 cm) against the other two: 8^2 = 64; 5^2 + 7^2 = 25 + 49 = 74.

Step 2: Since 64 < 74, the angle opposite the largest side is acute (by Theorems 1-2 comparison). The other angles, opposite smaller sides, are also acute.

Answer: The triangle is acute-angled.

Q10 Whether the triangle with sides 8 cm, 15 cm, 17 cm is acute, obtuse or right angled

Step 1: Test the largest side: 17^2 = 289; 8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289.

Step 2: Since 17^2 = 8^2 + 15^2 exactly, by the converse of Pythagoras' theorem the angle opposite the 17 cm side is a right angle.

Answer: The triangle is right-angled.

lessons.title: Theorems of Unit 9
lessons.notes_html:
Theorem 1 (9.1(i)) One and only one circle can pass through three non-collinear points

Given: A, B and C are three non-collinear points in a plane.

To prove: One and only one circle can pass through the three non-collinear points A, B and C.

Construction: Join A with B and B with C. Draw DF, the perpendicular bisector of AB, and HK, the perpendicular bisector of BC. The two bisectors are not parallel (A, B, C are non-collinear), so they intersect at a point O. Also join A, B and C with point O.

Proof:

Step 1: Every point on DF is equidistant from A and B (DF is the perpendicular bisector of AB). In particular OA = OB ... (i)

Step 2: Similarly every point on HK is equidistant from B and C. In particular OB = OC ... (ii)

Step 3: From (i) and (ii), OA = OB = OC; O is the only point common to DF and HK which is equidistant from A, B and C.

Step 4: Hence a circle with centre O and radius OA passes through A, B and C, and since O is unique, this circle is the only one. Proved.

Theorem 2 (9.1(ii)) A straight line, drawn from the centre of a circle to bisect a chord (which is not a diameter), is perpendicular to the chord

Given: M is the mid-point of any chord AB of a circle with centre O, where chord AB is not the diameter of the circle.

To prove: OM is perpendicular to the chord AB.

Construction: Join A and B with centre O. Write angle 1 = angle OMA and angle 2 = angle OMB as in the figure.

Proof:

Step 1: In triangles OAM and OBM: OA = OB (radii of the same circle); AM = BM (given, M is the midpoint); OM = OM (common).

Step 2: Therefore triangle OAM is congruent to triangle OBM (S.S.S = S.S.S), so angle 1 = angle 2 ... (i) (corresponding angles of congruent triangles).

Step 3: angle 1 + angle 2 = angle AMB = 180 deg (adjacent supplementary angles on the straight line AB) ... (ii)

Step 4: From (i) and (ii): angle 1 = angle 2 = 90 deg, i.e. OM is perpendicular to AB. Proved.

Theorem 3 (9.1(iii)) Perpendicular from the centre of a circle on a chord bisects it

Given: AB is the chord of a circle with centre O, so that OM is perpendicular to chord AB.

To prove: M is the mid-point of chord AB, i.e. AM = BM.

Construction: Join A and B with centre O.

Proof:

Step 1: In right triangles OAM and OBM: angle OMA = angle OMB = 90 deg (given); hypotenuse OA = hypotenuse OB (radii of the same circle); OM = OM (common).

Step 2: Therefore triangle OAM is congruent to triangle OBM (H.S = H.S in right triangles).

Step 3: Hence AM = BM (corresponding sides of congruent triangles), i.e. OM bisects the chord AB. Proved.

Corollary 1: The perpendicular bisector of the chord of a circle passes through the centre of the circle.

Corollary 2: The diameter of a circle passes through the mid-points of two parallel chords of the circle.

Theorem 4 (9.1(iv)) If two chords of a circle are congruent then they will be equidistant from the centre

Given: AB and CD are two equal chords of a circle with centre O, with OH perpendicular to AB and OK perpendicular to CD.

To prove: OH = OK.

Construction: Join O with A and O with C, giving right triangles OAH and OCK.

Proof:

Step 1: OH bisects chord AB (Theorem 3, perpendicular from centre), so AH = (1/2)AB ... (i)

Step 2: Similarly OK bisects chord CD, so CK = (1/2)CD ... (ii)

Step 3: But AB = CD (given) ... (iii), so from (i), (ii), (iii): AH = CK ... (iv)

Step 4: In right triangles OAH and OCK: hypotenuse OA = hypotenuse OC (radii), AH = CK (proved in (iv)), so triangle OAH is congruent to triangle OCK (H.S postulate).

Step 5: Hence OH = OK. Proved.

Theorem 5 (9.1(v)) Two chords of a circle which are equidistant from the centre, are congruent

Given: AB and CD are two chords of a circle with centre O. OH is perpendicular to AB and OK is perpendicular to CD, so that OH = OK.

To prove: AB = CD.

Construction: Join A and C with O, forming right triangles OAH and OCK.

Proof:

Step 1: In right triangles OAH and OCK: hypotenuse OA = hypotenuse OC (radii of the same circle); OH = OK (given). So triangle OAH is congruent to triangle OCK (H.S postulate), giving AH = CK ... (i) (corresponding sides).

Step 2: AH = (1/2)AB, because OH is perpendicular to chord AB (Theorem 3) ... (ii)

Step 3: Similarly CK = (1/2)CD ... (iii)

Step 4: From (i), (ii), (iii): (1/2)AB = (1/2)CD, so AB = CD. Proved.

Theorem 6 (Example of Unit 9) The diameter of a circle is the longest chord / the largest chord in a circle is the diameter

Given: AB is a chord and CD is the diameter of a circle with centre O.

To prove: If AB and CD are distinct, then CD > AB.

Construction: Join O with A and O with B to form triangle OAB.

Proof:

Step 1: In triangle OAB, the sum of two sides is greater than the third side: OA + OB > AB ... (i)

Step 2: OA and OB are radii of the same circle, and OA + OB = CD (the diameter is two radii) ... (ii)

Step 3: From (i) and (ii): CD > AB. Hence the diameter is greater than any other chord of the circle; the largest chord in a circle is the diameter. Proved.

mcqs.q: Through three non-collinear points, how many circles can pass?
mcqs.why: Theorem 9.1(i) states that one and only one circle can pass through three non-collinear points. The perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meet at a unique point O with OA = OB = OC.

mcqs.q: A straight line drawn from the centre of a circle to bisect a chord which is not a diameter is:
