mcqs.why: Theorem 9.1(ii) proves this. Triangles OAM and OBM are congruent by S.S.S., so the two adjacent angles at M are equal and sum to 180 degrees, hence each is 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle on a chord:
mcqs.why: Theorem 9.1(iii) proves that the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. Right triangles OAM and OBM are congruent by H.S., so AM = BM.

mcqs.q: If two chords of a circle are congruent, then they are:
options: At different distances from the centre
mcqs.why: Theorem 9.1(iv) proves that congruent chords are equidistant from the centre. With OH perpendicular to AB and OK perpendicular to CD, triangles OAH and OCK are congruent by H.S., so OH = OK.

mcqs.q: Two chords of a circle which are equidistant from the centre are:
mcqs.why: Theorem 9.1(v) is the converse of Theorem 9.1(iv). If OH = OK then triangles OAH and OCK are congruent by H.S., giving AH = CK, and therefore AB = 2AH = 2CK = CD.

mcqs.q: The largest chord in a circle is the:
mcqs.why: In triangle OAB, OA + OB > AB by the triangle inequality. Formula inside solution: OA + OB = radius + radius = diameter, so diameter > AB for every other chord AB.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 9.1(i), the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC intersect at one point because A, B and C are:
mcqs.why: Because A, B and C are non-collinear, the perpendicular bisectors DF and HK are not parallel, so they intersect at a unique point O which is equidistant from A, B and C.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 9.1(ii), triangles OAM and OBM are proved congruent by:
mcqs.why: OA = OB as radii, AM = BM because M is the midpoint of the chord, and OM is common. These are three equal sides, so the congruence used is S.S.S. = S.S.S.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 9.1(iii), right triangles OAM and OBM are proved congruent by:
mcqs.why: Both triangles are right-angled at M, their hypotenuses OA and OB are equal radii, and OM is common. This is the H.S. postulate for right-angled triangles.

mcqs.q: Corollary 1 of Theorem 9.1(iii) states that the perpendicular bisector of a chord of a circle passes through the:
mcqs.why: Corollary 1 states directly that the perpendicular bisector of the chord of a circle passes through the centre of the circle, which also appears as a book MCQ in Miscellaneous Exercise 9.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Prove that the diameters of a circle bisect each other

Step 1: Let AC and BD be two diameters of a circle with centre O.

Step 2: Every diameter passes through the centre O, and O is the midpoint of each diameter because OA = OC and OB = OD (radii of the same circle).

Step 3: So the two diameters meet at O, and each is bisected at O.

Hence the diameters of a circle bisect each other. Proved.

Q2 Two chords of a circle do not pass through the centre. Prove that they cannot bisect each other

Step 1: Suppose, if possible, that two chords AB and CD (neither passing through the centre O) bisect each other at a point E.

Step 2: E is then the midpoint of chord AB, so by Theorem 2 the line OE from the centre to E is perpendicular to AB.

Step 3: E is also the midpoint of chord CD, so by Theorem 2 the same line OE is perpendicular to CD.

Step 4: But through one point E only one line can be drawn perpendicular to OE; hence AB and CD would be the same line, contradicting that they are two different chords.

Hence two chords not passing through the centre cannot bisect each other. Proved.

Q3 If the length of the chord AB = 8 cm and its distance from the centre is 3 cm, then find the diameter of such a circle

Step 1: The perpendicular from the centre O to the chord meets it at its midpoint M (Theorem 3), so AM = 8/2 = 4 cm and OM = 3 cm.

Step 2: In right triangle OAM, OA is the radius: OA^2 = AM^2 + OM^2 = 16 + 9 = 25 (Pythagoras).

Step 3: Radius OA = 5 cm.

Step 4: Diameter = 2 x 5 = 10 cm.

Answer: Diameter = 10 cm.

Q4 Calculate the length of a chord which stands at a distance 5 cm from the centre of a circle whose radius is 9 cm

Step 1: Let M be the foot of the perpendicular from centre O to the chord AB. Then OM = 5 cm and OA = 9 cm (radius); M bisects AB (Theorem 3).

Step 2: In right triangle OAM: AM^2 = OA^2 - OM^2 = 81 - 25 = 56, so AM = sqrt(56) = 2sqrt(14) cm.

Step 3: Chord AB = 2 x AM = 4sqrt(14) = 14.97 cm (approx).

Answer: Chord = 4sqrt(14) cm (about 14.97 cm).

mcqs.q: The diameters of a circle bisect each other at the:
mcqs.why: Every diameter passes through the centre O, and O is the midpoint of each diameter because OA = OC and OB = OD are radii of the same circle, so the diameters bisect each other at O.

mcqs.q: Two chords of a circle which do not pass through the centre:
mcqs.why: If they bisected each other at E, line OE would be perpendicular to both chords by Theorem 9.1(ii). Only one perpendicular to OE can pass through E, so the chords would coincide, a contradiction.

mcqs.q: A chord AB = 8 cm is at a distance of 3 cm from the centre. The diameter of the circle is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: radius^2 = (half chord)^2 + (distance)^2. Step 1: AM = 8/2 = 4 cm. Step 2: OA^2 = 4^2 + 3^2 = 16 + 9 = 25. Step 3: radius OA = 5 cm. Step 4: diameter = 2 x 5 = 10 cm.

mcqs.q: A chord stands at a distance of 5 cm from the centre of a circle whose radius is 9 cm. The length of the chord is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: AM^2 = OA^2 - OM^2. Step 1: AM^2 = 9^2 - 5^2 = 81 - 25 = 56. Step 2: AM = square root 56 = 2 square root 14 cm. Step 3: chord AB = 2 x AM = 4 square root 14 cm, about 14.97 cm.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 9.1 Q3, with chord AB = 8 cm, the segment AM where M is the foot of the perpendicular from the centre is:
mcqs.why: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord by Theorem 9.1(iii). Formula: AM = AB/2 = 8/2 = 4 cm, which is then used with OM = 3 cm in right triangle OAM.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 9.1 Q4, with radius 9 cm and distance 5 cm, the half-chord AM is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: AM^2 = OA^2 - OM^2. Step 1: AM^2 = 81 - 25 = 56. Step 2: AM = square root 56. Step 3: square root 56 = square root (4 x 14) = 2 square root 14 cm.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 9.1 Q2, the contradiction arises because through one point E:
options: Only one line can be drawn perpendicular to OE
mcqs.why: E would be the midpoint of both chords, so OE would be perpendicular to AB and also perpendicular to CD. Through one point E only one line can be drawn perpendicular to OE, forcing AB and CD to be the same line.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 9.1 Q1, O is the midpoint of diameter AC because:
options: OA = OC as radii of the same circle
A and C are non-collinear points
mcqs.why: A diameter passes through the centre O and its endpoints are on the circle, so OA and OC are both radii and are equal. Hence O divides AC into two equal parts and is its midpoint.

mcqs.q: A chord of length 8 cm at distance 3 cm from the centre belongs to a circle of radius:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: radius^2 = (AB/2)^2 + distance^2. Step 1: half chord = 4 cm. Step 2: radius^2 = 16 + 9 = 25. Step 3: radius = square root 25 = 5 cm.

mcqs.q: Exercise 9.1 Q3 and Q4 both use which theorem to say the perpendicular from the centre meets the chord at its midpoint?
mcqs.why: Theorem 9.1(iii) states that the perpendicular from the centre of a circle on a chord bisects it. That is why AM is half of AB in both numerical questions.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Two equal chords of a circle intersect; show that the segments of the one are equal corresponding to the segments of the other

Given: Equal chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O intersect each other at E.

To prove: AE = CE and BE = DE.

Construction: Draw OH perpendicular to AB and OK perpendicular to CD; join O with E.

Proof:

Step 1: The equal chords are equidistant from the centre (Theorem 4): OH = OK.

Step 2: In right triangles OHE and OKE: hypotenuse OE is common, OH = OK, so the triangles are congruent (H.S), giving HE = KE ... (i)

Step 3: OH and OK bisect the chords (Theorem 3): AH = (1/2)AB and CK = (1/2)CD; since AB = CD, AH = CK ... (ii)

Step 4: From (i) and (ii), adding or subtracting the equal segments as the figure requires: AE = AH - HE = CK - KE = CE, and BE = DE.

Hence the segments of the one chord are equal corresponding to the segments of the other. Proved.

Q2 AB is the chord of a circle and the diameter CD is the perpendicular bisector of AB. Prove that AC = BC

Step 1: Let the diameter CD meet the chord AB at E. By hypothesis E is the midpoint of AB (AE = EB) and CD is perpendicular to AB (angle AEC = angle BEC = 90 deg).

Step 2: In triangles AEC and BEC: AE = EB (just shown); angle AEC = angle BEC = 90 deg; EC = EC (common).

Step 3: Therefore triangle AEC is congruent to triangle BEC (S.A.S = S.A.S).

Step 4: Hence AC = BC (corresponding sides of congruent triangles). Proved.

Q3 As shown in the figure, find the distance between two parallel chords AB and CD (chord AB = 6 cm above the centre, chord CD = 8 cm below the centre, radius = 5 cm)

Step 1: Distance of chord AB from the centre: the perpendicular from O bisects AB, so half of AB = 3 cm; distance d1 satisfies d1^2 = 5^2 - 3^2 = 25 - 9 = 16, so d1 = 4 cm.

Step 2: Distance of chord CD from the centre: half of CD = 4 cm; d2^2 = 5^2 - 4^2 = 25 - 16 = 9, so d2 = 3 cm.

Step 3: The chords lie on opposite sides of the centre (see the figure), so the distance between them = d1 + d2 = 4 + 3 = 7 cm.

Answer: 7 cm.

mcqs.q: Two equal chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at E. Then the segments satisfy:
mcqs.why: Equal chords are equidistant from the centre, so OH = OK. Congruent right triangles OHE and OKE give HE = KE, and AH = CK as halves of equal chords, hence AE = CE and BE = DE.

mcqs.q: AB is a chord and diameter CD is the perpendicular bisector of AB. Then AC is equal to:
mcqs.why: Triangles AEC and BEC are congruent by S.A.S.: AE = EB, both angles at E are 90 degrees, and EC is common. Therefore corresponding sides AC and BC are equal.

mcqs.q: Chords AB = 6 cm and CD = 8 cm lie on opposite sides of the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. The distance between the chords is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: distance^2 = radius^2 - (half chord)^2. Step 1: d1^2 = 25 - 9 = 16, so d1 = 4 cm. Step 2: d2^2 = 25 - 16 = 9, so d2 = 3 cm. Step 3: opposite sides, distance = 4 + 3 = 7 cm.

mcqs.q: For a chord of 6 cm in a circle of radius 5 cm, its distance from the centre is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: d^2 = r^2 - (half chord)^2. Step 1: half chord = 6/2 = 3 cm. Step 2: d^2 = 5^2 - 3^2 = 25 - 9 = 16. Step 3: d = square root 16 = 4 cm.

mcqs.q: For a chord of 8 cm in a circle of radius 5 cm, its distance from the centre is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: d^2 = r^2 - (half chord)^2. Step 1: half chord = 8/2 = 4 cm. Step 2: d^2 = 5^2 - 4^2 = 25 - 16 = 9. Step 3: d = square root 9 = 3 cm.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 9.2 Q1, OH = OK is obtained from which result about equal chords?
options: Equal chords are equidistant from the centre
Equal chords pass through the centre
mcqs.why: Theorem 9.1(iv) of Unit 9 states that if two chords of a circle are congruent then they are equidistant from the centre, so the perpendicular distances OH and OK are equal.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 9.2 Q1, right triangles OHE and OKE give HE = KE because they are congruent by:
mcqs.why: Hypotenuse OE is common to both right triangles and OH = OK because the equal chords are equidistant from the centre. Right triangles with equal hypotenuse and one side are congruent by H.S.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 9.2 Q2, triangles AEC and BEC are proved congruent by:
mcqs.why: AE = EB because E is the midpoint of AB, angle AEC = angle BEC = 90 degrees because CD is perpendicular to AB, and EC is common. Two sides and the included angle give S.A.S.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 9.2 Q3, half of chord AB = 6 cm used in the calculation is:
mcqs.why: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord by Theorem 9.1(iii). Formula: half chord = AB/2 = 6/2 = 3 cm, used in d1^2 = 5^2 - 3^2.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 9.2 Q1, AH = (1/2)AB holds because OH is:
mcqs.why: OH is drawn perpendicular to chord AB. By Theorem 9.1(iii), the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so H is the midpoint of AB and AH = (1/2)AB.

lessons.title: Miscellaneous Exercise 9
lessons.notes_html:
MCQ (i) In the circular figure, ADB is called (A and B are the ends of a chord, D a point on the circle below the chord)

(a) an arc
(b) a secant
(c) a chord
(d) a diameter
Correct answer: an arc

MCQ (ii) In the circular figure, arc ACB is called (A and B are the ends of a chord, C a point on the circle above)

(a) an arc
(b) a secant
(c) a chord
(d) a diameter
Correct answer: an arc

MCQ (iii) In the circular figure, AOB is called (O the centre, A and B on the circle, AOB a straight line)

(a) an arc
(b) a secant
(c) a chord
(d) a diameter
Correct answer: a diameter

MCQ (iv) In a circular figure, two chords AB and CD are equidistant from the centre. They will be

(a) parallel
(b) non congruent
(c) congruent
(d) perpendicular
Correct answer: congruent

MCQ (v) Radii of a circle are

(a) all equal
(b) double of the diameter
(c) all unequal
(d) half of any chord
Correct answer: all equal

MCQ (vi) A chord passing through the centre of a circle is called

(a) radius
(b) diameter
(c) circumference
(d) secant
Correct answer: diameter

MCQ (vii) Right bisector of the chord of a circle always passes through the

(a) radius
(b) circumference
(c) centre
(d) diameter
Correct answer: centre

MCQ (viii) The circular region bounded by two radii and the corresponding arc is called

(a) circumference of a circle
(b) sector of a circle
(c) diameter of a circle
(d) segment of a circle
Correct answer: sector of a circle

MCQ (ix) The distance of any point of the circle to its centre is called

(a) radius
(b) diameter
(c) a chord
(d) an arc
Correct answer: radius

MCQ (x) Line segment joining any point of the circle to the centre is called

(a) circumference
(b) diameter
(c) radial segment
(d) perimeter
Correct answer: radial segment

MCQ (xi) Locus of a point in a plane equidistant from a fixed point is called

(a) radius
(b) circle
(c) circumference
(d) diameter
Correct answer: circle

MCQ (xii) The symbol for a triangle is denoted by

(a) angle sign
(b) triangle sign (Delta)
(c) perpendicular sign
(d) circle sign
Correct answer: triangle sign (Delta)

MCQ (xiii) A complete circle is divided into

(a) 90 degrees
(b) 180 degrees
(c) 270 degrees
(d) 360 degrees
Correct answer: 360 degrees

MCQ (xiv) Through how many non-collinear points can a circle pass?

(a) one
(b) two
(c) three
(d) none
Correct answer: three

Q2 Differentiate: (i) Differentiate between a circle and a circumference

A circle is the locus of a moving point in a plane which is always equidistant from a fixed point (the centre); it is the whole plane figure (the region). The circumference is only the boundary traced by the moving point, i.e. the perimeter of the circle, of length 2.pi.r. Diagram (in words): shade the whole disc for the circle; draw only the boundary ring for the circumference.

Q2 Differentiate: (ii) Differentiate between a chord and the diameter of a circle

A chord is a line segment joining any two points on the circumference; it need not pass through the centre. The diameter is the special chord that passes through the centre; it is the longest chord and is twice the radius. Diagram (in words): draw a circle, a slanted segment joining two boundary points off-centre for a chord, and a segment through the centre for the diameter.

Q2 Differentiate: (iii) Differentiate between a chord and an arc of a circle

A chord is a straight line segment joining two points of the circle. An arc is a portion (curved part) of the circumference between two points of the circle. Diagram (in words): between points A and B, the straight segment is the chord and the curved boundary from A to B is the arc.

Q2 Differentiate: (iv) Differentiate between minor arc and major arc of a circle

An arc smaller than a semicircle is called a minor arc; an arc larger than a semicircle is called a major arc. The two arcs between the same two points together make the complete circle (360 degrees). Diagram (in words): mark points A and B; the short curved path is the minor arc and the long way round is the major arc.

Q2 Differentiate: (v) Differentiate between interior and exterior of a circle

The interior of a circle is the set of all points whose distance from the centre is less than the radius. The exterior is the set of all points whose distance from the centre is greater than the radius. Points at distance exactly equal to the radius lie on the circle itself. Diagram (in words): shade the inside of the ring for the interior and the region outside the ring for the exterior.

Q2 Differentiate: (vi) Differentiate between a sector and a segment of a circle

A sector is the plane figure bounded by two radii and the arc intercepted between them (like a slice of pie, OAIB in the book figure). A segment is the portion of a circle bounded by a chord and its corresponding arc. Diagram (in words): for a sector draw two radii with the arc between them; for a segment draw a chord and shade the cap between the chord and the arc.

mcqs.q: In the circular figure, ADB is called (A and B are the ends of a chord, D is a point on the circle):
mcqs.why: ADB is the curved part of the circumference joining A and B through D. A curved portion of the circumference between two points is called an arc, as in book MCQ (i).

mcqs.q: In the circular figure, arc ACB is called (A and B are the ends of a chord, C is a point on the circle):
mcqs.why: ACB is a portion of the circumference between points A and B passing through C. By definition a portion of the circumference is an arc, as in book MCQ (ii).

mcqs.q: In the circular figure, AOB is called (O is the centre, A and B are on the circle and AOB is a straight line):
mcqs.why: AOB is a straight line through the centre joining two points on the circle. A chord passing through the centre is called a diameter, as in book MCQ (iii).

mcqs.q: In a circular figure, two chords AB and CD are equidistant from the centre. They will be:
mcqs.why: By Theorem 9.1(v), two chords of a circle which are equidistant from the centre are congruent. This is exactly book MCQ (iv) of Miscellaneous Exercise 9.

mcqs.q: Radii of a circle are:
mcqs.why: Every radius joins the centre to a point on the circle, and all points on the circle are at the same distance from the centre. Hence all radii of a circle are equal, book MCQ (v).

mcqs.q: A chord passing through the centre of a circle is called:
mcqs.why: A chord is a segment joining two points on the circle. The special chord that also passes through the centre is the diameter, which is the longest chord, book MCQ (vi).

mcqs.q: The right bisector of the chord of a circle always passes through the:
mcqs.why: This is Corollary 1 of Theorem 9.1(iii): the perpendicular bisector, also called the right bisector, of a chord of a circle passes through the centre, book MCQ (vii).

mcqs.q: The circular region bounded by two radii and the corresponding arc is called:
mcqs.why: A sector is the plane region bounded by two radii and the arc intercepted between them, like a slice of pie. A segment is instead bounded by a chord and its arc, book MCQ (viii).

mcqs.q: The distance of any point of the circle from its centre is called:
mcqs.why: By the definition of a circle, every point on it is at a fixed distance from the centre, and that fixed distance is called the radius of the circle, book MCQ (ix).

mcqs.q: A line segment joining any point of the circle to the centre is called:
mcqs.why: The segment from a point on the circle to the centre is called a radial segment, and its length is the radius of the circle, as in book MCQ (x).

mcqs.q: The locus of a point in a plane equidistant from a fixed point is called:
mcqs.why: A circle is defined as the locus of a moving point in a plane which is always equidistant from a fixed point, the centre, as stated in book MCQ (xi) and the Q2 differentiation.

mcqs.q: The symbol for a triangle is denoted by:
mcqs.why: In geometry notation a triangle is denoted by the Greek letter Delta, written as a small triangle symbol before the three vertex letters, as in book MCQ (xii).

mcqs.q: A complete circle is divided into:
mcqs.why: One complete revolution around the centre measures 360 degrees. The two arcs between the same two points together also make the complete circle of 360 degrees, book MCQ (xiii).

mcqs.q: Through how many non-collinear points can a circle pass?
mcqs.why: Theorem 9.1(i) proves that one and only one circle can pass through three non-collinear points, so the number of non-collinear points required is three, book MCQ (xiv).

mcqs.q: An arc smaller than a semicircle is called a:
mcqs.why: From Q2 differentiation: an arc smaller than a semicircle is called a minor arc, while an arc larger than a semicircle is called a major arc. Together the two arcs make the complete circle.

lessons.title: Theorems of Unit 10
lessons.notes_html:
Theorem 1 (10.1(i)) If a line is drawn perpendicular to a radial segment of a circle at its outer end point, it is tangent to the circle at that point

Given: A circle with centre O and OC is the radial segment. Line AB is perpendicular to OC at its outer end C.

To prove: Line AB is a tangent to the circle at C.

Construction: Take any point P other than C on line AB; join O with P.

Proof:

Step 1: In triangle OCP, angle OCP = 90 deg (line AB is perpendicular to OC, given), and angle OPC < 90 deg (an acute angle of a right-angled triangle).

Step 2: The greater angle has the greater side opposite to it, so OP > OC.

Step 3: OC is the radius; OP > radius means P is a point outside the circle.

Step 4: Similarly every point on line AB except C lies outside the circle. Hence line AB intersects the circle at the one point C only, i.e. line AB is a tangent to the circle at C. Proved.

Corollary: There can only be one perpendicular to the radial segment OC at the point C; hence one and only one tangent can be drawn to the circle at a given point C on its circumference.

Theorem 2 (10.1(ii)) The tangent to a circle and the radial segment joining the point of contact and the centre are perpendicular to each other

Given: In a circle with centre O, OC is a radius and line AB is the tangent to the circle at point C.

To prove: Line AB and radial segment OC are perpendicular to each other.

Construction: Take any point P other than C on the tangent line AB. Join O with P so that OP meets the circle at D.

Proof:

Step 1: Line AB is tangent at C, while OP cuts the circle at D, so OC = OD (radii of the same circle) ... (i)

Step 2: But OD < OP, because P is outside the circle ... (ii)

Step 3: From (i) and (ii): OC < OP. So the radius OC is the shortest of all lines that can be drawn from O to the tangent line AB.

Step 4: The shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance, so OC is perpendicular to AB. Proved.

Theorem 3 (10.1(iii)) Two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it, are equal in length

Given: Two tangents PA and PB are drawn from an external point P to the circle with centre O (A and B are the points of contact).

To prove: PA = PB.

Construction: Join O with A, B and P, forming right triangles OAP and OBP.

Proof:

Step 1: In right triangles OAP and OBP: angle OAP = angle OBP = 90 deg (radius perpendicular to tangent, Theorem 2).

Step 2: Hypotenuse OP = hypotenuse OP (common); OA = OB (radii of the same circle).

Step 3: Therefore triangle OAP is congruent to triangle OBP (H.S = H.S).

Step 4: Hence PA = PB (corresponding sides). Proved.

Note: The length of a tangent is measured from the given point to the point of contact.

Corollary: OP is the right bisector of the chord of contact AB.

Theorem 4(A) (10.1(iv)) If two circles touch externally then the distance between their centres is equal to the sum of their radii

Given: Two circles with centres D and F respectively touch each other externally at point C, so that DC and FC are the radii of the two circles.

To prove: Point C lies on the join of centres D and F and DF = DC + CF.

Construction: Draw line ACB as a common tangent to the pair of circles at C.

Proof:

Step 1: Both circles touch externally at C, CD is a radial segment and ACB is the common tangent, so angle ACD = 90 deg (radius perpendicular to tangent) ... (i)

Step 2: Similarly CF is a radial segment of the second circle and ACB the common tangent, so angle ACF = 90 deg ... (ii)

Step 3: Adding (i) and (ii): angle ACD + angle ACF = 180 deg, i.e. angle DCF = 180 deg (sum of supplementary adjacent angles).

Step 4: Hence DCF is a straight line segment with C between D and F, and DF = DC + CF = sum of the radii. Proved.

Theorem 4(B) (10.1(v)) If two circles touch each other internally, then the point of contact lies on the line segment through their centres and the distance between their centres is equal to the difference of their radii

Given: Two circles with centres D and F touch each other internally at point C, so that DC and FC are the radii of the two circles.

To prove: Point C lies on the join of centres D and F (extended) and DF = DC - FC.

Construction: Draw line ACB as a common tangent to the pair of circles at C.

Proof:

Step 1: Both circles touch internally at C and ACB is the common tangent; DC is the radial segment of the first circle, so angle ACD = 90 deg ... (i)

Step 2: Similarly ACB is the common tangent and FC the radial segment of the second circle, so angle ACF = 90 deg ... (ii)

Step 3: From (i) and (ii), angle ACD = angle ACF = 90 deg; the two angles coincide, with point F between D and C. Hence DC = DF + FC.

Step 4: Therefore DF = DC - FC = difference of the radii. Proved.

Example 1 of Unit 10: AB is a diameter of a given circle with centre O. Tangents are drawn at the end points A and B. Show that the two tangents are parallel

Step 1: The radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent at A (Theorem 2), so the tangent at A makes a right angle with AB.

Step 2: Similarly the radius OB is perpendicular to the tangent at B, so the tangent at B also makes a right angle with AB.

Step 3: Two lines perpendicular to the same line AB are parallel to each other.

Hence the tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel. Proved.

Example 2 of Unit 10: In a circle, the tangents drawn at the ends of a chord make equal angles with that chord

Given: AB is the chord of a circle with centre O. Line CAD is the tangent at point A and line EBF is the tangent at point B.

To prove: angle BAD = angle ABF.

Construction: Join O with A and B to form triangle OAB; write angle 1 = OAB, angle 2 = OBA, angle 3 = OAD and angle 4 = OBF as in the figure.

Proof:

Step 1: In triangle OAB, OA = OB (radii of the same circle), so the angles opposite the equal sides are equal: angle 1 = angle 2 ... (i)

Step 2: OA is perpendicular to the tangent CD (radius to tangent), so angle 3 = angle OAD = 90 deg ... (ii)

Step 3: Similarly OB is perpendicular to the tangent EF, so angle 4 = angle OBF = 90 deg ... (iii). Hence angle 3 = angle 4 ... (iv)

Step 4: Adding (i) and (iv): angle 1 + angle 3 = angle 2 + angle 4, i.e. angle BAD = angle ABF. Proved.

mcqs.q: A line drawn perpendicular to a radial segment of a circle at its outer end point is:
options: A tangent to the circle at that point
mcqs.why: Theorem 10.1(i) proves this: for any other point P on the line, OP > OC, so P lies outside the circle. The line meets the circle only at C and is therefore a tangent at C.

mcqs.q: The tangent to a circle and the radial segment joining the point of contact and the centre are:
mcqs.why: Theorem 10.1(ii) proves that the radius OC is the shortest line from O to the tangent, and the shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance, so OC is perpendicular to the tangent.

mcqs.q: Two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are:
mcqs.why: Theorem 10.1(iii) proves PA = PB. Right triangles OAP and OBP are congruent by H.S., since OP is common and OA = OB are radii, so corresponding sides PA and PB are equal.

mcqs.q: If two circles touch externally, the distance between their centres is equal to:
mcqs.why: Theorem 10.1(iv) shows the point of contact C lies on the line of centres, with DF = DC + CF. Formula: distance between centres = r1 + r2 = sum of the radii.

mcqs.q: If two circles touch internally, the distance between their centres is equal to:
mcqs.why: Theorem 10.1(v) shows DC = DF + FC, so rearranging gives the formula DF = DC - FC, that is, distance between centres = difference of the radii.

mcqs.q: Tangents drawn at the end points of a diameter of a circle are:
mcqs.why: Each radius to an end of the diameter is perpendicular to its tangent by Theorem 10.1(ii), so both tangents are perpendicular to the same line AB. Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel.

mcqs.q: In a circle, the tangents drawn at the ends of a chord make with that chord:
mcqs.why: The example of Unit 10 proves angle BAD = angle ABF. Since OA = OB, base angles of triangle OAB are equal, and each radius is perpendicular to its tangent, adding the equal parts gives equal angles.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 10.1(i), OP > OC is concluded because in right triangle OCP:
options: The greater angle has the greater side opposite to it
mcqs.why: Angle OCP = 90 degrees is the greatest angle of triangle OCP and angle OPC is acute. The side opposite the greater angle is greater, so the side OP opposite the right angle exceeds OC.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 10.1(iii), right triangles OAP and OBP are congruent by:
mcqs.why: Both triangles are right-angled at A and B by Theorem 10.1(ii), hypotenuse OP is common, and OA = OB are radii of the same circle. This is the H.S. postulate.

mcqs.q: By the corollary of Theorem 10.1(i), at a given point C on the circumference of a circle:
options: Infinitely many tangents can be drawn
One and only one tangent can be drawn
mcqs.why: There can only be one perpendicular to the radial segment OC at the point C. Hence one and only one tangent can be drawn to the circle at a given point C on its circumference.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Prove that the tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter in a given circle must be parallel

Step 1: Let AB be a diameter of a circle with centre O, with tangents drawn at A and at B.

Step 2: By Theorem 2, the radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent at A; so the tangent at A is perpendicular to the line AB (since OA lies along AB).

Step 3: Similarly the radius OB is perpendicular to the tangent at B; so the tangent at B is also perpendicular to AB.

Step 4: Two straight lines both perpendicular to the same line AB are parallel to each other.

Hence the tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter are parallel. Proved.

Q2 The diameters of two concentric circles are 10 cm and 5 cm respectively. Look for (find) the length of any chord of the outer circle which touches the inner one. (Hint from the book: AB = 2x = 2.sqrt(25 - 6.25) = 2.sqrt(18.75), about 8.7 cm)

Step 1: Concentric circles share the same centre O. Outer radius = 10/2 = 5 cm; inner radius = 5/2 = 2.5 cm.

Step 2: Let AB be a chord of the outer circle touching the inner circle at C. The radius OC to the point of tangency is perpendicular to AB (Theorem 2), and the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so C is the midpoint of AB.

Step 3: In right triangle OCB (B on the outer circle): CB^2 = OB^2 - OC^2 = 25 - 6.25 = 18.75, so CB = sqrt(18.75) = 4.33 cm.

Step 4: AB = 2 x CB = 2sqrt(18.75) = 8.66 cm, about 8.7 cm.

Answer: The chord is about 8.7 cm long.

Q3 Lines AB and CD are the common tangents drawn to the pair of circles. If A and C are the points of tangency of the 1st circle while B and D are the points of tangency of the 2nd circle, then prove that AC is parallel to BD

Step 1: Let the centres of the two circles be O1 and O2. The radii to points of tangency are perpendicular to the tangents: O1A and O1C are perpendicular to the common tangents, and O2B and O2D are perpendicular to the common tangents.

Step 2: For the direct common tangent AB: O1A is perpendicular to AB and O2B is perpendicular to AB, with O1A and O2B on the same side; the figure O1ABO2 is a rectangle (both radii perpendicular to the same line and the line of centres perpendicular distance equal), so in particular the radii O1A and O2B are parallel and equal in direction.

Step 3: The same argument applied at C and D gives the radii O1C and O2D perpendicular to the tangent CD.

Step 4: The chord of contact directions: since the tangents at A and C make equal angles with the line of centres as those at B and D (corresponding radii are parallel), the segments AC and BD are equally inclined to the line of centres on the same side, hence AC is parallel to BD.

Hence AC // BD. Proved.

mcqs.q: The tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter in a given circle must be:
mcqs.why: By Theorem 10.1(ii) the radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent at A and radius OB is perpendicular to the tangent at B. Both tangents are perpendicular to AB, hence they are parallel.

mcqs.q: The diameters of two concentric circles are 10 cm and 5 cm. The length of any chord of the outer circle which touches the inner one is about:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: CB^2 = OB^2 - OC^2. Step 1: outer radius OB = 5 cm, inner radius OC = 2.5 cm. Step 2: CB^2 = 25 - 6.25 = 18.75. Step 3: CB = 4.33 cm. Step 4: AB = 2 x 4.33 = 8.66 cm, about 8.7 cm.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.1 Q2, the radius of the outer concentric circle is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: radius = diameter/2. Step 1: the outer diameter is given as 10 cm. Step 2: outer radius = 10/2 = 5 cm. This is OB in right triangle OCB.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.1 Q2, the radius of the inner concentric circle is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: radius = diameter/2. Step 1: the inner diameter is given as 5 cm. Step 2: inner radius = 5/2 = 2.5 cm. This is OC, the perpendicular distance from O to the chord.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.1 Q2, the half-chord CB is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: CB^2 = OB^2 - OC^2 by Pythagoras. Step 1: CB^2 = 5^2 - 2.5^2 = 25 - 6.25 = 18.75. Step 2: CB = square root 18.75 = 4.33 cm approximately.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.1 Q2, OC is perpendicular to chord AB because:
options: C is the midpoint of AB only
OC is the radius to the point where AB touches the inner circle
mcqs.why: AB touches the inner circle at C, so AB is a tangent to the inner circle at C. By Theorem 10.1(ii), the radial segment OC to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent AB.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.1 Q2, C is the midpoint of chord AB because:
options: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord
Tangents from a point are equal
mcqs.why: OC is perpendicular from the centre O to chord AB of the outer circle. By Unit 9 Theorem 3, the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so C is the midpoint and AB = 2CB.

mcqs.q: Lines AB and CD are common tangents to a pair of circles, with A, C points of tangency on the first circle and B, D on the second. Exercise 10.1 Q3 proves that:
options: AC is equal to the line of centres
mcqs.why: The radii to points of tangency are perpendicular to the common tangents, so corresponding radii are parallel and AC and BD are equally inclined to the line of centres on the same side, hence AC is parallel to BD.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.1 Q3, the radii O1A and O2B to the points of tangency are:
options: Parallel to the line of centres
Perpendicular to the common tangent AB
mcqs.why: By Theorem 10.1(ii), the radial segment joining the centre to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent. Hence both O1A and O2B are perpendicular to the common tangent AB.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.1 Q1, the tangent at A is perpendicular to line AB because:
options: OA lies along AB and the radius to a point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent
AB is a chord of maximum length
A is the centre of the circle
mcqs.why: OA is part of the diameter line AB. Theorem 10.1(ii) says the radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent at A, so the tangent at A is perpendicular to the whole line AB.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 AB and CD are two equal chords in a circle with centre O, and H and K are respectively the mid-points of the chords. Prove that HK makes equal angles with AB and CD

To prove: angle OHK... precisely, the line HK makes equal angles with the chords: the angle between HK and AB equals the angle between HK and CD.

Proof:

Step 1: H is the midpoint of chord AB, so by Theorem 2 of Unit 9, OH is perpendicular to AB. Similarly OK is perpendicular to CD.

Step 2: The chords are equal, so they are equidistant from the centre (Unit 9, Theorem 4): OH = OK.

Step 3: In triangle OHK, OH = OK, so the base angles are equal: angle OKH = angle OHK.

Step 4: The angle that HK makes with AB: since OH is perpendicular to AB, this angle = 90 deg - angle OHK. The angle that HK makes with CD = 90 deg - angle OKH.

Step 5: Since angle OHK = angle OKH, the two angles are equal.

Hence HK makes equal angles with AB and CD. Proved.

Q2 The radius of a circle is 2.5 cm. AB and CD are two chords 3.9 cm apart. If AB = 1.4 cm, then measure the other chord

Step 1: Distance of chord AB from the centre: the perpendicular from O bisects AB, so half of AB = 0.7 cm; d(AB)^2 = 2.5^2 - 0.7^2 = 6.25 - 0.49 = 5.76, so d(AB) = 2.4 cm.

Step 2: The two chords are 3.9 cm apart, so the distance of CD from the centre = 3.9 - 2.4 = 1.5 cm.

Step 3: Half of CD: sqrt(2.5^2 - 1.5^2) = sqrt(6.25 - 2.25) = sqrt(4) = 2 cm.

Step 4: CD = 2 x 2 = 4 cm.

Answer: The other chord CD measures 4 cm.

Q3 The radii of two intersecting circles are 10 cm and 8 cm. If the length of their common chord is 6 cm, then find the distance between the centres

Step 1: The line joining the centres bisects the common chord at right angles, so each half of the common chord is 3 cm.

Step 2: Distance from the first centre (radius 10) to the chord: sqrt(10^2 - 3^2) = sqrt(100 - 9) = sqrt(91) = 9.54 cm.

Step 3: Distance from the second centre (radius 8) to the chord: sqrt(8^2 - 3^2) = sqrt(64 - 9) = sqrt(55) = 7.42 cm.

Step 4: The circles intersect, so the centres lie on opposite sides of the common chord; distance between centres = 9.54 + 7.42 = 16.96 cm.

Answer: About 16.96 cm.

Q4 Show that the greatest chord in a circle is its diameter

Step 1: Let AB be any chord of a circle with centre O and let CD be a diameter.

Step 2: Join O with A and O with B, forming triangle OAB. By the triangle inequality (sum of two sides greater than the third): OA + OB > AB.

Step 3: OA + OB = radius + radius = diameter CD.

Step 4: Therefore CD > AB for every chord AB.

Hence the diameter is the greatest chord in a circle. Proved.

mcqs.q: AB and CD are two equal chords in a circle and H, K are their mid-points. The line HK makes with AB and CD:
mcqs.why: OH and OK are perpendicular to the chords and OH = OK since equal chords are equidistant from the centre. Base angles of triangle OHK are equal, so 90 degrees minus each gives equal angles with the chords.

mcqs.q: The radius of a circle is 2.5 cm. Chords AB and CD are 3.9 cm apart and AB = 1.4 cm. The length of CD is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: d^2 = r^2 - (half chord)^2. Step 1: d(AB)^2 = 6.25 - 0.49 = 5.76, d(AB) = 2.4 cm. Step 2: d(CD) = 3.9 - 2.4 = 1.5 cm. Step 3: half CD = square root(6.25 - 2.25) = 2 cm. Step 4: CD = 4 cm.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.2 Q2, the distance of chord AB = 1.4 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 2.5 cm is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: d^2 = r^2 - (AB/2)^2. Step 1: half of AB = 0.7 cm. Step 2: d^2 = 2.5^2 - 0.7^2 = 6.25 - 0.49 = 5.76. Step 3: d = square root 5.76 = 2.4 cm.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.2 Q2, the distance of chord CD from the centre is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Step 1: distance of AB from the centre is 2.4 cm, calculated from radius 2.5 cm and half-chord 0.7 cm. Step 2: the chords are 3.9 cm apart. Step 3: d(CD) = 3.9 - 2.4 = 1.5 cm.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.2 Q2, half the length of chord CD is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: (CD/2)^2 = r^2 - d^2. Step 1: (CD/2)^2 = 2.5^2 - 1.5^2 = 6.25 - 2.25 = 4. Step 2: CD/2 = square root 4 = 2 cm. Step 3: CD = 2 x 2 = 4 cm.

mcqs.q: The radii of two intersecting circles are 10 cm and 8 cm and their common chord is 6 cm. The distance between the centres is about:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: d = square root(r^2 - (half chord)^2). Step 1: d1 = square root(100 - 9) = square root 91 = 9.54 cm. Step 2: d2 = square root(64 - 9) = square root 55 = 7.42 cm. Step 3: distance = 9.54 + 7.42 = 16.96 cm.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.2 Q3, the distance from the centre of the circle of radius 10 cm to the common chord of length 6 cm is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: d^2 = r^2 - (half chord)^2. Step 1: half chord = 6/2 = 3 cm. Step 2: d^2 = 10^2 - 3^2 = 100 - 9 = 91. Step 3: d = square root 91 = 9.54 cm approximately.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.2 Q3, the distance from the centre of the circle of radius 8 cm to the common chord of length 6 cm is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: d^2 = r^2 - (half chord)^2. Step 1: half chord = 6/2 = 3 cm. Step 2: d^2 = 8^2 - 3^2 = 64 - 9 = 55. Step 3: d = square root 55 = 7.42 cm approximately.

mcqs.q: Exercise 10.2 Q4 shows that the greatest chord in a circle is its:
mcqs.why: For any chord AB, join O to A and B. By the triangle inequality OA + OB > AB, and OA + OB equals the diameter. Hence every chord is less than the diameter, so the diameter is the greatest chord.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 10.2 Q3, the line joining the centres of the two intersecting circles:
options: Is parallel to the common chord
Bisects the common chord at right angles
Is equal to the common chord
Passes through an endpoint of the chord
mcqs.why: The line of centres is the perpendicular bisector of the common chord of two intersecting circles. That is why each half of the common chord is 3 cm and right triangles are formed with each radius.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.3
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Two circles with radii 5 cm and 4 cm touch each other externally. Draw another circle with radius 2.5 cm touching the first pair, externally (construction)

Construction in words (the drawing is described step by step; see the flag in the manifest):

Step 1: Draw the two given circles with centres A (radius 5 cm) and B (radius 4 cm) touching externally, so AB = 5 + 4 = 9 cm (Theorem 4(A)).

Step 2: The required circle of radius 2.5 cm must touch both externally, so its centre C must satisfy CA = 5 + 2.5 = 7.5 cm and CB = 4 + 2.5 = 6.5 cm.

Step 3: With centre A and radius 7.5 cm draw an arc; with centre B and radius 6.5 cm draw another arc; let them intersect at C.

Step 4: With centre C and radius 2.5 cm draw the circle. It touches the first circle externally (CA = sum of radii 7.5) and the second externally (CB = 6.5). This is the required circle.

Q2 If the distance between the centres of two circles is the sum or the difference of their radii, they will touch each other (prove)

Case 1 (sum): Let the circles have centres D and F and radii r1 and r2, with DF = r1 + r2. Take the point C on segment DF with DC = r1; then CF = DF - DC = r2, so C lies on both circles. Every other point of the line of centres is at a distance from D different from r1 or from F different from r2, and the two circles meet at C only; hence they touch externally at C.

Case 2 (difference): Let DF = r1 - r2 (r1 > r2). Take C on the line DF extended beyond F with DC = r1; then FC = DC - DF = r1 - (r1 - r2) = r2, so C lies on both circles and is their only common point; hence they touch internally at C.

In both cases the circles touch each other. Proved (converse of Theorem 4).

mcqs.q: Two circles of radii 5 cm and 4 cm touch each other externally. The distance between their centres is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula for external touching: distance = sum of radii. Step 1: radii are 5 cm and 4 cm. Step 2: AB = 5 + 4 = 9 cm, by Theorem 10.1(iv).

mcqs.q: A circle of radius 2.5 cm is to touch a circle of radius 5 cm externally. The distance of its centre C from the centre A of the 5 cm circle must be:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: CA = sum of radii for external touching. Step 1: radii are 5 cm and 2.5 cm. Step 2: CA = 5 + 2.5 = 7.5 cm. An arc of this radius is drawn from A in the construction.

mcqs.q: A circle of radius 2.5 cm is to touch a circle of radius 4 cm externally. The distance of its centre C from the centre B of the 4 cm circle must be:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: CB = sum of radii for external touching. Step 1: radii are 4 cm and 2.5 cm. Step 2: CB = 4 + 2.5 = 6.5 cm. An arc of this radius is drawn from B in the construction.

mcqs.q: If the distance between the centres of two circles is the sum of their radii, the circles:
mcqs.why: Exercise 10.3 Q2 proves the converse of Theorem 10.1(iv): if DF = r1 + r2, the point C on DF with DC = r1 also satisfies CF = r2, so C lies on both circles and they touch externally.

mcqs.q: If the distance between the centres of two circles is the difference of their radii, the circles:
mcqs.why: Exercise 10.3 Q2 proves that if DF = r1 - r2 with r1 greater than r2, a point C on DF extended lies on both circles and is their only common point, so they touch internally.

mcqs.q: Exercise 10.3 Q2 is the converse of which theorem of Unit 10?
mcqs.why: Theorems 10.1(iv) and (v) say touching circles have centre distance equal to the sum or difference of radii. Exercise 10.3 Q2 proves the reverse: that centre distance forces the circles to touch.

mcqs.q: In the sum case of Exercise 10.3 Q2, point C on segment DF with DC = r1 satisfies CF equal to:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: CF = DF - DC. Step 1: DF = r1 + r2 and DC = r1. Step 2: CF = (r1 + r2) - r1 = r2. Hence C is at distance r2 from F and lies on the second circle also.

mcqs.q: In the difference case of Exercise 10.3 Q2, with DF = r1 - r2, the point of contact C lies:
options: On the line DF extended beyond F
mcqs.why: C is taken on the line DF extended beyond F with DC = r1. Then FC = DC - DF = r1 - (r1 - r2) = r2, so C lies on both circles and the touching is internal.

mcqs.q: In the construction of Exercise 10.3 Q1, the centre C of the required circle is found as the intersection of:
options: An arc of radius 7.5 cm from A and an arc of radius 6.5 cm from B
mcqs.why: The centre must be 7.5 cm from A and 6.5 cm from B for external touching with both circles. Drawing arcs of radii 7.5 cm and 6.5 cm from A and B, their intersection is C.

mcqs.q: The circle constructed in Exercise 10.3 Q1 has radius:
mcqs.why: The required circle is specified with radius 2.5 cm. Its centre C is located using CA = 7.5 cm and CB = 6.5 cm, and the circle drawn from C has radius 2.5 cm, touching both given circles externally.

lessons.title: Miscellaneous Exercise 10
lessons.notes_html:
MCQ (i) In the adjacent figure of the circle, the line PTQ is named as (T is the point where the line touches the circle)

(a) an arc
(b) a chord
(c) a tangent
(d) a secant
Correct answer: a tangent

MCQ (ii) In a circle with centre O, if OT is the radial segment and line PTQ is the tangent line, then

(a) OT is perpendicular to PQ
(b) OT is not perpendicular to PQ
(c) OT is parallel to PQ
(d) OT is the right bisector of PQ
Correct answer: OT is perpendicular to PQ

MCQ (iii) Find the semicircular area if pi = 3.1416 and OA = 20 cm (OA is the radius)

(a) 62.83 sq cm
(b) 314.16 sq cm
(c) 436.20 sq cm
(d) 628.32 sq cm
Correct answer: 628.32 sq cm

MCQ (iv) Find half the perimeter of a circle with centre O if pi = 3.1416 and OA = 20 cm

(a) 31.42 cm
(b) 62.832 cm
(c) 125.65 cm
(d) 188.50 cm
Correct answer: 62.832 cm

MCQ (v) A line which has two points in common with a circle is called

(a) sine of a circle
(b) cosine of a circle
(c) tangent of a circle
(d) secant of a circle
Correct answer: secant of a circle

MCQ (vi) A line which has only one point in common with a circle is called

(a) sine of a circle
(b) cosine of a circle
(c) tangent of a circle
(d) secant of a circle
Correct answer: tangent of a circle

MCQ (vii) Two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are _______ in length

(a) half
(b) equal
(c) double
(d) triple
Correct answer: equal

MCQ (viii) A circle has only one

(a) secant
(b) chord
(c) diameter
(d) centre
Correct answer: centre

MCQ (ix) A tangent line intersects the circle at

(a) three points
(b) two points
(c) a single point
(d) no point at all
Correct answer: a single point

MCQ (x) Tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are _______ to each other

(a) parallel
(b) non-parallel
(c) collinear
(d) perpendicular
Correct answer: parallel

MCQ (xi) The distance between the centres of two congruent touching circles externally is

(a) of zero length
(b) the radius of each circle
(c) the diameter of each circle
(d) twice the diameter of each circle
Correct answer: the diameter of each circle

MCQ (xii) In the adjacent circular figure with centre O and radius 5 cm, the length of the chord intercepted at 4 cm away from the centre of this circle is

(a) 4 cm
(b) 6 cm
(c) 7 cm
(d) 9 cm
Correct answer: 6 cm

MCQ (xiii) In the adjoining figure, there is a circle with centre O. If DC is parallel to diameter AB and angle AOC = 120 deg, then angle ACD is

(a) 40 deg
(b) 30 deg
(c) 50 deg
(d) 60 deg
Correct answer: 30 deg

mcqs.q: In the adjacent figure of the circle, the line PTQ is named as (T is the point where the line touches the circle):
mcqs.why: Line PTQ meets the circle at the single point T. A line which has only one point in common with a circle is called a tangent of the circle, book MCQ (i).

mcqs.q: In a circle with centre O, if OT is the radial segment and line PTQ is the tangent line, then:
options: OT is not perpendicular to PQ
OT is the right bisector of PQ
mcqs.why: By Theorem 10.1(ii), the tangent to a circle and the radial segment joining the point of contact and the centre are perpendicular to each other, book MCQ (ii).

mcqs.q: Find the semicircular area if pi = 3.1416 and OA = 20 cm, where OA is the radius:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: semicircular area = (1/2) x pi x r^2. Step 1: r = 20 cm, r^2 = 400. Step 2: area = 0.5 x 3.1416 x 400. Step 3: area = 3.1416 x 200 = 628.32 sq cm, book MCQ (iii).

mcqs.q: Find half the perimeter of a circle with centre O if pi = 3.1416 and OA = 20 cm:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: half perimeter = pi x r, half of circumference 2 pi r. Step 1: r = OA = 20 cm. Step 2: half perimeter = 3.1416 x 20 = 62.832 cm, book MCQ (iv).

mcqs.q: A line which has two points in common with a circle is called:
mcqs.why: A secant is a line that cuts the circle at two distinct points. A tangent, by contrast, has only one point in common with the circle, book MCQ (v).

mcqs.q: A line which has only one point in common with a circle is called:
mcqs.why: By definition, a line meeting the circle at exactly one point is a tangent of the circle, and that single point is the point of contact, book MCQ (vi).

mcqs.q: Two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are _______ in length:
mcqs.why: Theorem 10.1(iii) proves that two tangents drawn to a circle from an external point are equal in length, since right triangles OAP and OBP are congruent by H.S., book MCQ (vii).

mcqs.q: A tangent line intersects the circle at:
mcqs.why: A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point, the point of contact. Every other point of the tangent line lies outside the circle, as proved in Theorem 10.1(i), book MCQ (ix).

mcqs.q: Tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are _______ to each other:
mcqs.why: Each tangent is perpendicular to the diameter at its endpoint by Theorem 10.1(ii). Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel to each other, book MCQ (x).

mcqs.q: In a circle with centre O and radius 5 cm, the length of the chord intercepted at 4 cm away from the centre is:
mcqs.why: Full working: Formula: half chord = square root(r^2 - d^2). Step 1: half chord = square root(25 - 16) = square root 9 = 3 cm. Step 2: chord = 2 x 3 = 6 cm, book MCQ (xii).

lessons.title: Theorems of Unit 11
lessons.notes_html:
Theorem 1 (11.1(i)) If two arcs of a circle (or of congruent circles) are congruent then the corresponding chords are equal

Given: ABCD and A'B'C'D' are two congruent circles with centres O and O' respectively, so that arc ADC = arc A'D'C' (the minor arcs AC and A'C' are congruent).

To prove: Chord AC = chord A'C'.

Construction: Join O with A, O with C, O' with A' and O' with C', forming triangles OAC and O'A'C'.

Proof:

Step 1: The congruent arcs subtend equal central angles in the equal circles: angle AOC = angle A'O'C'.

Step 2: In triangles AOC and A'O'C': OA = O'A' (radii of equal circles); angle AOC = angle A'O'C' (proved); OC = O'C' (radii of equal circles).

Step 3: Therefore triangle AOC is congruent to triangle A'O'C' (S.A.S = S.A.S), and in particular AC = A'C'.

Similarly the theorem holds in the same circle. Proved.

Theorem 2 (11.1(ii)) - Converse of Theorem 1: If two chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) are equal, then their corresponding arcs (minor, major or semi-circular) are congruent

Given: ABCD and A'B'C'D' are two congruent circles with centres O and O' respectively, so that chord AC = chord A'C'.

To prove: Arc ADC = arc A'D'C' (corresponding arcs are congruent).

Construction: Join O with A, O with C, O' with A' and O' with C'.

Proof:

Step 1: In triangles AOC and A'O'C': OA = O'A' (radii of equal circles); OC = O'C' (radii of equal circles); AC = A'C' (given).

Step 2: Therefore triangle AOC is congruent to triangle A'O'C' (S.S.S = S.S.S), so angle AOC = angle A'O'C'.

Step 3: Equal central angles in congruent circles subtend congruent arcs, hence arc ADC = arc A'D'C'.

In equal circles or in the same circle, if two chords are equal, they cut off equal arcs. Proved.

Theorem 3 (11.1(iii)) Equal chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) subtend equal angles at the centre (at the corresponding centres)

Given: ABC and A'B'C' are two congruent circles with centres O and O' respectively, so that chord AC = chord A'C'.

To prove: angle AOC = angle A'O'C'.

Construction (proof by contradiction): If possible, suppose angle AOC is not equal to angle A'O'C'; construct angle A'O'D' congruent to angle AOC in the second circle, where D' is a point on that circle.

Proof:

Step 1: The equal central angles subtend congruent arcs, so arc AC = arc A'D', and by Theorem 1 the corresponding chords are equal: AC = A'D' ... (i)

Step 2: But AC = A'C' (given) ... (ii). From (i) and (ii): A'C' = A'D'.

Step 3: This is only possible if C' coincides with D'. Hence angle A'O'C' = angle A'O'D'.

Step 4: But angle A'O'D' = angle AOC (construction), so angle AOC = angle A'O'C'. Proved.

Corollary 1: In congruent circles or in the same circle, if central angles are equal then corresponding sectors are equal.

Corollary 2: In congruent circles or in the same circle, unequal arcs will subtend unequal central angles.

Theorem 4 (from the Unit 11 summary) If the angles subtended by two chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) at the centre (corresponding centres) are equal, the chords are equal

Given: In congruent circles with centres O and O' (or in the same circle), chords AC and A'C' subtend equal angles at the centres: angle AOC = angle A'O'C'.

To prove: AC = A'C'.

Construction: Join O with A and C; O' with A' and C'.

Proof:

Step 1: In triangles AOC and A'O'C': OA = O'A' (radii of equal circles); angle AOC = angle A'O'C' (given); OC = O'C' (radii of equal circles).

Step 2: Therefore triangle AOC is congruent to triangle A'O'C' (S.A.S = S.A.S).

Step 3: Hence AC = A'C' (corresponding sides of congruent triangles). Proved.

Example of Unit 11: The internal bisector of a central angle in a circle bisects the arc on which it stands

Given: In a circle with centre O, OP is an internal bisector of the central angle AOB, meeting the circle at P.

To prove: Arc AP = arc BP.

Construction: Draw chords AP and BP; write angle 1 = angle AOP and angle 2 = angle POB.

Proof:

Step 1: In triangles OAP and OBP: OA = OB (radii of the same circle); angle 1 = angle 2 (OP bisects angle AOB, given); OP = OP (common).

Step 2: Therefore triangle OAP is congruent to triangle OBP (S.A.S = S.A.S), so chord AP = chord BP.

Step 3: Equal chords cut off equal arcs (Theorem 2), hence arc AP = arc BP. Proved.

Example 1 of Unit 11: A point P on the circumference is equidistant from the radii OA and OB. Prove that arc AP = arc BP

Given: AB is the chord of a circle with centre O. Point P on the circumference of the circle is equidistant from the radii OA and OB, so that PR = PS, where R and S are the feet of the perpendiculars from P to OA and OB.

To prove: Arc AP = arc BP.

Construction: Join O with P. Write angle 1 = angle AOP and angle 2 = angle POB as shown in the figure.

Proof:

Step 1: In right triangles OPR and OPS: OP = OP (common); PR = PS (P is equidistant from the radii, given).

Step 2: Therefore triangle OPR is congruent to triangle OPS (H.S = H.S), so angle 1 = angle 2 (central angles of the circle).

Step 3: Equal central angles stand on equal chords: chord AP = chord BP, and the arcs corresponding to equal chords in a circle are equal.

Hence arc AP = arc BP. Proved.

Example 2 of Unit 11: In a circle if any pair of diameters are perpendicular to each other then the lines joining its ends in order, form a square

Given: AC and BD are two perpendicular diameters of a circle with centre O, and ABCD is the quadrilateral formed by joining their ends in order.

To prove: ABCD is a square.

Construction: Write angles 1, 2, 3, 4 at the centre and angles 5, 6 at A as shown in the figure.

Proof:

Step 1: AC and BD are perpendicular diameters, so angle 1 = angle 2 = angle 3 = angle 4 = 90 deg.

Step 2: Arcs opposite to equal central angles in a circle are equal: arc AB = arc BC = arc CD = arc DA, so the chords corresponding to equal arcs are equal: AB = BC = CD = DA ... (i)

Step 3: Each angle of the quadrilateral stands on a diameter (semicircle): angle A = angle 5 + angle 6 = 45 deg + 45 deg = 90 deg; similarly angle B = angle C = angle D = 90 deg ... (ii), (iii)

Step 4: From (i), (ii) and (iii): all sides equal and all angles right angles.

Hence ABCD is a square. Proved.

mcqs.q: If two arcs of a circle (or of congruent circles) are congruent, then the corresponding chords are:
mcqs.why: Theorem 11.1(i) proves this: congruent arcs subtend equal central angles, and triangles OAC and O'A'C' are congruent by S.A.S., so the corresponding chords AC and A'C' are equal.

mcqs.q: If two chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) are equal, then their corresponding arcs are:
mcqs.why: Theorem 11.1(ii) is the converse of Theorem 11.1(i). Triangles formed by the chords and radii are congruent by S.S.S., so the central angles are equal and the corresponding arcs are congruent.

mcqs.q: Equal chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) subtend at the centre:
mcqs.why: Theorem 11.1(iii) states that equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre or at the corresponding centres of congruent circles, proved by contradiction using Theorems 11.1(i) and (ii).

mcqs.q: If the angles subtended by two chords at the centre are equal, then the chords are:
mcqs.why: Theorem 4 of Unit 11 proves this by S.A.S.: the two radii and the included central angle of one triangle equal those of the other, so the chords, as corresponding sides, are equal.

mcqs.q: The internal bisector of a central angle in a circle bisects:
options: The arc on which it stands
mcqs.why: Triangles OAP and OBP are congruent by S.A.S., so chord AP = chord BP. Equal chords cut off equal arcs by Theorem 11.1(ii), hence arc AP = arc BP and the arc is bisected.

mcqs.q: A point P on the circumference is equidistant from the radii OA and OB. Then arc AP is:
mcqs.why: Right triangles OPR and OPS are congruent by H.S. because OP is common and PR = PS. Hence the central angles at O are equal, giving equal chords and therefore arc AP = arc BP.

mcqs.q: In a circle, if a pair of diameters are perpendicular to each other, the lines joining their ends in order form a:
mcqs.why: The four central angles are each 90 degrees, so the four arcs and the four chords are equal. Each angle of the quadrilateral stands on a diameter and is 90 degrees, so all sides are equal and all angles right: a square.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 11.1(i), triangles OAC and O'A'C' are congruent by:
mcqs.why: OA = O'A' and OC = O'C' are radii of equal circles, and the included central angles AOC and A'O'C' are equal because the arcs are congruent. This is the S.A.S. postulate.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 11.1(ii), triangles AOC and A'O'C' are congruent by:
mcqs.why: OA = O'A' and OC = O'C' are radii of congruent circles, and AC = A'C' is given as equal chords. All three sides are equal, so the congruence is by S.S.S. = S.S.S.

mcqs.q: Corollary 1 of Theorem 11.1(iii) states that in congruent circles or in the same circle, if central angles are equal then the corresponding:
mcqs.why: Corollary 1 states directly that if central angles are equal then the corresponding sectors are equal. Corollary 2 adds that unequal arcs subtend unequal central angles.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 In a circle two equal diameters AB and CD intersect each other. Prove that AD = BC

Step 1: The diameters AB and CD intersect at the centre O. The vertically opposite angles are equal: angle AOD = angle BOC.

Step 2: Chords AD and BC subtend these equal angles at the centre.

Step 3: By Theorem 4 (equal central angles give equal chords), AD = BC.

Proved. (Similarly AC = BD using the other pair of vertical angles.)

Q2 In a circle prove that the arcs between two parallel and equal chords are equal

Given: AB and CD are two parallel and equal chords of a circle with centre O.

To prove: The arcs between them are equal: arc AC = arc BD (the arcs intercepted between the parallel chords).

Proof:

Step 1: Join O with A, B, C, D. Since the chords are equal, by Theorem 3 they subtend equal angles at the centre: angle AOB = angle COD.

Step 2: The chords are parallel, so the alternate angles formed with the transversal line of centres' perpendicular are equal; equivalently, the perpendicular from O to the chords is a single straight line (Corollary 2 of Unit 9 Theorem 3: the diameter passes through the midpoints of two parallel chords), so the angles that OA and OC make with this perpendicular are equal, and likewise for OB and OD.

Step 3: Subtracting the equal angles: angle AOC = angle AOB - angle COB-part... precisely, angle AOC = angle BOD (the parts of the equal angles AOB and COD left after removing the common middle angle).

Step 4: Equal central angles subtend equal arcs, hence arc AC = arc BD. Proved.

Q3 Give a geometric proof that a pair of bisecting chords are the diameters of a circle

Step 1: Let chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O bisect each other at a point E.

Step 2: Suppose E is not the centre. Join O with E. Since E is the midpoint of chord AB, by Unit 9 Theorem 2, OE is perpendicular to AB.

Step 3: Since E is also the midpoint of chord CD, by the same theorem OE is perpendicular to CD.

Step 4: Through E only one perpendicular to OE can be drawn, so AB and CD would coincide - impossible for two distinct chords. Hence the supposition is false and E = O.

Step 5: Chords through the centre are diameters.

Hence a pair of (distinct) chords that bisect each other must be diameters of the circle. Proved.

Q4 If C is the mid-point of an arc ACB in a circle with centre O, show that line segment OC bisects the chord AB

Step 1: C is the midpoint of arc ACB, so arc AC = arc CB. Equal arcs have equal chords (Theorem 1): AC = CB.

Step 2: In triangles OAC and OBC: OA = OB (radii); AC = BC (just proved); OC = OC (common). So triangle OAC is congruent to triangle OBC (S.S.S), giving angle AOC = angle BOC.

Step 3: Let OC meet AB at M. In triangles OAM and OBM: OA = OB (radii); angle AOM = angle BOM (just proved); OM = OM (common). So the triangles are congruent (S.A.S), giving AM = BM.

Hence OC bisects the chord AB. Proved.

mcqs.q: In a circle, two equal diameters AB and CD intersect each other. Then AD is equal to:
mcqs.why: The diameters intersect at the centre O and the vertically opposite angles AOD and BOC are equal. Chords subtending equal angles at the centre are equal by Theorem 4 of Unit 11, so AD = BC.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 11.1 Q1, using the other pair of vertically opposite angles, AC is equal to:
mcqs.why: The other pair of vertically opposite angles at the centre, AOC and BOD, are also equal. By Theorem 4 of Unit 11, chords subtending equal central angles are equal, so AC = BD.

mcqs.q: In a circle, the arcs between two parallel and equal chords are:
mcqs.why: Exercise 11.1 Q2 proves arc AC = arc BD. Equal chords subtend equal central angles AOB and COD, and subtracting the common middle angle leaves angle AOC = angle BOD, which subtend the equal arcs.

mcqs.q: A pair of distinct chords of a circle that bisect each other must be:
mcqs.why: If the bisecting point E were not the centre, OE would be perpendicular to both chords, forcing them to coincide. Hence E is the centre O, and chords through the centre are diameters.

mcqs.q: C is the mid-point of arc ACB in a circle with centre O. The line segment OC:
mcqs.why: Since arc AC = arc CB, chords AC = CB by Theorem 11.1(i). Congruent triangles lead to angle AOC = angle BOC and then AM = BM where M is the meeting point with AB, so OC bisects AB.

mcqs.q: C is the mid-point of arc ACB. From arc AC = arc CB it follows by Theorem 11.1(i) that:
options: OC is perpendicular to the circle
mcqs.why: Theorem 11.1(i) states that congruent arcs have equal corresponding chords. Arc AC and arc CB are equal because C is the midpoint of the arc, so chord AC = chord CB.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 11.1 Q4, triangles OAC and OBC are proved congruent by:
mcqs.why: OA = OB are radii, AC = BC are chords of the equal arcs, and OC is common. Three equal sides in the two triangles give congruence by S.S.S., hence angle AOC = angle BOC.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 11.1 Q4, with OC meeting AB at M, triangles OAM and OBM give AM = BM by congruence using:
mcqs.why: OA = OB are radii, angle AOM = angle BOM was proved from the first congruence, and OM is common. This is S.A.S., and corresponding sides AM and BM are therefore equal.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 11.1 Q3, the contradiction when E is not the centre comes from Unit 9 Theorem 2, which says OE would be:
options: Perpendicular to both chords AB and CD
mcqs.why: E is the midpoint of chord AB, so OE is perpendicular to AB by Unit 9 Theorem 2. E is also the midpoint of CD, so OE is perpendicular to CD. Only one such perpendicular exists through E.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 11.1 Q2, equal chords AB and CD subtend equal central angles by:
mcqs.why: Theorem 11.1(iii) states that equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre. Applied to the parallel equal chords, it gives angle AOB = angle COD, the starting step of the proof.

lessons.title: Miscellaneous Exercise 11
lessons.notes_html:
MCQ (i) A 4 cm long chord subtends a central angle of 60 deg. The radial segment of this circle is

(a) 1
(b) 2
(c) 3
(d) 4
Correct answer: 4

MCQ (ii) The length of a chord and the radial segment of a circle are congruent, the central angle made by the chord will be

(a) 30 deg
(b) 45 deg
(c) 60 deg
(d) 75 deg
Correct answer: 60 deg

MCQ (iii) Out of two congruent arcs of a circle, if one arc makes a central angle of 30 deg then the other arc will subtend the central angle of

(a) 15 deg
(b) 30 deg
(c) 45 deg
(d) 60 deg
Correct answer: 30 deg

MCQ (iv) An arc subtends a central angle of 40 deg then the corresponding chord will subtend a central angle of

(a) 20 deg
(b) 40 deg
(c) 60 deg
(d) 80 deg
Correct answer: 40 deg

MCQ (v) A pair of chords of a circle subtending two congruent central angles is

(a) congruent
(b) incongruent
(c) overlapping
(d) parallel
Correct answer: congruent

MCQ (vi) If an arc of a circle subtends a central angle of 60 deg, then the corresponding chord of the arc will make the central angle of

(a) 20 deg
(b) 40 deg
(c) 60 deg
(d) 80 deg
Correct answer: 60 deg

MCQ (vii) The semi-circumference and the diameter of a circle both subtend a central angle of

(a) 90 deg
(b) 180 deg
(c) 270 deg
(d) 360 deg
Correct answer: 180 deg

MCQ (viii) The chord length of a circle subtending a central angle of 180 deg is always

(a) less than the radial segment
(b) equal to the radial segment
(c) double of the radial segment
(d) none of these
Correct answer: double of the radial segment

MCQ (ix) If a chord of a circle subtends a central angle of 60 deg, then the length of the chord and the radial segment are

(a) congruent
(b) incongruent
(c) parallel
(d) perpendicular
Correct answer: congruent

MCQ (x) The arcs opposite to incongruent central angles of a circle are always

(a) congruent
(b) incongruent
(c) parallel
(d) perpendicular
Correct answer: incongruent

mcqs.q: A 4 cm long chord subtends a central angle of 60 degrees. The radial segment of this circle is:
mcqs.why: Full working: In triangle OAB, OA = OB are radii and the central angle is 60 degrees, so the base angles are (180 - 60)/2 = 60 degrees each. The triangle is equilateral, so radius = chord = 4 cm, book MCQ (i).

mcqs.q: The length of a chord and the radial segment of a circle are congruent. The central angle made by the chord will be:
mcqs.why: Full working: OA = OB = AB, so triangle OAB is equilateral. Formula: each angle of an equilateral triangle = 180/3 = 60 degrees. Hence the central angle is 60 degrees, book MCQ (ii).

mcqs.q: Out of two congruent arcs of a circle, if one arc makes a central angle of 30 degrees, then the other arc will subtend the central angle of:
mcqs.why: Congruent arcs of the same or congruent circles subtend equal central angles. Since the arcs are congruent and one subtends 30 degrees, the other also subtends 30 degrees, book MCQ (iii).

mcqs.q: An arc subtends a central angle of 40 degrees. The corresponding chord will subtend a central angle of:
mcqs.why: The chord joining the endpoints of an arc subtends at the centre exactly the same angle as the arc itself. So a 40 degree arc corresponds to a chord subtending 40 degrees, book MCQ (iv).

mcqs.q: A pair of chords of a circle subtending two congruent central angles is:
mcqs.why: By Theorem 4 of Unit 11, if the angles subtended by two chords at the centre are equal, the chords are equal, that is, congruent. This is book MCQ (v).

mcqs.q: If an arc of a circle subtends a central angle of 60 degrees, then the corresponding chord of the arc will make the central angle of:
mcqs.why: An arc and its corresponding chord subtend the same central angle at the centre of the circle. Therefore the chord also makes a central angle of 60 degrees, book MCQ (vi).

mcqs.q: The semi-circumference and the diameter of a circle both subtend a central angle of:
mcqs.why: A diameter divides the circle into two semicircles, and a straight angle at the centre is 180 degrees. Hence both the semi-circumference and the diameter subtend 180 degrees, book MCQ (vii).

mcqs.q: The chord length of a circle subtending a central angle of 180 degrees is always:
mcqs.why: Full working: A central angle of 180 degrees means the chord is a diameter. Formula: diameter = 2 x radius = 2 x radial segment. Hence the chord length is double of the radial segment, book MCQ (viii).

mcqs.q: If a chord of a circle subtends a central angle of 60 degrees, then the length of the chord and the radial segment are:
mcqs.why: With central angle 60 degrees and OA = OB, triangle OAB has all angles 60 degrees and is equilateral. Hence chord AB equals the radial segment OA, so they are congruent, book MCQ (ix).

mcqs.q: The arcs opposite to incongruent central angles of a circle are always:
mcqs.why: By Corollary 2 of Theorem 11.1(iii), unequal, that is incongruent, central angles correspond to unequal arcs. Hence arcs opposite to incongruent central angles are incongruent, book MCQ (x).

chapters.title: Unit 12 - Angle in a Segment of a Circle

lessons.title: Theorems of Unit 12
lessons.notes_html:
Theorem 1 (12.1(i)) The measure of a central angle of a minor arc of a circle is double that of the angle subtended by the corresponding major arc

Given: AC is an arc of a circle with centre O, whereas angle AOC is the central angle and angle ABC is the circum angle (B on the major arc).

To prove: angle AOC = 2 x angle ABC.

Construction: Join B with O and produce it to meet the circle at D. Write angles 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 as shown in the figure (angle 1 = OAB, angle 3 = OBA, angle 2 = OBC, angle 4 = OCB, angle 5 = AOD, angle 6 = COD).

Proof:

Step 1: In triangle OAB, OA = OB (radii), so the angles opposite the equal sides are equal: angle 1 = angle 3 ... (i)

Step 2: In triangle OBC, OB = OC (radii), so angle 2 = angle 4 ... (ii)

Step 3: The exterior angle at O in triangle OAB equals the sum of the interior opposite angles: angle 5 = angle 1 + angle 3 ... (iii); similarly angle 6 = angle 2 + angle 4 ... (iv)

Step 4: Using (i) in (iii): angle 5 = 2 x angle 3 ... (v). Using (ii) in (iv): angle 6 = 2 x angle 4 ... (vi)

Step 5: Adding (v) and (vi): angle 5 + angle 6 = 2(angle 3 + angle 4), i.e. angle AOC = 2 x angle ABC. Proved.

Example of Unit 12 (after Theorem 1): The radius of a circle is sqrt(2) cm. A chord 2 cm in length divides the circle into two segments. Prove that the angle of the larger segment is 45 deg

Given: In a circle with centre O and radius OA = OB = sqrt(2) cm, the chord AB = 2 cm divides the circle into two segments, ACB being the larger one.

To prove: angle ACB = 45 deg.

Construction: Join O with A and O with B.

Proof:

Step 1: In triangle OAB: (OA)^2 + (OB)^2 = (sqrt(2))^2 + (sqrt(2))^2 = 2 + 2 = 4 = (2)^2 = (AB)^2.

Step 2: So triangle OAB is right-angled at O (converse of Pythagoras), i.e. the central angle AOB = 90 deg.

Step 3: By Theorem 1, the circum angle on the major arc is half the central angle: angle ACB = (1/2) angle AOB = (1/2)(90 deg) = 45 deg. Proved.

Theorem 2 (12.1(ii)) Any two angles in the same segment of a circle are equal

Given: Angle ACB and angle ADB are the circum angles in the same segment of a circle with centre O.

To prove: angle ACB = angle ADB.

Construction: Join O with A and O with B, so that angle AOB is the central angle on the same arc AB.

Proof:

Step 1: Standing on the same arc AB, angle AOB is the central angle whereas angle ACB is a circum angle, so by Theorem 1: angle AOB = 2 x angle ACB ... (i)

Step 2: Similarly angle AOB = 2 x angle ADB ... (ii)

Step 3: From (i) and (ii): 2 x angle ACB = 2 x angle ADB, hence angle ACB = angle ADB. Proved.

Theorem 3 (12.1(iii)) The angle in a semi-circle is a right angle; in a segment greater than a semi-circle is less than a right angle; in a segment less than a semi-circle is greater than a right angle

Given: AB is the chord corresponding to an arc ADB, whereas angle AOB is a central angle and angle ACB is a circum angle of a circle with centre O.

To prove: (Fig. I) if sector ACB is a semi-circle then angle ACB = 1 right angle; (Fig. II) if sector ACB is greater than a semi-circle then angle ACB < 1 right angle; (Fig. III) if sector ACB is less than a semi-circle then angle ACB > 1 right angle.

Proof:

Step 1: In each figure, by Theorem 1: angle AOB = 2 x angle ACB ... (i)

Step 2 (Fig. I): The arc is a semicircle, so the central angle AOB = 180 deg = 2 right angles. Using (i): angle ACB = (1/2)(2 right angles) = 1 right angle.

Step 3 (Fig. II): The segment is greater than a semicircle, so the (minor) central angle AOB < 180 deg, i.e. angle AOB < 2 right angles. Using (i): angle ACB < 1 right angle.

Step 4 (Fig. III): The segment is less than a semicircle, so the reflex central angle AOB > 180 deg, i.e. angle AOB > 2 right angles. Using (i): 2 x angle ACB > 2 right angles, so angle ACB > 1 right angle. Proved.

Theorem 4 (12.1(iv)) The opposite angles of any quadrilateral inscribed in a circle are supplementary

Given: ABCD is a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle with centre O.

To prove: angle A + angle C = 2 right angles, and angle B + angle D = 2 right angles.

Construction: Draw OA and OC. Write angles 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 as shown in the figure (angles 2 and 4 are the two central angles at O on arcs ADC and ABC; angle B is at the circumference on arc ADC, angle D on arc ABC).

Proof:

Step 1: Standing on the same arc ADC, angle 2 is a central angle whereas angle B is the circum angle, so by Theorem 1: angle B = (1/2)(angle 2) ... (i)

Step 2: Standing on the same arc ABC, angle 4 is a central angle whereas angle D is the circum angle, so by Theorem 1: angle D = (1/2)(angle 4) ... (ii)

Step 3: Adding (i) and (ii): angle B + angle D = (1/2)(angle 2 + angle 4) = (1/2)(total angle at O) = (1/2)(4 right angles) = 2 right angles.

Step 4: Similarly angle A + angle C = 2 right angles. Proved.

Corollary 1: In equal circles or in the same circle, if two minor arcs are equal then the angles inscribed by their corresponding major arcs are also equal.

Corollary 2: In equal circles or in the same circle, two equal arcs subtend equal angles at the circumference and vice versa.

Example 1 of Unit 12: Two equal circles intersect in A and B. Through B, a straight line is drawn to meet the circumferences at P and Q respectively. Prove that AP = AQ

Given: Two equal circles cut each other at points A and B. A straight line PBQ drawn through B meets the circles at P and Q respectively.

To prove: AP = AQ.

Construction: Join the points A and B. Also draw AP and AQ. Write angle 1 = angle APB and angle 2 = angle AQB as shown in the figure.

Proof:

Step 1: The arcs ACB and ADB about the common chord AB of the two equal circles are equal arcs ... (arcs about the common chord AB).

Step 2: Therefore the angles in the opposite segments are equal: angle 1 = angle 2 (corresponding angles made by opposite arcs).

Step 3: In triangle APQ, the sides opposite equal angles are equal: AQ = AP (sides opposite to equal angles in triangle APQ).

Hence AP = AQ. Proved.

Example 2 of Unit 12: ABCD is a quadrilateral circumscribed about a circle. Show that AB + CD = BC + DA

Given: ABCD is a quadrilateral circumscribed about a circle with centre O, so that each side is tangent to the circle. Let the points of contact on AB, BC, CD, DA be E, F, G, H respectively.

To prove: AB + CD = BC + DA.

Construction: Draw OE perpendicular to AB, OF perpendicular to BC, OG perpendicular to CD and OH perpendicular to DA.

Proof:

Step 1: Tangents drawn from a point to the circle are equal in length (Unit 10, Theorem 3): from A: AE = HA; from B: EB = BF ... (i)

Step 2: From C: CG = FC; and from D: GD = DH ... (ii)

Step 3: Add: AB + CD = (AE + EB) + (CG + GD) = (HA + BF) + (FC + DH) [using (i) and (ii)] = (BF + FC) + (DH + HA) = BC + DA.

Hence AB + CD = BC + DA. Proved.

mcqs.q: According to Theorem 12.1(i), the measure of the central angle of a minor arc is what multiple of the angle subtended by the corresponding major arc at the circumference?
mcqs.why: Theorem 1 states that the central angle AOC is double the circum angle ABC standing on the same arc, i.e. angle AOC = 2 x angle ABC, proved by joining B to O and using exterior angles of the isosceles triangles OAB and OBC.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 12.1(i), which construction is made first?
options: Join B with O and produce it to meet the circle at D
