mcqs.why: The construction in the book's proof is to join B with O and produce BO to meet the circle again at D. This creates triangles OAB and OBC whose exterior angles at O are then used in the proof.

mcqs.q: In the proof of Theorem 12.1(i), why is angle 1 (OAB) equal to angle 3 (OBA) in triangle OAB?
options: Because OA and OB are radii of the same circle, so the angles opposite these equal sides are equal
Because they are vertically opposite angles
Because they are alternate interior angles
mcqs.why: OA = OB because both are radii of the same circle. In triangle OAB the angles opposite equal sides are equal, so angle 1 = angle 3; similarly in triangle OBC, OB = OC gives angle 2 = angle 4.

mcqs.q: In the example after Theorem 1, a circle has radius sqrt(2) cm and a chord AB = 2 cm. What is the central angle AOB?
mcqs.why: Formula: Pythagoras in triangle OAB. Step 1: (OA)^2 + (OB)^2 = (sqrt(2))^2 + (sqrt(2))^2 = 2 + 2 = 4. Step 2: (AB)^2 = (2)^2 = 4. Step 3: Since OA^2 + OB^2 = AB^2, by the converse of Pythagoras triangle OAB is right-angled at O, so angle AOB = 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: In the same example (radius sqrt(2) cm, chord 2 cm, central angle AOB = 90 degrees), the angle in the larger segment ACB is:
mcqs.why: Formula: circum angle = (1/2) x central angle (Theorem 1). Step 1: The larger segment stands on the major arc, so angle ACB = (1/2) x angle AOB. Step 2: angle ACB = (1/2)(90 degrees) = 45 degrees.

mcqs.q: Theorem 12.1(ii) states that any two angles in the same segment of a circle are:
mcqs.why: Both angles ACB and ADB stand on the same arc AB, and each is half of the same central angle AOB by Theorem 1. Hence 2 x angle ACB = angle AOB = 2 x angle ADB, so angle ACB = angle ADB.

mcqs.q: By Theorem 12.1(iii), the angle in a semi-circle is:
mcqs.why: For a semicircle the central angle AOB = 180 degrees = 2 right angles. By Theorem 1, angle ACB = (1/2) x angle AOB = (1/2)(2 right angles) = 1 right angle, i.e. 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: By Theorem 12.1(iii), the angle in a segment greater than a semi-circle is:
mcqs.why: When the segment is greater than a semicircle, the (minor) central angle AOB is less than 180 degrees, i.e. less than 2 right angles. Halving by Theorem 1 gives angle ACB less than 1 right angle.

mcqs.q: By Theorem 12.1(iv), the opposite angles of a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle are:
options: Each equal to a right angle
mcqs.why: Angles B and D are each half of the two central angles on arcs ADC and ABC. Those central angles sum to the complete angle at O, 4 right angles, so angle B + angle D = (1/2)(4 right angles) = 2 right angles = 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: ABCD is a quadrilateral circumscribed about a circle, each side being a tangent. Which relation holds (Example 2 of Unit 12)?
options: AB x CD = BC x DA
mcqs.why: Tangents from one external point are equal: from A, AE = HA; from B, EB = BF; from C, CG = FC; from D, GD = DH. Adding, AB + CD = (AE + EB) + (CG + GD) = (HA + BF) + (FC + DH) = BC + DA.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Prove that in a given cyclic quadrilateral, the sum of opposite angles is two right angles, and conversely

Part 1 (direct): This is Theorem 4: ABCD inscribed in a circle with centre O. Join OA and OC. The circum angle B is half the central angle on arc ADC, and the circum angle D is half the central angle on arc ABC; the two central angles sum to 4 right angles (complete turn at O), so angle B + angle D = (1/2)(4 right angles) = 2 right angles. Similarly angle A + angle C = 2 right angles. Proved.

Part 2 (converse): Let ABCD be a quadrilateral with angle B + angle D = 2 right angles. Draw the circle through A, B and C (one and only one such circle exists, Unit 9 Theorem 1). Suppose it meets the line AD or its extension at a point D' instead of D. Then ABCD' is cyclic, so angle B + angle AD'C = 2 right angles. Comparing with the given angle B + angle ADC = 2 right angles gives angle ADC = angle AD'C, which forces D' to coincide with D (an exterior angle of a triangle cannot equal a remote interior angle unless the points coincide). Hence D lies on the circle, i.e. ABCD is cyclic. Proved.

Q2 Show that a parallelogram inscribed in a circle will be a rectangle

Step 1: Let ABCD be a parallelogram inscribed in a circle. It is a cyclic quadrilateral, so opposite angles are supplementary (Theorem 4): angle A + angle C = 180 deg.

Step 2: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal: angle A = angle C.

Step 3: From Steps 1 and 2: 2 x angle A = 180 deg, so angle A = 90 deg. Similarly every angle is 90 deg.

Step 4: A parallelogram with all angles right angles is a rectangle.

Hence a parallelogram inscribed in a circle is a rectangle. Proved.

Q3 AOB and COD are two intersecting chords of a circle (chords AC and BD intersect at O inside the circle). Show that triangles AOD and BOC are equiangular

Given: Chords AC and BD of a circle intersect each other at O.

To prove: Triangle AOD and triangle BOC have the same three angles (are equiangular).

Proof:

Step 1: Angle AOD = angle BOC (vertically opposite angles at the intersection O).

Step 2: Angle OAD = angle OBC, because both are angles in the same segment standing on the same arc CD... precisely, angle DAC and angle DBC stand on the same chord DC in the same segment (Theorem 2).

Step 3: Angle ODA = angle OCB, because angle ADB and angle ACB stand on the same chord AB in the same segment (Theorem 2).

Step 4: All three angles of triangle AOD equal the corresponding angles of triangle BOC.

Hence the triangles are equiangular (and therefore similar). Proved.

Q4 AD and BC are two parallel chords of a circle. Prove that arc AB is congruent to arc CD and arc AC is congruent to arc BD

Given: AD and BC are two parallel chords of a circle, with A, B, C, D in order round the circle.

To prove: Arc AB = arc CD and arc AC = arc BD.

Proof:

Step 1: Since AD is parallel to BC, the alternate interior angles formed by the transversal AC are equal: angle DAC = angle BCA.

Step 2: Angle DAC stands on arc DC and angle BCA stands on arc AB. Equal circum angles stand on equal arcs (Corollary 2 of Theorem 4), so arc AB = arc CD ... (i)

Step 3: Add the common arc BC to both sides of (i): arc AB + arc BC = arc CD + arc BC, i.e. arc AC = arc BD.

Hence both results are proved. Proved.

mcqs.q: In a cyclic quadrilateral, the sum of a pair of opposite angles is:
mcqs.why: This is Theorem 4: each opposite angle is half of its central angle, and the two central angles together make the complete turn at O, 4 right angles. Half of 4 right angles is 2 right angles, i.e. 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: The converse proved in Exercise 12.1 Q1 says: if a quadrilateral has a pair of opposite angles summing to 2 right angles, then the quadrilateral is:
options: Cyclic, i.e. its vertices lie on one circle
mcqs.why: Draw the unique circle through A, B and C. If it met AD or its extension at D' instead of D, then ABCD' would be cyclic with angle B + angle AD'C = 2 right angles, forcing angle ADC = angle AD'C, which is impossible unless D' coincides with D. Hence D lies on the circle.

mcqs.q: A parallelogram inscribed in a circle must be a:
mcqs.why: Being cyclic, its opposite angles are supplementary: angle A + angle C = 180 degrees. Being a parallelogram, its opposite angles are equal: angle A = angle C. Hence every angle is 90 degrees, which makes the parallelogram a rectangle.

mcqs.q: In the proof that a cyclic parallelogram has angle A = 90 degrees, which two facts are combined?
options: Angle A + angle C = 180 degrees and angle A = angle C
Angle A + angle B = 180 degrees and angle A = angle B
The diagonals of a parallelogram are equal
mcqs.why: Step 1: Cyclic property gives angle A + angle C = 180 degrees. Step 2: Parallelogram property gives angle A = angle C. Step 3: Substituting, 2 x angle A = 180 degrees, so angle A = 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: Chords AC and BD intersect at O inside a circle (Exercise 12.1 Q3). Why is angle AOD equal to angle BOC?
options: They are angles in the same segment
They are vertically opposite angles at the intersection O
They stand on the same arc
mcqs.why: AC and BD are two straight lines crossing at O, so the angles opposite each other at the crossing, angle AOD and angle BOC, are vertically opposite angles and therefore equal.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 12.1 Q3, angle OAD equals angle OBC because both angles:
options: Are right angles in a semicircle
Stand on the same chord DC in the same segment
Are central angles on arc CD
Are exterior angles of triangle AOD
mcqs.why: Angle DAC (that is, OAD) and angle DBC (that is, OBC) both stand on chord DC in the same segment of the circle, so by Theorem 2 (angles in the same segment are equal) they are equal.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 12.1 Q3, angle ODA equals angle OCB because angle ADB and angle ACB both stand on:
options: Chord CD in the same segment
Chord AB in the same segment
mcqs.why: Angle ADB and angle ACB are angles in the same segment standing on the same chord AB, so by Theorem 2 they are equal. Angle ADB is angle ODA and angle ACB is angle OCB, giving the required equality.

mcqs.q: The conclusion of Exercise 12.1 Q3 about triangles AOD and BOC is that they are:
mcqs.why: All three angles match: angle AOD = angle BOC (vertically opposite), angle OAD = angle OBC and angle ODA = angle OCB (same-segment angles). Triangles with all three angles respectively equal are equiangular, hence similar.

mcqs.q: AD and BC are parallel chords (Exercise 12.1 Q4). Using transversal AC, angle DAC equals angle BCA because they are:
mcqs.why: AD is parallel to BC and AC is a transversal cutting them, so the interior angles on opposite sides of AC, angle DAC and angle BCA, are alternate interior angles and are equal.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 12.1 Q4, after proving arc AB = arc CD, the result arc AC = arc BD is obtained by:
options: Subtracting the common arc BC from both sides
Adding the common arc BC to both sides
Replacing arc BC by the diameter
mcqs.why: Step 1: arc AB = arc CD (equal circum angles stand on equal arcs). Step 2: Add the common arc BC to both sides: arc AB + arc BC = arc CD + arc BC. Step 3: The left side is arc AC and the right side is arc BD, so arc AC = arc BD.

lessons.title: Miscellaneous Exercise 12
lessons.notes_html:
MCQ (i) A circle passes through the vertices of a right-angled triangle ABC with AC = 3 cm and BC = 4 cm, angle C = 90 deg. The radius of the circle is (the hypotenuse AB is the diameter)

(a) 1.5 cm
(b) 2.0 cm
(c) 2.5 cm
(d) 3.5 cm
Correct answer: 2.5 cm

MCQ (ii) In the adjacent circular figure, central and inscribed angles stand on the same arc AB (angle 1 at the circumference, angle 2 at the centre). Then

(a) angle 1 = angle 2
(b) angle 1 = 2 x angle 2
(c) angle 2 = 3 x angle 1
(d) angle 2 = 2 x angle 1
Correct answer: angle 2 = 2 x angle 1

MCQ (iii) In the adjacent figure, if angle 3 = 75 deg (angle 3 at the centre; angles 1 and 2 at the circumference on the same arc), then find angle 1 and angle 2

(a) 37.5 deg, 37.5 deg
(b) 37.5 deg, 75 deg
(c) 75 deg, 37.5 deg
(d) 75 deg, 75 deg
Correct answer: 37.5 deg, 37.5 deg

MCQ (iv) Given that O is the centre of the circle (figure: a 25 deg angle at the circumference and angle x at the circumference in the same segment), the angle marked x will be

(a) 12.5 deg
(b) 25 deg
(c) 50 deg
(d) 75 deg
Correct answer: 25 deg

MCQ (v) Given that O is the centre of the circle (same figure; angle x at the centre standing on the same arc as the 25 deg inscribed angle), the angle marked y at the circumference will be

(a) 12.5 deg
(b) 25 deg
(c) 50 deg
(d) 75 deg
Correct answer: 25 deg

MCQ (vi) In the figure, O is the centre of the circle and line ABN is a straight line; the exterior angle at B is 64 deg and the reflex angle at O is twice the interior angle at B. The obtuse angle AOC = x is

(a) 32 deg
(b) 64 deg
(c) 96 deg
(d) 128 deg
Correct answer: 128 deg

MCQ (vii) In the figure, O is the centre of the circle and the central angle is 110 deg; the inscribed angle x on the major arc is

(a) 55 deg
(b) 110 deg
(c) 220 deg
(d) 125 deg
Correct answer: 125 deg

MCQ (viii) In the figure, O is the centre of the circle, a diameter is drawn, and the radius to a point on the circle equals the chord from that point to one end of the diameter (equilateral triangle at the centre). Then angle x at the other end of the diameter is

(a) 15 deg
(b) 30 deg
(c) 45 deg
(d) 60 deg
Correct answer: 30 deg

mcqs.q: A circle passes through the vertices of right-angled triangle ABC with AC = 3 cm, BC = 4 cm and angle C = 90 degrees. The radius of the circle is:
mcqs.why: Formula: hypotenuse AB = sqrt(AC^2 + BC^2); radius = AB/2 since the hypotenuse is a diameter (angle in a semicircle). Step 1: AB = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 cm. Step 2: Radius = 5/2 = 2.5 cm. This is the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: Central angle (angle 2) and inscribed angle (angle 1) stand on the same arc AB. Then:
mcqs.why: By Theorem 1 the central angle on an arc is double the inscribed angle on the same arc, so angle 2 = 2 x angle 1. This is the book's keyed answer for MCQ (ii).

mcqs.q: The central angle on an arc is 75 degrees, and angles 1 and 2 are inscribed angles on the same arc. Angle 1 and angle 2 are respectively:
mcqs.why: Formula: inscribed angle = (1/2) x central angle. Step 1: Angle 1 = (1/2)(75 degrees) = 37.5 degrees. Step 2: Angle 2 stands on the same arc in the same segment, so by Theorem 2 it equals angle 1 = 37.5 degrees. This is the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: O is the centre and an inscribed angle in a segment measures 25 degrees. Another inscribed angle x in the same segment measures:
mcqs.why: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal (Theorem 2). Both angles stand in the same segment, so x equals the given angle in that segment, x = 25 degrees. This is the book's keyed answer for MCQ (iv).

mcqs.q: With O as centre, the angle y at the circumference standing in the same segment as a 25 degree inscribed angle measures:
mcqs.why: By Theorem 2, all angles in the same segment are equal, whatever point of the segment they are taken at. Hence y equals the given 25 degree angle in that segment: y = 25 degrees, the book's keyed answer for MCQ (v).

mcqs.q: O is the centre, ABN is a straight line, the exterior angle at B is 64 degrees and the reflex angle AOC is twice the interior angle at B. The obtuse angle AOC = x is:
mcqs.why: Formula: central angle = 2 x inscribed angle on the same arc. The inscribed angle subtending arc AC at B is 64 degrees (the angle in the alternate relation shown in the figure), so Step 1: x = 2 x 64 degrees = 128 degrees, an obtuse angle. This is the book's keyed answer for MCQ (vi).

mcqs.q: O is the centre and the (minor) central angle is 110 degrees. The inscribed angle x subtended by the major arc is:
mcqs.why: Formula: inscribed angle = (1/2) x reflex central angle on the same (major) arc. Step 1: Reflex angle at O = 360 - 110 = 250 degrees. Step 2: x = (1/2)(250 degrees) = 125 degrees. This is the book's keyed answer for MCQ (vii).

mcqs.q: A diameter is drawn and the radius to a point on the circle equals the chord from that point to one end of the diameter, forming an equilateral triangle at the centre. The angle x at the other end of the diameter is:
mcqs.why: The equilateral triangle gives a central angle of 60 degrees on the arc. Formula: inscribed angle = (1/2) x central angle. Step 1: x = (1/2)(60 degrees) = 30 degrees. This is the book's keyed answer for MCQ (viii).

mcqs.q: For the right-angled triangle of MCQ (i) with legs 3 cm and 4 cm, the hypotenuse AB, which is the diameter of the circumcircle, measures:
mcqs.why: Formula: Pythagoras, AB = sqrt(AC^2 + BC^2). Step 1: AC^2 + BC^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25. Step 2: AB = sqrt(25) = 5 cm. Since angle C = 90 degrees, this hypotenuse is the diameter of the circle through A, B and C.

mcqs.q: If an inscribed angle on an arc is 37.5 degrees, the central angle on the same arc is:
mcqs.why: Formula: central angle = 2 x inscribed angle (Theorem 1). Step 1: Central angle = 2 x 37.5 degrees = 75 degrees, which matches the central angle used in the book's MCQ (iii) of this exercise.

lessons.title: Constructions of Unit 13 (steps as given in the book)
lessons.notes_html:
Construction 13.1(i) To locate the centre of a given circle

Given: A circle (centre not marked).

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Draw two chords AB and CD of the circle.

Step 2: Draw line EFG as the perpendicular bisector of chord AB.

Step 3: Draw line PQR as the perpendicular bisector of chord CD.

Step 4: The perpendicular bisectors EFG and PQR intersect each other at O.

O is the centre of the circle (Unit 9, Theorem 1: the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre).

Construction 13.1(ii) Draw a circle passing through three given non-collinear points

Given: Three non-collinear points A, B and C.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Join A with B and B with C.

Step 2: Draw line LM and line PQ as the right (perpendicular) bisectors of AB and BC respectively; LM and PQ intersect at point O.

Step 3: Draw a circle with radius OA = OB = OC having centre at O.

This is the required circle (unique, by Unit 9 Theorem 1).

Construction 13.1(iii-a) To complete the circle by finding the centre when a part of a circumference is given

Given: Arc AB is a part of the circumference of a circle.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Let C, D, E and F be four points on the given arc AB.

Step 2: Draw chords CD and EF.

Step 3: Draw line PQ as perpendicular bisector of CD and line LM as perpendicular bisector of EF.

Step 4: LM and PQ intersect at O, so O is equidistant from points A, B, C, D, E and F.

Step 5: Complete the circle with centre O and radius OA = OB = OC = OD = OE = OF; it passes through all the points on the given part of the circumference.

Construction 13.1(iii-b) To complete the circle without finding the centre when a part of its circumference is given

Given: Arc AB is the part of the circumference of a circle.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Take two chords CD and DE of the suitable same length, which are chords of arc AB.

Step 2: Produce CD to D' and DE to E' to get the external angle D'DE'.

Step 3: Construct angle E'EF congruent to angle D'DE' and take EF = CD = DE; produce EF to F'.

Step 4: Construct angle F'FG congruent to angle E'EF' and take FG = CD; produce FG to G'.

Step 5: Points F and G are on the circumference of the required circle; the dotted arcs EF and FG are as shown in the book's figure.

Step 6: Continue this process of external angles of equal measure to complete the circumference of the circle.

Note (from the book): Constructing internal angles of equal measure, the circumference of the circle can also be completed.

Construction 13.2(i) Circumscribe a circle about a given triangle

Given: Triangle ABC.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Draw line LMN as perpendicular bisector of side AB.

Step 2: Draw line PQR as perpendicular bisector of side AC.

Step 3: LN and PR intersect at point O.

Step 4: With centre O and radius OA = OB = OC, draw a circle.

This circle passes through A, B and C; O is the circumcentre. Remember: the circle passing through the vertices of triangle ABC is the circumcircle, its radius the circumradius and its centre the circumcentre.

Construction 13.2(ii) Inscribe a circle in a given triangle

Given: A triangle ABC.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Draw ray BE and ray CF to bisect the angles ABC and ACB respectively; rays BE and CF intersect each other at point O.

Step 2: O is the centre of the inscribed circle.

Step 3: From O draw OP perpendicular to BC.

With centre O and radius OP draw a circle; this circle is the inscribed circle of triangle ABC.

Remember: a circle which touches the three sides of a triangle internally is known as incircle, its radius as in-radius and centre as in-centre.

Construction 13.2(iii) Escribe a circle to a given triangle (opposite to vertex A)

Given: A triangle ABC.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Produce the sides AB and AC of triangle ABC.

Step 2: Draw bisectors of the exterior angles at B and C (the exterior angles ABC-side and ACB-side); these bisectors of exterior angles meet at I1.

Step 3: From I1 draw a perpendicular on side BC of triangle ABC, meeting BC at D; I1D is the radius of the escribed circle with centre I1.

Step 4: Draw the circle with radius I1D and centre I1; it touches the side BC externally and the produced sides AB and AC.

Remember: the circle touching one side of the triangle externally and the two produced sides internally is called the escribed circle (e-circle); its centre is the e-centre and radius the e-radius.

Construction 13.2(iv) Circumscribe an equilateral triangle about a given circle

Given: A circle with centre O of reasonable radius.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Draw AB, a diameter of the circle, for locating.

Step 2: Draw an arc of radius OA with centre at A for locating points C and D on the circle.

Step 3: Join O to the points C and D.

Step 4: Draw tangents to the circle at points B, C and D.

Step 5: These tangents intersect at points E, F and G.

Triangle EFG is the required equilateral triangle circumscribed about the circle.

Construction 13.2(v) Inscribe an equilateral triangle in a given circle

Given: A circle with centre at O.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Draw any diameter AB of the circle.

Step 2: Draw an arc of radius OA from point A; the arc cuts the circle at points C and D.

Step 3: Join the points B, C and D to form the straight line segments BC, CD and BD.

Triangle BCD is the required inscribed equilateral triangle.

Construction 13.2(vi) Circumscribe a square about a given circle

Given: A circle with centre at O.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Draw two diameters PR and QS which bisect each other at right angle.

Step 2: At points P, Q, R and S draw tangents to the circle.

Step 3: Produce the tangents to meet each other at A, B, C and D.

ABCD is the required circumscribed square.

Construction 13.2(vii) Inscribe a square in a given circle

Given: A circle, with centre at O.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Through O draw two diameters AC and BD which bisect each other at right angle.

Step 2: Join A with B, B with C, C with D and D with A.

ABCD is the required square inscribed in the circle.

Construction 13.2(viii) Circumscribe a regular hexagon about a given circle

Given: A circle with centre at O.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Draw any diameter AD.

Step 2: From point A draw an arc of radius AO (the radius of the circle), which cuts the circle at points B and F.

Step 3: Join B with O and extend it to meet the circle at E.

Step 4: Join F with O and extend it to meet the circle at C.

Step 5: Draw tangents to the circle at points A, B, C, D, E and F intersecting one another at points P, Q, R, S, T and U respectively.

Thus PQRSTU is the circumscribed regular hexagon.

Construction 13.2(ix) Inscribe a regular hexagon in a given circle

Given: A circle, with centre at O.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Take any point A on the circle and join it with O.

Step 2: From point A, draw an arc of radius OA which intersects the circle at points B and F.

Step 3: Join O and A with points B and F; triangles OAB and OAF are equilateral, so angles AOB and AOF are 60 deg each, and OA = AB = AF.

Step 4: Produce FO to meet the circle at C; join B to C. Since angle BOC = 60 deg, BC = OA.

Step 5: From C and F, draw arcs of radius OA, which intersect the circle at points D and E.

Step 6: Join C to D, D to E and E to F; we have OA = OB = OC = OD = OE = OF.

Thus the figure ABCDEF is a regular hexagon inscribed in the circle.

Construction 13.3(i) To draw a tangent to a given arc without using the centre, through a given point P - Case (i): P is the middle point of the arc

Given: P is the mid-point of arc AB.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Join A and B to form the chord AB.

Step 2: Draw the perpendicular bisector of chord AB, which passes through the mid-point P of arc AB and the mid-point R of AB.

Step 3: At point P construct a right angle TPR.

Step 4: Produce PT in the direction of P beyond point S; thus line TP (produced) is the required tangent to the arc AB at point P.

Construction 13.3(i) Case (ii): P is at the end point of the arc

Given: P is the end point of arc PQR.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Take a point A on the arc PQR.

Step 2: Join the points A and P.

Step 3: Draw perpendicular AS at A which intersects the arc PQR at B.

Step 4: Join the points B and P.

Step 5: Draw angle APD of measure equal to that of angle ABP.

Step 6: Now angle BPD = angle BPA + angle APD = angle BPA + angle ABP = 90 deg (since angle APD = angle ABP, and angle BAP = 90 deg as the angle in a semicircle, so angle BPA + angle ABP = 90 deg).

Thus line PD is the required tangent.

Construction 13.3(i) Case (iii): Point P is outside the arc

Given: Point P is a point outside the arc ABC without knowing its centre.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Join A to P; AP cuts the arc at E.

Step 2: Find the mid-point M of AP.

Step 3: Draw a semi-circle of radius AM = MP with centre at M.

Step 4: Draw a perpendicular at point E which meets the semi-circle at D.

Step 5: Draw an arc of radius PD with P as its centre.

Step 6: This arc cuts the given arc ABC at point T.

Step 7: Join P with T; line PTQ is the required tangent.

Construction 13.3(ii-a) To draw a tangent to a circle from a given point P at a given point on the circumference

Given: A circle with centre O and some point P on the circumference.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Join point P to the centre O, so that OP is the radius of the circle.

Step 2: Draw a line TPS which is perpendicular to the radius OP.

Therefore line TPS is the required tangent to the circle at the given point P (Unit 10, Theorem 1).

Construction 13.3(ii-b) To draw a tangent to a circle from a given point P which lies outside the circle

Given: A circle with centre O and some point P outside the circle.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Join point P to the centre O.

Step 2: Find M, the mid-point of OP.

Step 3: Construct a semi-circle on diameter OP, with M as its centre; this semi-circle cuts the given circle at T.

Step 4: Join P with T and produce PT on both sides; then line PT is the required tangent (the angle in the semicircle at T is a right angle, so OT is perpendicular to PT).

Construction 13.3(iii) To draw two tangents to a circle meeting each other at a given angle

Given: A circle with centre O; angle MNS is a given angle.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Take a point A on the circumference of the circle having centre O.

Step 2: Join the points O and A.

Step 3: Draw angle COA of measure equal to that of angle MNS.

Step 4: Produce CO to meet the circle at B.

Step 5: So angle AOB = 180 deg - angle COA.

Step 6: Draw line AD perpendicular to OA.

Step 7: Draw line BE perpendicular to OB.

Step 8: Lines AD and BE intersect at P.

Step 9: Angle AOB + angle APB = 180 deg, i.e. angle AOB = 180 deg - angle APB.

Step 10: From Steps 5 and 9: 180 deg - angle COA = 180 deg - angle APB, so angle COA = angle APB, and hence angle APB = angle MNS (since angle COA = angle MNS).

Step 11: Lines AP and BP are the required tangents meeting at the given angle MNS.

Construction 13.3(iv-a) To draw direct (external) common tangents to equal circles

Given: Two circles of equal radii with centres O and O' respectively.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Join the centres O and O'.

Step 2: Draw diameter AOB of the first circle so that AOB is perpendicular to OO'.

Step 3: Draw diameter A'O'B' of the second circle so that A'O'B' is perpendicular to OO'.

Step 4: Draw lines AA' and BB', which are the required common (direct) tangents.

Construction 13.3(iv-b) To draw transverse (internal) common tangents to two equal circles

Given: Two equal circles with centres O and O' respectively.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Join the centres O and O'.

Step 2: Find the mid-point M of OO'.

Step 3: Find the mid-point N of MO'.

Step 4: Taking point N as centre and radius equal to MN, draw a circle intersecting the circle with centre O' at points P and P'.

Step 5: Draw a line through the points M and P touching the second circle at the point Q.

Step 6: Draw a line through the points M and P' touching the second circle at the point Q'.

Thus lines PQ and P'Q' are the required transverse common tangents to the given circles.

Construction 13.3(v-a) To draw direct (external) common tangents to two unequal circles

Given: Two unequal circles with centres O, O' and radii r, r' (r > r') respectively.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Join the points O and O'.

Step 2: On diameter OO', construct a new circle with centre M, the mid-point of OO'.

Step 3: Draw another circle with centre at O and radius r - r', cutting the circle with diameter OO' at P and Q.

Step 4: Produce OP and OQ to meet the first (bigger) circle at A and B respectively.

Step 5: Draw O'A' parallel to OA and O'B' parallel to OB, meeting the smaller circle at A' and B'.

Step 6: Join AA' and BB', which are the required direct common tangents.

Construction 13.3(v-b) To draw transverse (internal) common tangents to two unequal circles

Given: Two unequal circles with centres O, O' and radii r, r' respectively.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Join the centres O and O' of the given circles.

Step 2: Find the mid-point M of OO'.

Step 3: On diameter OO', construct a new circle with centre M.

Step 4: Draw another circle with centre O and radius r + r', intersecting the circle of diameter OO' at P and Q.

Step 5: Join O with P and Q; OP and OQ meet the circle with radius r at A and B respectively.

Step 6: Draw O'B' parallel to OA and O'A' parallel to OB (on the opposite sides).

Step 7: Join A with B' and A' with B; thus AB' and A'B are the required transverse common tangents.

Construction 13.3(vi-a) To draw a tangent to two unequal touching circles

Case I (one circle inside the other, touching internally): Given two unequal touching circles with centres O and O'.

Steps: Step 1: Join O with O' and produce OO' to meet the circles at the point A where the circles touch each other. Step 2: The tangent is perpendicular to the line segment OA. Step 3: Draw the perpendicular to OA at the point A, which is the required tangent.

Case II (circles touching externally): Given two unequal touching circles with centres O and O'.

Steps: Step 1: Join O with O'; OO' intersects the circles at the point B where they touch each other. Step 2: The tangent is perpendicular to the line segment containing the centres of the circles. Step 3: Draw the perpendicular to OO' at the point B, which is the required tangent.

Construction 13.3(vi-b) To draw a (direct common) tangent to two unequal intersecting circles

Given: Two intersecting circles with centres A and B (radii r and r1, r > r1).

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Take the line segment AB joining the centres.

Step 2: Draw the two circles of radii r and r1 with centres A and B respectively.

Step 3: Taking centre at A, draw a circle of radius r - r1.

Step 4: Bisect the line segment AB at point M.

Step 5: Taking centre at M and radius AM = BM, draw a circle intersecting the circle of radius r - r1 at P and Q.

Step 6: Join A with P and produce it to meet the circle with centre A at D; also join A with Q and produce it to meet the circle with centre A at C.

Step 7: Draw BN parallel to AD, intersecting the circle with centre B at T.

Step 8: Join D and T; line DT is a common tangent to the given two circles.

Step 9: Repeat the same process on the other side of AB; line CT' is also a common tangent to the given two circles.

Construction 13.3(vii-a) To draw a circle which touches both the arms of a given angle

Given: An angle BAC.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Draw ray AD bisecting angle BAC.

Step 2: Take any point E on AD.

Step 3: Draw line ET perpendicular to AC, intersecting AC at the point F.

Step 4: Draw a circle with centre E and radius EF.

This circle touches both the arms of angle BAC (every point on the bisector is equidistant from the arms).

Construction 13.3(vii-b) To draw a circle touching two convergent lines and passing through a given point between them

Given: Lines BS and CT are two converging lines, and P is a given point between them.

Steps of Construction:

Step 1: Produce BS and produce CT; they intersect at A.

Step 2: Draw ray AD bisecting angle BAC.

Step 3: Take any point E on AD.

Step 4: Draw EF perpendicular to line AB.

Step 5: Draw a circle with centre E and radius EF.

Step 6: This circle touches lines AB and AC.

Step 7: Draw ray AP, which cuts this circle at the point H; join E and H.

Step 8: Through P, draw line PZ parallel to HE, intersecting AD at the point O.

Step 9: Draw a new circle with centre O and radius OP; this circle touches both the lines and passes through P.

Construction 13.3(vii-c) To draw a circle which touches three converging lines

Note (from the book): It is not possible to draw a circle touching three converging lines.

Reason: The centre of a circle touching two converging lines must lie on the bisector of the angle between them; for a third converging line the centre would also have to lie on another bisector, and the single intersection point of the bisectors is at a different distance from the third line in general - so no single circle can touch all three converging lines.

mcqs.q: To locate the centre of a given circle (Construction 13.1(i)), the centre O is found as:
options: The intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of two chords AB and CD
The intersection of two chords AB and CD
The midpoint of a chord AB
mcqs.why: Draw two chords AB and CD, then draw the perpendicular bisector of each chord. The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre, so the two bisectors meet at O, the centre of the circle.

mcqs.q: To draw a circle through three given non-collinear points A, B and C (Construction 13.1(ii)), the centre O is:
options: The intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC, with radius OA = OB = OC
The midpoint of the longest side
The intersection of the angle bisectors of triangle ABC
mcqs.why: Join A to B and B to C, draw the perpendicular bisectors LM of AB and PQ of BC; they meet at O. With centre O and radius OA (= OB = OC) the circle passes through all three points, and it is unique.

mcqs.q: To complete a circle when part of its circumference (arc AB) is given, using the centre (Construction 13.1(iii-a)), you take points C, D, E, F on the arc, draw chords CD and EF, and then:
options: Draw tangents at C and F
Draw the perpendicular bisectors of CD and EF; their intersection is the centre O
Join C to E and D to F
mcqs.why: The perpendicular bisector PQ of chord CD and the perpendicular bisector LM of chord EF intersect at O, which is equidistant from A, B, C, D, E and F. The circle with centre O and radius OA completes the given part of the circumference.

mcqs.q: To complete a circle from a given arc WITHOUT finding the centre (Construction 13.1(iii-b)), the method used is to construct repeatedly:
options: External angles of equal measure at successive points of the arc
Tangents at the ends of the arc
mcqs.why: Take equal chords CD and DE, produce them to get the external angle D'DE', then construct a congruent external angle at E with EF = CD, and so on. Continuing with external angles of equal measure completes the circumference; equal internal angles can be used instead.

mcqs.q: To circumscribe a circle about triangle ABC (Construction 13.2(i)), the circumcentre O is the intersection of:
options: The bisectors of two angles of the triangle
The perpendicular bisectors of two sides of the triangle
mcqs.why: Draw the perpendicular bisector LMN of AB and the perpendicular bisector PQR of AC; they intersect at O. The circle with centre O and radius OA = OB = OC passes through A, B and C and is the circumcircle.

mcqs.q: To inscribe a circle in triangle ABC (Construction 13.2(ii)), after finding the in-centre O as the meeting of two angle bisectors, the in-radius is taken as:
options: OA, the distance to a vertex
The perpendicular OP from O to side BC
The length of an angle bisector
mcqs.why: Bisect angles ABC and ACB by rays BE and CF meeting at O, the in-centre. From O draw OP perpendicular to BC; the circle with centre O and radius OP touches all three sides internally and is the incircle.

mcqs.q: To escribe a circle opposite vertex A (Construction 13.2(iii)), the e-centre I1 is the meeting point of:
options: The perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC
The interior bisectors of angles B and C
The bisectors of the exterior angles at B and C, after producing sides AB and AC
The tangents at B and C
mcqs.why: Produce sides AB and AC, then bisect the exterior angles at B and C; these exterior bisectors meet at I1. The perpendicular I1D from I1 to BC is the e-radius, and the circle touches BC externally and the produced sides AB and AC.

mcqs.q: To inscribe an equilateral triangle in a given circle (Construction 13.2(v)), after drawing diameter AB and an arc of radius OA from A cutting the circle at C and D, the required triangle is:
options: Triangle BCD, formed by joining B, C and D
Triangle formed by the tangents at B, C and D
mcqs.why: Draw any diameter AB, then an arc of radius OA from A cutting the circle at C and D. Joining B to C, C to D and D to B gives triangle BCD, the required equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle.

mcqs.q: To inscribe a square in a given circle (Construction 13.2(vii)), the first step is to draw:
options: Four tangents at the ends of one diameter
Two diameters AC and BD through O which bisect each other at right angles
An arc of radius OA from a point on the circle
The perpendicular bisector of one radius
mcqs.why: Through the centre O draw two diameters AC and BD at right angles to each other. Joining A to B, B to C, C to D and D to A gives the square ABCD inscribed in the circle.

mcqs.q: In the construction of a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle (Construction 13.2(ix)), each side of the hexagon is equal to:
options: Half the radius of the circle
The radius OA of the circle
Twice the radius of the circle
mcqs.why: Triangles OAB and OAF formed with an arc of radius OA are equilateral, so angle AOB = 60 degrees and AB = OA. Stepping the radius around the circle gives six equal chords, each equal to the radius, forming the regular hexagon ABCDEF.

mcqs.q: To draw a tangent at a given point P on the circumference (Construction 13.3(ii-a)), the tangent line TPS is drawn:
options: Perpendicular to the radius OP at P
At 45 degrees to the radius OP
mcqs.why: Join P to the centre O so OP is a radius, then draw line TPS perpendicular to OP at P. A line perpendicular to a radius at its outer end is the tangent to the circle at that point.

mcqs.q: To draw a tangent from an external point P to a circle with centre O (Construction 13.3(ii-b)), the point of contact T is found by:
options: Drawing a circle on OP as diameter, with centre at the midpoint M of OP, cutting the given circle at T
Drawing a line from P parallel to a radius
Taking T as the midpoint of OP
mcqs.why: Join P to O, find the midpoint M of OP, and draw the semicircle on diameter OP with centre M; it cuts the given circle at T. Joining P to T gives the tangent, because the angle in the semicircle at T is a right angle, so OT is perpendicular to PT.

mcqs.q: In drawing two tangents meeting at a given angle MNS (Construction 13.3(iii)), the angle AOB between the two radii to the points of contact satisfies:
options: Angle AOB + angle APB = 180 degrees, so angle APB equals the given angle
mcqs.why: Tangents AD and BE are drawn perpendicular to radii OA and OB, meeting at P. In quadrilateral OAPB the angles at A and B are right angles, so angle AOB + angle APB = 180 degrees. The construction makes angle COA equal to angle MNS, which forces angle APB = angle MNS.

mcqs.q: To draw direct (external) common tangents to two unequal circles of radii r and r' with r > r' (Construction 13.3(v-a)), the auxiliary circle drawn with centre O has radius:
mcqs.why: Join the centres O and O', draw the circle on OO' as diameter, then draw a circle with centre O and radius r - r' cutting it at P and Q. Producing OP and OQ to the bigger circle and drawing parallel radii in the smaller circle gives the points joined by the direct common tangents AA' and BB'.

mcqs.q: To draw transverse (internal) common tangents to two unequal circles of radii r and r' (Construction 13.3(v-b)), the auxiliary circle drawn with centre O has radius:
mcqs.why: For transverse tangents the auxiliary circle at O has radius r + r' (the sum, not the difference) and cuts the circle on diameter OO' at P and Q. Radii drawn parallel on opposite sides then give the transverse common tangents AB' and A'B.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Divide an arc of any length (i) into two equal parts (ii) into four equal parts

Construction (in words): Given an arc AB of a circle.

(i) Into two equal parts: Step 1: Draw the chord AB. Step 2: Draw the perpendicular bisector of chord AB (arcs of equal radius from A and B cutting each other on both sides; join the intersection points). Step 3: The perpendicular bisector meets the arc AB at its mid-point M, because the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre and bisects the arc. Arc AM = arc MB.

(ii) Into four equal parts: Step 1: First bisect the arc as in (i), getting the mid-point M. Step 2: Draw chords AM and MB and bisect each of them by the same perpendicular-bisector construction, getting points P on arc AM and Q on arc MB. Step 3: Then arc AP = arc PM = arc MQ = arc QB: the arc is divided into four equal parts.

Q2 Practically find the centre of an arc ABC

Construction (in words): Step 1: On the arc ABC take the three points A, B and C. Step 2: Draw chords AB and BC. Step 3: Draw the perpendicular bisector of chord AB and the perpendicular bisector of chord BC (equal-radius arcs from the endpoints of each chord, joined). Step 4: The two perpendicular bisectors intersect at a point O. Step 5: O is equidistant from A, B and C (OA = OB = OC), so O is the centre of the arc ABC (Construction 13.1(i)/(ii)).

Q3(i) If AB = 3 cm and BC = 4 cm are the lengths of two chords of an arc, then locate the centre of the arc

Construction (in words): Step 1: Draw the arc's two chords AB = 3 cm and BC = 4 cm meeting at B on the arc. Step 2: Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB: with centres A and B and radius more than half of AB, draw arcs cutting each other at two points; join them. Step 3: Draw the perpendicular bisector of BC = 4 cm in the same way. Step 4: The two perpendicular bisectors meet at O. O is the centre of the arc; check by measuring OA = OB = OC.

Q3(ii) If AB = 3.5 cm and BC = 5 cm are the lengths of two chords of an arc, then locate the centre of the arc

Construction (in words): Step 1: Draw chords AB = 3.5 cm and BC = 5 cm of the arc. Step 2: Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB (equal arcs from A and B, radius more than 1.75 cm, cutting on both sides; join the cuts). Step 3: Draw the perpendicular bisector of BC in the same way. Step 4: Their intersection O is the centre of the arc, with OA = OB = OC as the radius.

Q4 For an arc, draw two perpendicular bisectors of the chords PQ and QR of this arc; construct a circle through P, Q and R

Construction (in words): Step 1: On the given arc mark the points P, Q and R and draw chords PQ and QR. Step 2: Draw the perpendicular bisector of chord PQ. Step 3: Draw the perpendicular bisector of chord QR. Step 4: The bisectors intersect at O. Step 5: With centre O and radius OP (= OQ = OR) draw the circle; it passes through P, Q and R and completes the given arc (Construction 13.1(ii)).

Q5 Describe a circle of radius 5 cm passing through points A and B, 6 cm apart. Also find the distance from the centre to the line segment AB

Construction (in words): Step 1: Draw segment AB = 6 cm. Step 2: Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB, meeting AB at its mid-point M (AM = 3 cm). Step 3: With centre A and radius 5 cm draw an arc cutting the perpendicular bisector at O (two choices, one on each side). Step 4: With centre O and radius OA = 5 cm draw the circle; it passes through A and B.

Distance from the centre to AB: Formula (Pythagoras in triangle OMA): OM = sqrt(OA^2 - AM^2).

Step 1: OA = 5 cm (radius), AM = 6/2 = 3 cm.

Step 2: OM = sqrt(25 - 9) = sqrt(16) = 4 cm.

The distance from the centre to the line segment AB is 4 cm.

Q6 If AB = 4 cm and BC = 6 cm, such that AB is perpendicular to BC, construct a circle through points A, B and C. Also measure its radius

Construction (in words): Step 1: Draw AB = 4 cm and BC = 6 cm perpendicular to AB at B; join A to C. Step 2: Since angle ABC = 90 deg, the hypotenuse AC must be a diameter of the circle through A, B, C (angle in a semicircle, Unit 12 Theorem 3). Step 3: Find the mid-point O of AC by its perpendicular bisector. Step 4: With centre O and radius OA draw the circle through A, B and C.

Radius: Formula: AC = sqrt(AB^2 + BC^2); radius = AC/2.

Step 1: AC = sqrt(16 + 36) = sqrt(52) = 2 x sqrt(13) cm.

Step 2: Radius = sqrt(13) cm = about 3.61 cm (measured on the construction: about 3.6 cm).

mcqs.q: To divide a given arc AB into two equal parts (Exercise 13.1 Q1), the mid-point M of the arc is obtained where:
options: The tangent at A meets the chord AB
The perpendicular bisector of chord AB meets the arc AB
The angle bisector at the centre meets chord AB
mcqs.why: Draw chord AB and its perpendicular bisector (equal-radius arcs from A and B joined). The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre and bisects the arc, meeting arc AB at its mid-point M, so arc AM = arc MB.

mcqs.q: To divide an arc AB into four equal parts (Exercise 13.1 Q1), after bisecting arc AB at M you must:
options: Draw tangents at A, M and B
Bisect arc AM at P and arc MB at Q by the same perpendicular-bisector construction
Halve the chord AB twice with a ruler only
mcqs.why: First bisect the whole arc at M. Then draw chords AM and MB and bisect each arc by its chord's perpendicular bisector, giving P on arc AM and Q on arc MB. Then arc AP = arc PM = arc MQ = arc QB.

mcqs.q: To find the centre of an arc ABC practically (Exercise 13.1 Q2), the centre O is:
options: The intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of chords AB and BC
The intersection of chords AB and BC
mcqs.why: Take points A, B, C on the arc, draw chords AB and BC and the perpendicular bisector of each chord. Their intersection O satisfies OA = OB = OC, so O is the centre of the arc ABC.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 13.1 Q3(i), chords AB = 3 cm and BC = 4 cm of an arc are given. The centre is located by drawing:
options: Circles of radii 3 cm and 4 cm at B
The perpendicular bisectors of AB and of BC; their meeting point O is the centre
The bisector of angle ABC only
mcqs.why: Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB = 3 cm (arcs from A and B with radius more than half of AB) and of BC = 4 cm in the same way. They meet at O, the centre, checked by measuring OA = OB = OC.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 13.1 Q3(ii), AB = 3.5 cm. For the perpendicular bisector of AB, the arcs from A and B must be drawn with radius:
options: More than 1.75 cm, i.e. more than half of AB
mcqs.why: Half of AB = 3.5/2 = 1.75 cm. The compass radius must be more than half the chord so that the arcs from A and B actually cross each other on both sides; joining the crossings gives the perpendicular bisector.

mcqs.q: For an arc with points P, Q, R (Exercise 13.1 Q4), the circle through P, Q and R is drawn with centre at the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of chords PQ and QR, and with radius:
options: OP, which equals OQ and OR
mcqs.why: The bisectors of PQ and QR meet at O, which is equidistant from the three points: OP = OQ = OR. The circle with centre O and radius OP passes through P, Q and R and completes the given arc.

mcqs.q: A circle of radius 5 cm passes through A and B with AB = 6 cm (Exercise 13.1 Q5). The centre O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, and AM, where M is the midpoint of AB, equals:
mcqs.why: Formula: M is the midpoint of AB, so AM = AB/2. Step 1: AM = 6/2 = 3 cm. The centre O is found where an arc of radius 5 cm from A cuts the perpendicular bisector of AB.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 13.1 Q5 (radius OA = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm), the distance OM from the centre to the chord AB is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Pythagoras in triangle OMA, OM = sqrt(OA^2 - AM^2). Step 1: OA = 5 cm, AM = 3 cm. Step 2: OM = sqrt(25 - 9) = sqrt(16) = 4 cm. So the centre is 4 cm from the line segment AB.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 13.1 Q6, AB = 4 cm is perpendicular to BC = 6 cm, and a circle is drawn through A, B and C. The hypotenuse AC must be a diameter of this circle because:
options: Every chord of a circle is a diameter
Angle ABC = 90 degrees is an angle in a semicircle, so AC subtends it as a diameter
AB and BC are radii of the circle
mcqs.why: Angle ABC = 90 degrees stands on arc AC. By the converse of the semicircle theorem (Unit 12, Theorem 3), a right angle at the circumference means AC is a diameter, so the centre is the midpoint of AC.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 13.1 Q6 (AB = 4 cm, BC = 6 cm, right angle at B), the radius of the circle through A, B and C is:
mcqs.why: Formula: AC = sqrt(AB^2 + BC^2); radius = AC/2. Step 1: AC = sqrt(16 + 36) = sqrt(52) = 2 x sqrt(13) cm. Step 2: Radius = (2 x sqrt(13))/2 = sqrt(13) cm, which is about 3.61 cm, matching the measured value of about 3.6 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 Circumscribe a circle about a triangle ABC with sides AB = 6 cm, BC = 3 cm, CA = 4 cm. Also measure its circum radius

Construction (in words): Step 1: Construct triangle ABC with AB = 6 cm, BC = 3 cm, CA = 4 cm (arcs from A and B). Step 2: Draw the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC (Construction 13.2(i)); they meet at the circumcentre O. Step 3: With centre O and radius OA draw the circumcircle.

Circumradius (check by formula): Formula: R = abc / (4 x Area), Area by Heron: s = (3 + 4 + 6)/2 = 6.5; Area = sqrt(6.5 x 3.5 x 2.5 x 0.5) = sqrt(28.4375) = 5.33 cm^2.

Step 1: R = (3 x 4 x 6) / (4 x 5.33) = 72 / 21.33 = 3.38 cm.

Measured circumradius: about 3.4 cm.

Q2 Inscribe a circle in a triangle ABC with sides AB = 5 cm, BC = 3 cm, CA = 3 cm. Also measure its in-radius

Construction (in words): Step 1: Construct triangle ABC with the given sides. Step 2: Bisect angles B and C (Construction 13.2(ii)); the bisectors meet at the in-centre O. Step 3: From O drop a perpendicular OP to BC. Step 4: With centre O and radius OP draw the incircle.

In-radius (check by formula): Formula: r = Area / s. s = (5 + 3 + 3)/2 = 5.5; Area = sqrt(5.5 x 0.5 x 2.5 x 2.5) = sqrt(17.1875) = 4.15 cm^2.

Step 1: r = 4.15 / 5.5 = 0.75 cm.

Measured in-radius: about 0.75 cm.

Q3 Escribe a circle opposite to vertex A to a triangle ABC with sides AB = 6 cm, BC = 4 cm, CA = 3 cm. Find its radius also

Construction (in words): Step 1: Construct triangle ABC with the given sides. Step 2: Produce AB and AC beyond B and C... (for the circle opposite A: produce AB and AC and bisect the exterior angles at B and C, Construction 13.2(iii)); the bisectors meet at the e-centre I1. Step 3: From I1 drop a perpendicular I1D to BC. Step 4: With centre I1 and radius I1D draw the escribed circle opposite A.

E-radius (check by formula): Formula: r_a = Area / (s - a), where a = BC = 4. s = (6 + 4 + 3)/2 = 6.5; Area = sqrt(6.5 x 0.5 x 2.5 x 3.5) = sqrt(28.4375) = 5.33 cm^2.

Step 1: r_a = 5.33 / (6.5 - 4) = 5.33 / 2.5 = 2.13 cm.

The escribed radius is about 2.13 cm.

Q4 Circumscribe a circle about an equilateral triangle ABC with each side of length 4 cm

Construction (in words): Step 1: Construct the equilateral triangle ABC with side 4 cm. Step 2: Draw the perpendicular bisectors of two sides; they meet at the circumcentre O (for an equilateral triangle this is also the centroid). Step 3: With centre O and radius OA draw the circumcircle.

Circumradius: Formula: R = a / sqrt(3). Step 1: R = 4 / 1.732 = 2.31 cm.

Measured: about 2.3 cm.

Q5 Inscribe a circle in an equilateral triangle ABC with each side of length 5 cm

Construction (in words): Step 1: Construct the equilateral triangle ABC with side 5 cm. Step 2: Bisect two angles; the bisectors meet at the in-centre O (same point as the circumcentre). Step 3: Drop a perpendicular from O to a side and draw the circle with that radius.

In-radius: Formula: r = a / (2 x sqrt(3)). Step 1: r = 5 / 3.464 = 1.44 cm.

Measured: about 1.44 cm.

Q6 Circumscribe and inscribe circles with regard to a right-angle triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm

Construction (in words): Step 1: Construct the right-angled triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and hypotenuse 5 cm. Step 2 (circumcircle): The hypotenuse is a diameter (angle in a semicircle), so take the mid-point of the hypotenuse as centre O and radius half the hypotenuse; draw the circle. Circumradius = 5/2 = 2.5 cm. Step 3 (incircle): Bisect two angles to get the in-centre; drop a perpendicular to a side and draw the circle.

In-radius: Formula: r = (sum of legs - hypotenuse)/2. Step 1: r = (3 + 4 - 5)/2 = 1 cm.

So circumradius = 2.5 cm and in-radius = 1 cm.

Q7 In and around the circle of radius 4 cm draw a square

Construction (in words): Step 1: Draw the circle of radius 4 cm with centre O. Step 2 (inscribed square): Draw two diameters at right angles to each other and join their four ends (Construction 13.2(vii)); the inscribed square has diagonal 8 cm, so its side = 8/sqrt(2) = 4 x sqrt(2) = about 5.66 cm. Step 3 (circumscribed square): Draw tangents at the ends of the two perpendicular diameters and produce them to meet (Construction 13.2(vi)); the circumscribed square has side equal to the diameter = 8 cm.

Q8 In and around the circle of radius 3.5 cm draw a regular hexagon

Construction (in words): Step 1: Draw the circle of radius 3.5 cm. Step 2 (inscribed hexagon): From a point A on the circle step the radius 3.5 cm around the circle with the compass (Construction 13.2(ix)) and join the six points; each side of the inscribed regular hexagon equals the radius = 3.5 cm. Step 3 (circumscribed hexagon): Draw tangents at those six points and let them meet (Construction 13.2(viii)); each side of the circumscribed regular hexagon = 2 x 3.5 x tan(30 deg) = about 4.04 cm.

Q9 Circumscribe a regular hexagon about a circle of radius 3 cm

Construction (in words): Follow Construction 13.2(viii) with the circle of radius 3 cm: draw a diameter, step the radius from one end to get points B and F, produce the radii to get all six points of contact, and draw tangents at the six points; the tangents form the circumscribed regular hexagon PQRSTU.

Each side of this hexagon = 2 x 3 x tan(30 deg) = about 3.46 cm.

mcqs.q: For triangle ABC with AB = 6 cm, BC = 3 cm, CA = 4 cm (Exercise 13.2 Q1), the measured circumradius of its circumcircle is about:
mcqs.why: Formula: R = abc/(4 x Area), s = (3 + 4 + 6)/2 = 6.5, Area = sqrt(6.5 x 3.5 x 2.5 x 0.5) = sqrt(28.4375) = 5.33 cm^2. Step 1: R = (3 x 4 x 6)/(4 x 5.33) = 72/21.33 = 3.38 cm, i.e. about 3.4 cm measured. The centre is the meeting of the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC.

mcqs.q: For triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, BC = 3 cm, CA = 3 cm (Exercise 13.2 Q2), the measured in-radius of its incircle is about:
mcqs.why: Formula: r = Area/s. Step 1: s = (5 + 3 + 3)/2 = 5.5. Step 2: Area = sqrt(5.5 x 0.5 x 2.5 x 2.5) = sqrt(17.1875) = 4.15 cm^2. Step 3: r = 4.15/5.5 = 0.75 cm. The in-centre is the meeting of the bisectors of angles B and C.

mcqs.q: For triangle ABC with AB = 6 cm, BC = 4 cm, CA = 3 cm (Exercise 13.2 Q3), the radius of the escribed circle opposite vertex A is about:
The circumradius of an equilateral triangle of side 4 cm (Exercise 13.2 Q4) is about:
mcqs.why: Formula: For an equilateral triangle, R = a/sqrt(3). Step 1: R = 4/1.732 = 2.31 cm, measured about 2.3 cm. The circumcentre is the meeting of the perpendicular bisectors of two sides.

mcqs.q: The in-radius of an equilateral triangle of side 5 cm (Exercise 13.2 Q5) is about:
mcqs.why: Formula: For an equilateral triangle, r = a/(2 x sqrt(3)). Step 1: r = 5/(2 x 1.732) = 5/3.464 = 1.44 cm. The in-centre is the same point as the circumcentre for an equilateral triangle.

mcqs.q: For the right-angled triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm (Exercise 13.2 Q6), the circumradius is:
mcqs.why: Formula: The hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumcircle (angle in a semicircle), so R = hypotenuse/2. Step 1: R = 5/2 = 2.5 cm, with the centre at the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

mcqs.q: For the same right-angled triangle with legs 3 cm and 4 cm and hypotenuse 5 cm (Exercise 13.2 Q6), the in-radius is:
mcqs.why: Formula: For a right-angled triangle, r = (sum of legs - hypotenuse)/2. Step 1: r = (3 + 4 - 5)/2 = 2/2 = 1 cm. The incircle is drawn from the in-centre found by bisecting two angles.

mcqs.q: In and around a circle of radius 4 cm (Exercise 13.2 Q7), the side of the inscribed square is about:
mcqs.why: Formula: The diagonal of the inscribed square is the diameter = 8 cm, so side = diagonal/sqrt(2). Step 1: Side = 8/1.414 = 4 x sqrt(2) = about 5.66 cm. The square is formed by joining the ends of two diameters drawn at right angles.

mcqs.q: In and around the same circle of radius 4 cm (Exercise 13.2 Q7), the side of the circumscribed square equals:
mcqs.why: The circumscribed square is formed by tangents at the ends of two perpendicular diameters. Its side spans the full width of the circle, so side = diameter = 2 x 4 = 8 cm.

mcqs.q: In and around a circle of radius 3.5 cm (Exercise 13.2 Q8), each side of the inscribed regular hexagon equals:
mcqs.why: Stepping the compass set to the radius around the circle marks the six vertices, because each side of a regular inscribed hexagon equals the radius. Here each side = 3.5 cm. The circumscribed hexagon in the same question has side about 4.04 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.3
lessons.notes_html:
Q1 In an arc ABC the length of the chord BC = 2 cm. Draw a secant PBC = 8 cm, where P is the point outside the arc. Draw a tangent through point P to the arc

Construction (in words): Use Construction 13.3(i) Case (iii) (point outside the arc): Step 1: On the given arc ABC, chord BC = 2 cm; place P outside so that the secant PBC measures 8 cm (P-B-C along a straight line). Step 2: Join A to P; AP cuts the arc at E. Step 3: Find the mid-point M of AP and draw the semi-circle on AP with centre M. Step 4: Draw the perpendicular at E meeting the semi-circle at D. Step 5: With centre P and radius PD draw an arc cutting the given arc at T. Step 6: Join P with T; PT is the required tangent from P.

Q2 Construct a circle with diameter 8 cm. Indicate a point C, 5 cm away from its circumference. Draw a tangent from point C to the circle without using its centre

Construction (in words): Step 1: Draw the circle with diameter 8 cm (radius 4 cm) - centre not to be used afterwards. Step 2: Mark point C outside, 5 cm away from the circumference (i.e. 9 cm from the centre along any ray). Step 3: Draw any chord of the circle through... apply Construction 13.3(i) Case (iii) treating the circumference as the given arc: join a point A of the circle to C, bisect AC, draw the semi-circle on AC, erect the perpendicular where AC re-meets the circle, transfer that length from C to find the contact point T, and join C with T. CT is the required tangent, drawn without using the centre.

Q3 Construct a circle of radius 2 cm. Draw two tangents making an angle of 60 deg with each other

Construction (in words): Use Construction 13.3(iii) with the given angle 60 deg: Step 1: Draw the circle of radius 2 cm with centre O; take a point A on it and join OA. Step 2: Construct at O an angle COA equal to 60 deg and produce CO to meet the circle at B, so angle AOB = 180 - 60 = 120 deg. Step 3: Draw the tangent at A (perpendicular to OA) and the tangent at B (perpendicular to OB). Step 4: The two tangents meet at P with angle APB = 180 - 120 = 60 deg, as required.

Q4 Draw two perpendicular tangents to a circle of radius 3 cm

Construction (in words): Step 1: Draw the circle of radius 3 cm with centre O. Step 2: Draw two radii OA and OB at right angles to each other (angle AOB = 90 deg). Step 3: Draw the tangent at A perpendicular to OA and the tangent at B perpendicular to OB. Step 4: The tangents meet at P; in quadrilateral OAPB, angle APB = 360 - 90 - 90 - 90 = 90 deg, so the two tangents are perpendicular, as required. (Equivalently, Construction 13.3(iii) with given angle 90 deg.)

Q5 Two equal circles are at 8 cm apart. Draw two direct common tangents of this pair of circles

Construction (in words): Use Construction 13.3(iv-a): Step 1: Draw the two equal circles with centres O and O' 8 cm apart. Step 2: Join OO'. Step 3: In each circle draw the diameter perpendicular to OO'. Step 4: Join the corresponding ends of these diameters (top to top, bottom to bottom); the two joining lines are the direct common tangents, each of length 8 cm (equal to OO').

Q6 Draw two equal circles of each radius 2.4 cm. If the distance between their centres is 6 cm, then draw their transverse tangents

Construction (in words): Use Construction 13.3(iv-b): Step 1: Draw the two equal circles of radius 2.4 cm with centres O, O' 6 cm apart; join OO'. Step 2: Find the mid-point M of OO' and the mid-point N of MO'. Step 3: With centre N and radius MN draw a circle cutting the O' circle at P and P'. Step 4: Lines through M and P, and through M and P', touching the second circle, are the two transverse common tangents; they cross OO' at its mid-point M.

Q7 Draw two circles with radii 2.5 cm and 3 cm. If their centres are 6.5 cm apart, then draw two direct common tangents

Construction (in words): Use Construction 13.3(v-a): Step 1: Draw the circles with centres O (radius 3 cm) and O' (radius 2.5 cm), OO' = 6.5 cm. Step 2: Construct the circle on OO' as diameter (centre = mid-point M). Step 3: With centre O draw a circle of radius 3 - 2.5 = 0.5 cm cutting the diameter-circle at P and Q. Step 4: Produce OP, OQ to meet the big circle at A, B; draw O'A' parallel to OA and O'B' parallel to OB. Step 5: Join AA' and BB' - the two direct common tangents.

Q8 Draw two circles with radii 3.5 cm and 2 cm. If their centres are 6 cm apart, then draw two transverse common tangents

Construction (in words): Use Construction 13.3(v-b): Step 1: Draw the circles with centres O (radius 3.5 cm) and O' (radius 2 cm), OO' = 6 cm. Step 2: Construct the circle on OO' as diameter. Step 3: With centre O draw a circle of radius 3.5 + 2 = 5.5 cm cutting the diameter-circle at P and Q. Step 4: Join O to P and Q to get A and B on the big circle; draw the radii O'B' parallel to OA and O'A' parallel to OB on opposite sides. Step 5: Join AB' and A'B - the two transverse common tangents.

Q9 Draw two common tangents to two touching circles of radii 2.5 cm and 3.5 cm

Construction (in words): Step 1: Draw the two circles of radii 2.5 cm and 3.5 cm touching externally, centres O, O' with OO' = 2.5 + 3.5 = 6 cm. Step 2: The common tangent at the point of contact: join OO', mark the contact point B on it, and draw the perpendicular to OO' at B (Construction 13.3(vi-a) Case II) - this is one common tangent. Step 3: A direct common tangent: apply Construction 13.3(v-a) with r - r' = 1 cm to draw one of the two direct common tangents. (Two touching circles have exactly 3 common tangents in total: the one at the contact point and two direct ones.)

Q10 Draw two common tangents to two intersecting circles of radii 3 cm and 4 cm

Construction (in words): Step 1: Draw the two circles of radii 3 cm and 4 cm with centres close enough to intersect (centres, say, 5 cm apart, since 4 - 3 < 5 < 4 + 3). Step 2: Apply Construction 13.3(vi-b): with centre A (radius 4 cm) draw a circle of radius 4 - 3 = 1 cm; bisect AB at M; with centre M draw the circle on AB as diameter cutting the 1 cm circle at P and Q. Step 3: Produce AP to meet the big circle at D and draw the radius of the small circle parallel to AD, giving T. Step 4: DT is one direct common tangent; repeat on the other side for the second. (Intersecting circles have exactly 2 common tangents, both direct.)

Q11 Draw circles which touch both the arms of angles (i) 45 deg (ii) 60 deg

Construction (in words): Use Construction 13.3(vii-a) for each angle: Step 1: Draw the angle (45 deg, then separately 60 deg) with vertex A. Step 2: Bisect the angle by ray AD. Step 3: Take any point E on AD and drop the perpendicular EF to one arm. Step 4: Draw the circle with centre E and radius EF; it touches both arms of the angle. (Any point of the bisector may be chosen as centre, giving a family of such circles.)

mcqs.q: Point P lies outside arc ABC with secant PBC = 8 cm (Exercise 13.3 Q1). In the tangent construction from P, the point of contact T on the arc is found by drawing:
options: A circle with centre P and radius PB
An arc of radius PD with centre P, cutting the given arc at T; then PT is the tangent
mcqs.why: Following Construction 13.3(i) Case (iii): join A to P meeting the arc at E, bisect AP at M, draw the semicircle on AP, erect the perpendicular at E meeting it at D, then swing an arc of radius PD from P to cut the arc at T. Joining P to T gives the required tangent.

mcqs.q: Two tangents to a circle of radius 2 cm are to make an angle of 60 degrees with each other (Exercise 13.3 Q3). The angle AOB between the radii to the points of contact must be:
mcqs.why: Formula: angle between tangents + angle between radii = 180 degrees. Step 1: Construct angle COA = 60 degrees and produce CO to B, so angle AOB = 180 - 60 = 120 degrees. Step 2: Tangents at A and B then meet at P with angle APB = 180 - 120 = 60 degrees, as required.

mcqs.q: To draw two perpendicular tangents to a circle of radius 3 cm (Exercise 13.3 Q4), the radii OA and OB to the points of contact are drawn with angle AOB equal to:
mcqs.why: Draw radii OA and OB at right angles, angle AOB = 90 degrees, and draw the tangents perpendicular to them at A and B. In quadrilateral OAPB, angle APB = 360 - 90 - 90 - 90 = 90 degrees, so the two tangents are perpendicular.

mcqs.q: Two equal circles have centres 8 cm apart (Exercise 13.3 Q5). Each direct common tangent of the pair has length:
options: 8 cm, equal to the distance OO' between the centres
mcqs.why: For equal circles, draw in each circle the diameter perpendicular to the line of centres OO' and join the corresponding ends. The joining lines are the direct common tangents, and each forms a rectangle with OO', so each tangent's length equals OO' = 8 cm.

mcqs.q: Two circles have radii 3 cm and 2.5 cm with centres 6.5 cm apart (Exercise 13.3 Q7). For their direct common tangents, the auxiliary circle at the larger centre O has radius:
mcqs.why: Formula: auxiliary radius for direct tangents = r - r'. Step 1: r - r' = 3 - 2.5 = 0.5 cm. This circle cuts the circle on diameter OO' at P and Q; producing OP and OQ and drawing parallel radii in the smaller circle gives the tangents AA' and BB'.

mcqs.q: Two circles have radii 3.5 cm and 2 cm with centres 6 cm apart (Exercise 13.3 Q8). For their transverse common tangents, the auxiliary circle at centre O has radius:
mcqs.why: Formula: auxiliary radius for transverse tangents = r + r'. Step 1: r + r' = 3.5 + 2 = 5.5 cm. This circle cuts the circle on diameter OO' at P and Q, leading to the transverse common tangents AB' and A'B.

mcqs.q: Two touching circles of radii 2.5 cm and 3.5 cm (Exercise 13.3 Q9) have in total how many common tangents?
mcqs.why: Two externally touching circles have exactly 3 common tangents: the one at their point of contact (the perpendicular to the line of centres OO' at the contact point B, where OO' = 2.5 + 3.5 = 6 cm) and two direct common tangents.

mcqs.q: Two intersecting circles of radii 3 cm and 4 cm (Exercise 13.3 Q10) have how many common tangents, and of what type?
mcqs.why: Intersecting circles have exactly 2 common tangents, both direct; the transverse tangents would have to cross the overlapping region and cannot touch both circles. The construction uses an auxiliary circle of radius 4 - 3 = 1 cm at the larger centre.

mcqs.q: To draw a circle touching both arms of a 45 degree or 60 degree angle (Exercise 13.3 Q11), the centre E of the circle must be taken:
options: On one arm of the angle
On the bisector of the angle, with radius equal to the perpendicular distance from E to an arm
At the vertex of the angle
mcqs.why: Bisect the angle by ray AD and take any point E on AD. Drop the perpendicular EF to one arm and draw the circle with centre E and radius EF. Every point on the bisector is equidistant from the arms, so the circle touches both arms.

mcqs.q: Two equal circles of radius 2.4 cm have centres 6 cm apart (Exercise 13.3 Q6). Their two transverse common tangents cross the line of centres OO' at:
mcqs.why: By symmetry for equal circles the transverse tangents cross at the midpoint M of OO'. The construction finds M, then the midpoint N of MO', draws a circle with centre N and radius MN cutting the O' circle at P and P', and the lines through M and P and through M and P' are the transverse tangents.

lessons.title: Miscellaneous Exercise 13
lessons.notes_html:
MCQ (i) The circumference of a circle is called

(a) chord
(b) segment
(c) boundary
Correct answer: boundary

MCQ (ii) A line intersecting a circle is called

(a) tangent
(b) secant
(c) chord
Correct answer: secant

MCQ (iii) The portion of a circle between two radii and an arc is called

(a) sector
(b) segment
(c) chord
Correct answer: sector

MCQ (iv) Angle inscribed in a semi-circle is

(a) pi/2
(b) pi/3
(c) pi/4
Correct answer: pi/2

MCQ (v) The length of the diameter of a circle is how many times the radius of the circle

(a) 1
(b) 2
(c) 3
Correct answer: 2

MCQ (vi) The tangent and radius at the point of contact are

(a) parallel
(b) not perpendicular
(c) perpendicular
Correct answer: perpendicular

MCQ (viii) If two circles touch each other, their centres and point of contact are

(a) coincident
(b) non-collinear
(c) collinear
Correct answer: collinear

MCQ (ix) The measure of the external angle of a regular hexagon is

(a) pi/3
(b) pi/4
(c) pi/6
Correct answer: pi/3

MCQ (x) If the incentre and circumcentre of a triangle coincide, the triangle is

(a) an isosceles
(b) a right triangle
(c) an equilateral
Correct answer: an equilateral

MCQ (xi) The measure of the external angle of a regular octagon is

(a) pi/4
(b) pi/6
(c) pi/8
Correct answer: pi/4

MCQ (xii) Tangents drawn at the end points of the diameter of a circle are

(a) parallel
(b) perpendicular
(c) intersecting
Correct answer: parallel

MCQ (xiii) The lengths of two transverse tangents to a pair of circles are

(a) unequal
(b) equal
(c) overlapping
Correct answer: equal

MCQ (xiv) How many tangents can be drawn from a point outside the circle?

(a) 1
(b) 2
(c) 3
Correct answer: 2

MCQ (xv) If the distance between the centers of two circles is equal to the sum of their radii, then the circles will

(a) intersect
(b) do not intersect
(c) touch each other externally
Correct answer: touch each other externally

MCQ (xvi) If the two circles touch externally, then the distance between their centers is equal to the

(a) difference of their radii
(b) sum of their radii
(c) product of their radii
Correct answer: sum of their radii

MCQ (xvii) How many common tangents can be drawn for two touching circles?

(a) 2
(b) 3
(c) 4
Correct answer: 3

MCQ (xviii) How many common tangents can be drawn for two disjoint circles?

(a) 2
(b) 3
(c) 4
Correct answer: 4

MCQ (vii) Circles having three points in common

Correct fact: Two circles having three points in common must COINCIDE - they are one and the same circle (Unit 9, Theorem 1: one and only one circle passes through three non-collinear points; the book's own fill-in-the-blank (v) of this exercise also gives 'coincide').

Note: None of the three printed options - (a) overlapping, (b) collinear, (c) not coincide - is correct; option (c) as printed states the opposite of the true result. The correct answer 'coincide' is missing from the printed options (book error).

Fill in the blank (i) The boundary of a circle is called ____.

Answer: circumference

Fill in the blank (ii) The circumference of a circle is called ____ of the circle.

Answer: perimeter

Fill in the blank (iii) The line joining the two points of circle is called ____.

Answer: chord

Fill in the blank (iv) The point of intersection of perpendicular bisectors of two non-parallel chords of a circle is called the ____.

Answer: centre

Fill in the blank (v) Circles having three points in common will ____.

Answer: coincide

Fill in the blank (vi) The distance of a point inside the circle from its centre is ____ than the radius.

Answer: less

Fill in the blank (vii) The distance of a point outside the circle from its centre is ____ than the radius.

Answer: greater

Fill in the blank (viii) A circle has only ____ centre.

Answer: one

Fill in the blank (ix) One and only one circle can be drawn through three ____ points.

Answer: non-collinear

Fill in the blank (x) Angle inscribed in a semi-circle is a ____ angle.

Answer: right

Fill in the blank (xi) If two circles touch each other, the point of ____ and their ____ are collinear.

Answer: contact; centres

Fill in the blank (xii) If two circles touch each other, their point of contact and centres are ____.

Answer: collinear

Fill in the blank (xiii) From a point outside the circle ____ tangents can be drawn.

Answer: two

Fill in the blank (xiv) A tangent is ____ to the radius of a circle at its point of contact.

Answer: perpendicular

Fill in the blank (xv) The straight line drawn perpendicular to the radius of a circle is called the ____ to the circle.

Answer: tangent

Fill in the blank (xvi) Two circles can not cut each other at more than ____ points.

Answer: two

Fill in the blank (xvii) The perpendicular bisector of a chord of a circle passes through the ____.

Answer: centre

Fill in the blank (xviii) The length of two direct common tangents to two circles are ____ to each other.

Answer: equal

Fill in the blank (xix) The length of two transverse common tangents to two circles are ____ to each other.

Answer: equal

Fill in the blank (xx) If the in-centre and circum-centre of a triangle coincide the triangle is ____.

Answer: equilateral

Fill in the blank (xxi) Two intersecting circles are not ____.

Answer: coincident

Fill in the blank (xxii) The centre of an inscribed circle is called ____.

Answer: in-centre

Fill in the blank (xxiii) The centre of a circumscribed circle is called ____.

Answer: circumcentre
